I'm not indebted t) my crest For people's deep attention. It may be I am Fortune's gust, Or some other's I won't mention. With honks and eyes magnificent— Ah the Fs ars tru!y lovable I have fastened on the fast vent, And made the scent quite provable. I'm NA dependent n niv clique For tactics s• ingenicus ; In fact. I think my party's weak, Whereas I'm strong in genius. • Eince Benny dfed our Tory slip Must have felt a lack of principle; B it, now I've got his n-Cghtv And, like him, shall pose invincib7e. I have p-dicias pecnliir That. wit give my views vitality; • Though the work would be more easy, were There much I,ss of liad rascality. My political agility Has no rival on the twist, sfr; And when the moment enures, ability Will assume its proper part, sir Warrington. VESTJAMIN SA.WDON.

Fine youths and maids, who never will be seen More blithe and gladsome than at se,enteen; Though you.may think not so, yet, as your mien We view and scan, we say, "bright seventeeu," Neer will von be more happy than you've been (0 golden lad and Irks) at seventeen; No sorrows deep are yo-rrs—at least. I ween You are not mu.tx depressed at seventeen. How happy Lady Grey ere she was queen:37,:.:7; So fair, so learned, so good at severteen And fresh you seem ; though some look not !o green As others are at verdant seventeen. Or tier or poor, form entbunpoint or lean, You're much to be observed at seventeen. In broadcloth clad, or silk, or bombazine, 0, how we envy you at seventeen 1 Before you know this sharp world s practise keen, You're artless at true honest seventeen Ala.)! soon passes off this pretty scene; You cannot always be fair seventeen; Clouds may, ere long, obsqure your sky serene, Aud storms may ruffle e'en calm seventeen. How will you all turn out,.-Jane, Imogene; • Alonzo, Charles? Who knows, at seventeen? A risky time for Patrick and Kathleen— In fact, fur any one at seventeen. At one of the customary school examinations an urchin was ked, " What is the Chief use of bread ?" to which be replied, with an archuess that Implied, What a simpleton you must be to ask such e question! "To spread butter upon." • Alexander Dames at one time was vely poor, and rarely bad any money. One of his friends was telling him Af a duel he had recently fought, in which the ball of his adver- eery bad been turned aside by a five-frarc piece be bad in his waistcoat pocket. " Ah, you're a lucky fellow," said the great Alexander; "if I had been in your place I should beve been killed." • A woman called at a grocer's the other day and asked for , quirt of vinegar. It was measured out, and she put it in a gallon jog. She then asked for another quart to be put In the same vessel. "And why not ask for half a gallon and have done with it ?" impatiently wired the grocer. "Ocb, bless yet little soul," aneweted Bridge:, knowingly, "isn't It for two that I want it !" A. person once made it a practice to buy six loaves every day, and a friend observ,ng this, staked *hat he did with th,n. keep c.f.:tilos!, another I give away. Iwo 103703 T. rezurn, and the two remaining over I le.-d." Tae trirEd paid. " I don't nanerazd you ; speak a littlg more plainly." He replied, "The loaf which I keep I eat, ant the one which I give away I give to a poor neighbour; the two which I re!n,n I give to my father and moth r, and I lend two byres to my sons." It is related *bet Seeretary Everts of the United States was once one of a petty who were vieitieg tbe natural bridge In Virginia. As It usual, after tarrying at the top, they de- scended and viewed the wonder from below. While there the story was told that Gecrge Washington had orice stood there and thrown a silver dcelar corn nletPiv over the bridge. Some of the party pooh-proned this assertion; but Mr. Everts gravely rebuked tlarn, Paying, "You forget how much farther a dollar went in those days." A good story comes from the South-East. A cettler, who suppos-al he had meeicel tastes, went to the nearest town- ship and purchased a music-stool, taking it home with him in his trete Jo the course of a few days, however, he brought it bark, and demanded restitution of the money paid, as it was no good—no good at all. The seller exa- mined it, and paid that it was in perfect order, and the screw all right: and therefore tbat it should not be thrown back on his hands. " WEI the settler, "I took it home careful, as you ccted see for yourself, and I gave it a tarn, and the missis she gave it a turn, and every, one of the children gave it a turn, and -never a tune could one and all , of us screw Out of it. It's no more a musicoitool then the four-legged washing-stool the miesis sets her tubs on." Coats° 13ve.pecns.—A sad domestic aftllction has re- - • eently overtiken a New Zealand household owing to the overweening confidence of its master to "doctor himself." Tnis gentleman, we are told, was suffering from a violent headeche, and, throwing " physic to the doge," sought his I own remedy. It proved eventually worse than the disease, though the sufferer, like other discoverers, pretends to be delighted with his experiment. A gum tree flourished at the bottom of his paddock, and, arguing that if it would dispel a miasma it might possibly cure a headache, he made a poultice of gum leaves and applied it to his head. After soaking his head in the mash for some time he WAS as well as ever, but at the expense of a strange metamorohosis. His hair had changed in celone, -and was now a blueish green. Soip is useless; the Colonial True6tte are eon- plas!ed, not being accuttomed to deal in fast colours, and according to the latest accounts, his wife and relations were in despair. HATS OFF.—When lewd John Russell appeared at the bar on the 21st of June, 1867, to deliver a message from the , - Crown, in spite of the cries of " Hathepff !" and the I Speaker's intimation that Members must urcover, Sir James Graham did not bare his head until Lord John had got well on with his reading. Next day he exclaimed that he meast no disrespect either to the Crown or the House, but had acted in strict accordance with old usage, which decreed that Members should remain covered until they heard the word Rex or Regina proncunced, and for that he had waited. The Speaeer admitted that the Member for East Cumber- land was in the right as to the practice of the House, and excused his own apparent deviation from the rules on the score of desiring to save time and preserve order. Crom- well flung his hat on his head when he pronounced sentence Of extinction ra the Long Parliament. Maier Harrison took off his hat very ceremoniously as he approached the. Spiker, bowed low, and, kissing his hand, took possession if It, and handed hill out of the House "as a gentleman does a lady, the whole House following." Chancellor Seafield made no such pretence of politeness in dismissing the last national Parliament held in Scotland. He pat on his hat, saying, "There is an end of an acid song!' Au Eliza- bethan vereifier sang— Before the Prince none covered are, But those that to themselves go bare. —4V the Year Round. To SeWOOL AGAlS.—Great work is given to the world but we are ignorant Of the many days which went perhaps slowly by before that work was born. Genius, boys! There Is no such genius as labour; it is the greatest wonder-worker the world has ever seen. Work! whatever you do, do it with your might. Of all the miserable creature!, there is none nacre miserable than the hulking biped who calls him- self boy; yet who loafs about with his hands in his pockets, and w-11l neither work when he works, nor play when he plays. Avoid him, boys! Already in his youth he is like the tree which curebereth the ground; he Is as incapable and as uedeeireble an acqneintance as the lunatics in our asylums. We do not wish you to be i prig, full of airs and graces, thinking yousssll better than all the other fellows in the world; but we would sooner you were that Man a nincornnoon, who loafs his life away. Note two simple trathe That every bay who would be a zeae, and be worthy of hie manhood, should have an aim in life. 11. That the higher your aim, so much the greater will be your achieeement. It is easy enough to aini too low, impossible to aim too high.• And whatever your aim, so long as it is • worthy, stick to It; under no conditions let it go. Do not be cast do-en by failure; the oftener you fail she better it - will be her you; there is no school like the school of disap- pointment. The greatest men have risen from the lowed peace! ; the most succenful men have failed the oftenest. One weapon is necessary, and with that one weapon you will In the long, run win every battle. It is earnestness—ea- thug:tam if Jou prefer to call it so. Be in earnest; be so much in earnest that you will be satisfied with nothing short Of vi ;tory, entire and complete; so much in earnest that you will not know when you are beaten; so much in earnest ' ' - that from every defeat you will learn how to avoid another. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, eLe. A poisonous weed is doing a good deal of damage among sheep in some parts of California. One man is reported to have lost 500 head from this cause. The French Ministry of Agriculture require a special grant of £53,780, over half of which would be devoted to the conflict with the phyllcxera, while £18,820 are re- quired for the enlargement and re-establishment of the agricultural school at Montpelier, and £2,300 for the de- etruction of wolves. The following subjects have been proposal for discussion at the next congress of German Agriculture:-1. Vega- bondage and the means of prevention afforded by employing vagabonds in land labour. 2. The improved cultivation of heath and moor land. 3. The tariff on roads and railways, also the most practical means of transporting g.oods by rail. 4. The rent of land considered from a social and political point of view. 5. The harm done in towns by Free Trade, and kow the same may be met. DADaY INDUSTRY IN FEANCIL—To give an idea of the dairy industry in France, Mr. Herve Mangon recently stated at an agricultural gathering that the milk produced in the country would. if colleoad, form a stream about one metre in width and 33 centimetres in depth (say, 3(1. 4ia. by Ift. lin.), flowing night and day all the year, with a mean velo- city of one metre per second. Young animals drink a part of this enormous volume of llk, men takes a good part of it, and the rest is transformed into cheese and butter. No branch of agricultural industry has eo provessed during the i last 50 years as the making of butter. In 1833 France bought abroad 1,200,000 kiloarammes of butter, and sold to foreigners only 1,100,000 kilogrammes. She now exports 34 to 35 milli= kilogrammee of butter annually, and re- ceives in return hoe-. abroad (especially from England) a sum of more than 100 million francs. La Manche alone furnishes more than one-third of the total exportation. .Nature. ture. Tag US7B OF SHIM-MILK AND IVDEY.—.Professor Alex. Mueller, of Berlin, has recently called attention to this sub- ject in the German Milch-Zeituv, and has described some improved methods of preservation, devised for the purpose of increeeing the use of skim-milk and whey in that city. He urges that the chief reasons why so little use has hitherto been made of these products in populous places are the ignorance which prevails in respect to their high physiolo- gical value as food; the lack of practical knowledge as to the maulfold, useful, and appetising purposes which they ' could bz• macio to serve in cooking and baking; and perticu- larly the difficulty of marketing such cheap and perishatle materials ; that is, of transporting them cheaply, and at ereeerving them effectively for periods long enough to re- lieve both buyer and seller from anxiety as to the risk of spoiling. With regard to the troable last namrel, he con- siders it as good as proved that partial concentration of sk,irnm.;ilk or of whey, by evaporating in vacaum-pate, will be sufficient for all ordinary requirements. By evaporating skim-milk to one-fourth or one-fifth its bulk a product is obtained which can be kept without special care for a week or fortnight, according to the season and the temperature. Whey concentrated to one-seventh or one-eighth its bulk, or still further, or even to dryness, if it is to be carried far, is by no means a perishable article. It has, in fact, long been prepared, in a somewhat crude way, in Nor- way and in Switzer' trid. As regards the city cf Berlin at j the present time, the concentration of whey seems to be more important than the preservation of. skim-milk, since l the common practice there is to sell, in its ralural state, as much aid:it-milk as there is demand for, and to make cheese from the remainder. The whey thus obtained was formerly thrown away, because of the difficulty of keeping a large number of hogs in the city. The ceecentrated whey has been found, prectically, to serve an extremely useful pur- pose in bread-making. Professor Mueller remarks that the quality of the bread is surprisingly improve, and that for this p‘rticular purpose, whey is decidedly better than fresh milk.

DOGS—TREATMENT OF PUPPIES.—Y oung preppies can scarcely be fed too often, if they are fed regularly. When very young they should have feed five or six times a day, but when a couple of months old, four times will suffice until they are four or five months cld, and then three times a day until they reach the age of one year, after which twice a day will be sufficient. To follow the system adopted by some breeders who give puppies as much as they will eat at one meal, and imagine that the lethargic semi-sleepy state that follows, is conducive to health and growth is a very great mistake. The best plan is to feed little and often, therethe puppies will knock about and play, both before and after their meals,and when tired and their food is partially digested, they go to sleep and sleep soundly, waking up ready for another feed; whereae, if gorged they lie about, and if they sleep do not get rid of the load, for digestiost gm on much more slowly when an animal is asleep than when It is awake. If puppies stomachs are accustomed to be over-loaded when they are young, their digestive powers become impaired, and they have thus weak loins and big bellies ween full-grown, and what is a more immediate danger are subject to worms. pley feet and bowed legs may be traced to the same cause. In order to get puppies to grow a good size they mutt be induced to eat as much as possible, that is if the right kind of food is provided, but the food most be given little and often. By feeding in this way the puppies will cat more food, and at the same time have a better appetite for their meals, than if the acme quantity •of food were given In one or two meale, in wbioh eft*e they would he overloaded at the first meet arei have no Ceeire for the second one. For hod as much variation should be given as is possible, and hence Spratt'a biscuits mixed with broth, boiled meat of various kinds, dry bread, oatmeal, and green food are all useful. Perhaps the biscuits should be made the staple 4iet, and the others used as variatioes. Kennels should not at this time of the year be swilled out with water, but the floer had better be covered with dry sawdust or ear h, on which a little quicklime may be scattered, and the whole swept out and the floor resprinkled every day. PIGEONS.—THE CARRIER--Of all the various breeds of pigeons, the carrier undoubtedly stands in the first position, having only the pouter as a rival, and hence we generally see one or other of thees varietiee in the first place. The carrier undoubtedly at one time was known for its carrying or bearing properties, and derived its name from the acme ; but many yeere, if not centuriee, of bretdicei have taken areey diets properties, and made it what it now is—puiely a•fancy breed. Certein paints have been unduly developed,' with toe Tcmtlit that the carrier has been weakened in con- etitution, and is certainly not now one of the most beautiful breeds we possess. Very high prices are given for good specimens, and £lOO has been occasionally paid for a first- class bird. some two or three years ago one breweler told six birds for .£5O each, and another one refused £l3O far a pair, a cock and a hem There is no other breed so difficult to excel in, and that cost so much money to commence— that jai? it ía intended to make a position. The great points of the carrier are (1) the beak with its wattle, which is an exeresence of a wart-like nature, growing thereon. This covers the greater portion of the beak, extending from the heed to within a short distance of the end. It is both on the upper and lower mandible, and is judged according to its size, shape, and proportions. The length of beak is me isered from the centre of the eye, and Isi to 2 inches are deemed good lengths. The great difficulty is to breed and, if bred, to preserve this wattle in its proper shape, ars it is very liable to get misshapen. (2) The eye with its wattle, which is of a similar nature to the beak wattle, and sur- rounds the eye. This is small, or should be, and is preferred when perfectly circular. It is very liable to get coarse and to apout—i e., that is the weight of the wattle to draw it downwards, and to form a spout on the under side, which when it occurs, is very difficulty of cure, and causes an in- flarnmation of the eyes. (3) The fine tapering neck, which In a really good one gives the bird a very stylish appear- ance. In those birds that are heavy in wattle there is a great dange: of the strain upon the neck causing it to get' coarse and thick. (4) The tail and wings should he long, and the legs firmly set. Of the colours, black is the Com- monest, hut in addition there are dune, blues, and whites, the last two of which have not, however, been brought to the same state of perfection as the former. The great eecret of getting strong carriers is not to in-breed, and not to give the young ones liberty until they are four or five months old. CANARlES.—Esmatus.—This is a disease usually met with in ceee birds and is simple inflammation of the intes- tines. The first symptoms are swelling and tenderness of the abdomen, and on blowing aside the feathers the veins will appear enlarged and dark in colour. At first there is constipation, which, if not speedily relieved, is followed by diarrecsa, and this causes rapid loss of flesh and of warmth, and death at the end of two or three days. The best remedy, 'lf used eirly, is a drop of castor oil warmed. If the bird draws up its limbs as if cramped and in pain, add to the oil a drop of laudanum; and as the commencement of inflant• nsation is generally marked by shivering, keep the bird as warm as poseible. A warm bath is a tempting but very dangerous remedy unless the bird is very strong, for a weakly bird hail not strength to dry itself, and the handling which the process entails is very exhausting. If the oil relieves the bird, feed it sparingly for some days on canary seed, crushed if the bird is very feeble, and mixed with moistened bread or biscuit; and as this food is very plain, keep up the temperature of the room until the ordinary mixed food can be resumed with safety. When diarrheas has set in, the evacuations are watery and greenish coloured, but in the worst cases it may be blood stained. The bird rapidly loses strength, refuses all food, and soon dies. In such at case the best treatment would be to use soft food only, say a little sponge-cake dipped in sherry wine, and medicated with laudanum, but it is very seldom that birds recover that are so far gone as that. The causes of enteritis are very simple. In the Gm of single birds the disease is generally due to cold, as from a bath, or from overfeeding, or the use of unsound food. Young birds will gorge themselves with egg food, and old and young alike suffer when they are allowed to eat soar food, or wet and unripe green food. Bat this disease, or one closely allied to It, occasionally appears as an epidemic, which devastates the birdeoocc, sparing neither young nor old. Of its nature, we, as yet, know next to nothing, but it may fairly be set down to improper food, overcrowding, and unhealthy Bur- ronedinge, and as it has not been knoten to be contagions, immediate measeares taken to remove any suspected exciting c Aliso, will probably result in saving the rest of the stock. RABBITS —KR/MING FOR PROFIT.—Thoee who have ground and time to attend to them, will find that common rabbits can be kept very profitably indeed. The outlay need not be very large, and as they are most prolific as breeders, the reavery large one. The extent of the opt,nrrin it jon% generallyw iu, of course, depend upon the amount of gi mend at disposal, but however much there is, unless it be i unlimited in extent, t should be wired in, and the netting sunk into the ground about eighteen inches, to prevent the rabbits burrowing their way out. Hess rabbits can be turned down, and will soon begin to make holes for themselves.

div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

The Academy hears that the "Novae Madonna" of Raphael, formerly in the Idnuro collection, has crossed the Atlantic and found a temporary home in the Metropolitan Museum of Art at New York. There is little chance that it will ever come back to us. ' Mr. George M. Tweddell, of Stokesley, author of a Popu- lar History of Cleveland, and many other kcal works, pro- poses to issue by subscription, "A Hundred Masonic Son- ; nets." We regret to hear that the veteran anther is threatened with the loss of his eyesight. —Academy. Meesrs. Uampson Low will be the publishers of Mr. Archi- bald R. Colquhouu's narrative of his journey of exploration through the South China border-lands from Canton to Man- dalay. The title chosen by the author is "Across Chryee," and th'e book will appear as early as possible next year. Mr. Ellis Lever, of Manchester, has offered a premium of £5OO to the inventor of the best portable electric lamp for use in coal mines. Mr:Bart, M.P., and Mr. Crawford, the secretary of the Miners' National Union,, are to rend es' as- sistance to Mr. Lever in promoting the object which he has in view. M. de Nenville, the celebrated painter of battle-scenes,has received a commission from the French Govermnent to paint the taking of Tel-el-Kebir. He was present at the review held by the Queen, and he has already made a number of sketches for his work, including one of Sir Garnet Wolseley at the head of his troops.— Academy. Td. Barthelemy Brillion, a distinguished metallurgist of Rive de Gier, of the district of the Loire, says the Journal des Mines, has made some new experiments on iron ore with very remarkable results. Thirty-two pounds weight of Af- rican iron ore was placed in fragments is a crucible. When the ore was heated to a red heat a reacting substance was added, and in three minutes the liquefaction of the ore was complete, the prcduce obtained being pure iron. By means of this process a blast furnace will, it is said, turn out twenty-two tons of iron every fourteen minutes, instead of as at present twenty-two tons every twelve hours. At a meeting of the Somerset Arches )logic .l Society which was held at Taunton recently, it was announded thet Mr. Methyr Guest had presented the members with a piece at furniture known as "the Fielding table." It was made for Fielding during his residence at East Stour Manor House, and was left there by him. The table haa remained in the house till quite recently, although the estate (which now belongs the Machioness of Westminster) has changed hands more than once and the old manor house is now occupied by a farmer. It is a large, massive oak table, and a brass plate affixed to it bears the following inscription —" This table belonged to Henry Fielding, Esq.,novelist. He hunted from East Stone, 1718, and in three years diesipated his for- tune keeping hounds." METALLURGICAL DISCOVERY.—PERSEVER NCE REWARDED.

The most important Metallurgical discovery since the in- vention of Bessemer steel and the basic process of steel- making has been made by a Birmingham metal manufac- turer, after thirty years of constent experiments, in' vrhich he expended over £30,000. The invention has just been patented in Great Britain, France, Germany, Rnssia, Austria, Belgium, Sweden, Italy, Spain, the United States, Canada, and India. It consists of a new process of making alumina, from which aluminum can be manufactured at about one- tenth- the cost by ordinary methods; and an aluminum is recognised as the most valuable metal for forming workable alloys, the importance of the discovery cannot be over- animated. This, indeed, is shown by the fact that eons- penies in France have jest offered upwards of a quarter of a million sterling for the patent-right for that country alose, while the aggregate offers of American, German, Belgian, and other companies amount to more than a million of pounds. The inventor is Mr. James Webster, of Hollywood, who has organised a company under the style of the Alu- minum Crown Metal Works Compaay, Limited, sever' pro- prietors to work the patent. Under the ordinary process alumina costs £l,OOO a ton, whereas by Mr. Webster pro- cess it is less thin £lOO, besides which all the by products are utilised, and from these a blue dye is made, which, it is believed, will supersede indigo for calico printing, inasmuch as it permanently retains its colour, and is not affected by acids. Mr. Webster's alumina deposit is certified by an eminent analyst to contain 84 per cent, of pure alumina as compared with 65 per cent. realised by the ordinary process, and the oxide can now be made in any quantity in the course of a few days, while hitherto it could only be pro- duced in limited quantities, and the process required neajiy

Owing, however, to the expense of production, and the limited qeantities of the metal produced, alumisum has hitherto only been used for small ornaments el jewelry, masical and mathematical instruments, the caatiegs of machinery, &c., but it can now be used in combination with other metals for multitudinous purposes. Many tons of bismuth-bronze, manufactured from the aluminum, have been sent to Mall for conversion into propellers for the Eastern Steamship Company, the advantage claimed tor the bronze being that it has nearly one hundred more resisting power than any other material used for the parpese, while in the event of a collision it will bend rather than break, and, further, it will not corrode from the action of the salt weter. it is also used for ship fittings, and is rolled into sheets for all kinds of purposes for which electroplating is now applied, spoons, knives and forks, dish covers, railway carriage and tool handles, and other articles being made from it by 'a leading Sheffield firm. Aluminum bronze is also made which is adapted for the manufacture of artillery, and several consinmeats have been made to the Royal Gun Factory at Woolwich by order of the War Office. T.re nectar has a strairaing power of 42 tons to the inch, as against 28 of gun metal. The bronze is also converted into wire for electrie telegraph purposes, and is being Introduced' for post-office purposes in London; while samples are now being tested in Glasgow for similar purposes. Among the numerous other purposes to which the metal is beipg ap- plied are for bell making, pianoforte wire making, and the manufacture of jewel tinge and other jewelry, which are ix demand for the United States. The new *metal can also be united by a soldering or welding procees with any other metal, a result which has never before been effected.

"Suffering sisters," exclaimed the speaker, energetically shaking the hair•pins from her head in her excitement, ",women will never obtain their rights until they display more courage. Let me say to you, in the words of a famous French orator, 'Courage, courage, courage !' " At this stage of the proceedings somebody threw a box of black beetles upon the platform, and the meeting broke up in great terror and confusion.

ON PRACTISING MUSlC.—Beginners are not fond of prac- tising ; bat to a musician it is absolute delight. No one knows really what practising means until he has come to enjoy I;; it is a pleasure far greater than playing over in society what has been already learnt; it ifs an occupation as exciting, though in a different way, as the excitement of reading new music. When we play we are liable to become depressed by the poverty of our performance; when we practise hope spore us on; it does not matter what faults we commit if we are only practicing, and it is encouraging to reel that, as time goes on, our difficulties are conquered and overcome. They meet us half-way, and melt and vanish from us, even as when we travel by rail the landscapes through which we pass seem to advance toward us and re- cede behind us, and we are scarcely aware that it Is our- selves who. press steadily forwards, whilst they stand Still. ABYSSINIAN LAW.—The courts of justice in Abyssinia are somewhat primitive places. Tbe advocates plead tied to. gether by their robes. While one is speaking no interrup- tion is permitted, but as some concession must be made to long-suffering human nature pent up under the agony of hearing vituperations and allegations known to be false, the other advocate is allowed to grunt when he considers some passage in his opponent's speech particularly objectionable. A case is often settled by bets. For instance, a man will wager so many cows that he is in the right, and the other will do the same. The result is that the loser must pay his bet to the chief as a fine. In this manner a dispute about.a matter of five shillings will coat a wordy individual who lies trusted to the "glorious uncertainty" of Abyssinian law ten or twelve pounds. We had something not very wilsly different once amongst ourselves, when cases could be de- cided by a wager of battle to an opponent in a court of, law. An Lbyksinian is a quarrelsome and excessively vain per- ionage, and his 11tig2u5 disposition is greatly owing lo the possession of these Bubiottaly commendable qualitlea.—The Peoples of the World.. - - - - -

Tua GRFAT Srohat or 1703.—The great storm in No- vember, 1703, described by Defoe, b still commemorated by an annual sermon, preached in pursuance of a bequest. De- foe, who was one of the founders of this memorial discourse, states that the wind, which for some fourteen days pre- viously had been blowing strongly, appeared to have reached Its climax at from five till eight o'clock on November 27th, and had it not ceased at that time it is supposed that no building in London could have withstood it. Whole streets of houses were unroofed, and so great Was the demand for tiles that the price, which had been one guinea per thou- zand, suddenly rose to £6, and even than the supply was not equal to the demand. In fact, deal boards had to be aubstituted, and for twelve months afterwards continued to be used. It was found that upwards of two thousand stacks of chimneys had been blown down, and Defoe, who, out of curiosity, rode round London for the purpose, counted seventeen thousand fallen trees, and then got tired. Dam- age to the extent of two millions sterling was done in the City of London alone, and the first Eddystone lighthouse was swept away. The storm appeared to be most destruc- tive in the south of England, as hundreds of vessels, includ- ing a frigate with Admiral Beaumont, were lost. —Sunday at Home.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 16, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 16, 1882.
THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Richard Bolger, town councillor, has been appointed High Sheriff of Dublin for the coming year. A man named Richard Walsh, who had recently arrived from America, and purchased the interest of a widow in her holding at Moghastin, near Westport, was fired at on Mon- day, but escaped injury. The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland as been pleased to com- mute the capital sentence passed on the five men wile ',leaded guilty to participating in the Maamtrasna massacre to penal servitude for life. The first arrests under the Curfew Clause was made in Deblin on Monday night, a printer zamed James Bunn° hay- iny been arrested by a detective, charged with being away from his place of abode, intending to commit a crime.

Mr. Parnell, it is stated, has filkl a petition in the Irish Land Court, for the sale of his estate in County Wicklow. There are noarly 5,000 acres to be disposed of, subject to 150111 Q leases, and the Tyllole amount of alio charges affecting the entail is 13,0400. - At a full sitting of the Land Commission Court, on Mon- day, Mr. Justice O'Hagan delivered the unanimous judg- ment of tile Court upholding on appeal the decision previously given by Mr. Commissioner Litton on the " hanging gale" proviso of the Arrears Act. . _

At bilge, on Tuesday, a farmer, named Kilmartin, from. Arran Island, Galway, was indicted for shooting at and woundidg a bailiff named Hernoux. The latter swore he saw the prisoner fire at him and the bullet lodged in his chest. Prisoner was convicted, and he was Sentenced to transportation for life. Briefs have been issued for the next sitting of the Land Commissioners in an application for a conditional order of attachment against the proprietor of the Freeman's Journal for alleged contempt in publishing articles on the 11th ult. and subsequent dates concerning Lord Talbot de Malahide and his Balbriggan tenantry, whose rents were reduced by the Sub-Commissioners, and against whose decision no appeal has been brought. A Dublin correspondent says that late on Tuesday night notices were served upon Messrs. Devitt, Healy, and Quinn to the effect that a meeting of judges had been held, and it was found that a divisional court could not be constituted for the.purpose of hearing the application in the Qaeen's Bench Division on Thursday. It is, tlerefore, notifiecil that the application will be renewed on the first opportunity, of which reasonable notice will be given, informing the Crown solicitor for Dublin county or any place in Dublin, at which such notice may be left for them. THE DISTRESS IN THE IrVEST.—A special correspondent of the Daily News, travelling in the west of Ireland, de- scribes a state of considerable privation, but says :—" It is encouraging that the nearer you come to he scene of dis- tress, or reported distress, the more the reports become modified. It would be an exaggeration to compare it to the mirage of the desert, but it would be no exaggeration to say that'the representations made in some, of the newspapers are considerably overdrawn." A short time ago, Mr. Justice Chitty made an order against the Laud Corporation of Ireland, Limited, restrain- in z the company from applying capital issued on " B " shares in paying a secured dividend of 5 per cent. no " A " shares. This order was appealed against by the company, and the Lords Justices have dismissed the appeal with costs, on the ground that the application of one portion of the company's capital as a guarantee fund for the payment ,of dividends on another portion of the capital waultra vireo.

In the Longhrea district on Sunday there was an unsuc- cessful attempt made to hold a meeting of the National pLeague. The Lord Lieutenant had prohibited the meeting, and the resident magistrates appeared on the spot and warned the peasantry of the risk they were running. It is said that after being dispersed the meeting assembled in a. field and formed a branch of the League. The prohibited meeting was to have been addressed by several Boman Catholic priests, and it bad the sanction of Bishop Duggan. At C,:,rk winter assizes, on Monday, David Fleming was indicted for the attempted murder of John Cullotty, at Cat her, county Kerry, in ApciL Cullotty was a rent warner, and he was about to serve writs of ejeittnent upon some tenants, when he was visited at his house by two men armed and disguised. One of them knocked Cullotty down, and •the other fired his revolver twice, seriously wounding Cul- lotty, and necessitating amputation of his right leg. Daring the struggle the disguise of one of these men fell off, and he was recognised as Fleming. The jury cmvicted the prisoner, and sentence was deferred.

GUARDING AN lettsa Jureen.—ExtraordinarY precautions are being adopted for securing the safety of -Judge Barry in Cork. Travelling from Dublin he was accompanied by detectives, and at. each station where the train stopped a force of police was present. On arrival he was escorted to his lodgings by a troop of Scots Greys with drawn swords, and at. his lodging a temporary police barrack has been con- structed. Similar precautions were adopted in court. Al/ the passages were manned by polite, who excluded all of suspicious appearance, and, for that matter, all who did not present a respectable exterior. The passage fretn the bench to the judge's chamber was guarded by detectives. PRESENTATION TO SEROBANT DANTERS.—An interesting scene took piece on Saturday afternoon, at Trinity College, Dublin, when, at four o'clock, a numerously-attended meet- ing of the fellows and students of Trinity College was held, undee the presidency of the Provost, in one of the examination haUs, for the purpose of presenting a silver salver and spirit 'and to Sergeant Danvers, of the King's Own Rifles, for his gallant conduct up n thteoccasion of the murder of Detec- tire-officer Cox. The proceedings were most enthusiastic throughout. The Provost was warmly cheered ekaiing his speech. Sergeant Danvers returned thanks. He said speech-making was no part of his drill and educat ,on, and they would not expect a speech from him. At to one part of the presentation, a spirit stand, be could Assure tleetn that, it would never be used without drinking the. health, of tee students of Trieity College. (Leughter and cheers.)—At the conclusion, of the Provost's speech, "God EA'Ve the Queen" was sung by the ladies and other members of the Choral Societyrunder the direction of Sir Robert Stewart. At the close of the proceedings Sergeaat Denver was chaired, with a college cap on his head, by the studente around the preeinete. A watch will next week be pre- sented by the Irish Bar to Sergeant Danvers, for whom, in addition, between ..-areTe and £4OO Las already heen sub- ecribed. Tem NTIRDFIR OW Tan HUDDTS.—The trial of the first of the three prisoners (Patrick Higgins) indicted for the murder of the Huddys-in the neighbourhood of Lough Mask has proved a failure. Mr.. Justice O'Brien, in summing upe the 'evidence, begged the jury, to do their duty "boldly,- manfully, and fearlessly." An hour after they had retired the foreman reported that there was not the least possibility of the jury agreeing, eating, "The dissenting portion of them sav that they do not, wish to go into the matter further because there is no use in arguing." A juror protested
ttu Sergenni Dkur.

against the term "they." His Lordship discharged the 'jury. It is said that edema of the jury were in favour of conviction, and only one for acquittal.—The trial of Higgins was recommenced in the Dublin Special Corinnission Court on Monday' before Mr. Jhatice O'Brien and a fresh jury. At .the outset Mr. Teeling, the prisoner's counsel, sought to obtain' a postponement of. the trial on the ground that aertain comments indulged in by several L-mden and Dab. ho journals would influence the jury anti prejudice his client's C 490. His Lordship:overruled the application, and the trial proceeded. It concluded on Wednesday, Mr. Justice o;Brien, in an able eharge extending over three hours, con- cludycl by exhorting the j.i:ry not to be influenced by any- thing they had beard outside this trial, and by fearlessly doing their duty. The jury returned into court after an hour's absence With a verdiat of guilty. The prisoner, ad- dressing the Court through an interpreter, declared, in the name of God and the Yirghs, that he never raised his hand against the lluddys. Jude g'Brien sentenced the prisoner to be hanged in Galway Gaol on the 11:h of January. His Lordship said he was of coinion that the murder did not' originate with th 3 prisoner,, and that he was probably the least.guilty of the parties concerned. The foreman of the jary said this was their opinion also. The Judge said he 'would take care to lay the itry's opinion before the proper authorities.

The negotiations between M. de (Hers and the Vatican have, according to the Roman correspondent of the IVeue Freie Presse, of Vienna, alraady led to some result. The Vatican has agreed to contribute by such means as lie in its power to eradicate disaffection in Russian Poland. Russia, on the other hand, it is said, has made important conces- sions to the Pope, and it is probable that the Consistory will preconise the Polish Bishops. gift of twenty valuable horses and twenty-four mules, laden with presents, is quite Oriental in character, and may be taken as indicating more than ordinary regard. Such is the tribute of friendship aud high esteem which the Atneer of Cabal has, by special messenger, sent to the Viceroy of India, who no doubt will, with equal ceremony, send return• gifts expressive of the goodwill and high regard of his excellency for the Araeer. It is better to be engaged in the exchange of horsv, mules, and valuable gifts than of re- criminatory language and cannon balls.

_ A correspondent at Brussels states that Canon Bernard, now a prisoner at T9urnay, on the charge of absconding with the treaSure Of the diootae of Tournay to America, has given powers to M. Bourgeois, COMmivary of Police, to ob- tain at Boston 700,000 f., and New York 2,000,0001., deposited out of the stolen treasury. This will carry the amount re- covered to 5,000,000 f. The coming trial of Bernard is interesting, the correspondent adds, because the diocese not being a legal corporation, there is, consequefttly, a difficulty in deciding to whom the money belongs. DEATH. OF A GREAT FRINCII ADVOCITIL—A Paris cor- respondent telegraphed on Sunday ;—The French Bar has sustained a great loss in the death, on Saturday, of M. Lac- haud,.at the age of 64. His reputation was made by his defence of Madame Lafarge, and had kept up ever since. From the Boc irme to the Bazaine trial there was scarcely a great criminal case in which M. Lachaud's services were not sought. While listaning to his eloquence it was useless to reflect that it was an advocate speaking; it was impossible to rest unmoved, and even the judges seldom escaped the infection. He was certainly one of the most brilliant figures in French society. He leaves a-son uho has won esteem as an advocate and publicist. A MURDER IN GALrbrA.—A Vienna correspondent says that at Lemberg on -Monday an entire Jewish family were arraigned on a charge of murder, the circumstances of which are very extraordinary. The principal prisoner is Hoses Ritter, described as a land proprietor, and he, his wife Gittei, and two daughters, Chaie and Belle, are accused of having decoyed away a Christian peasant girl, Franciska Mulch, put her to death, and horribly mutilated her re- mains. The motive of the crime is alleged to have arisen out of some religious superstition. it is proved that the girl's mutilated body was found near Ritter's house, in the Galician village of Luteza. The excitement caused by the case is the greater as it comes before the court at a time ' when the public miad is stillogitated about a mystery of a very similar chiractsr connected with another part ot the Empire. I refer to the murder by a Jewish butcher at Tiszla Edar, in Hungary, of a Christian peasant girl, of whom no trace has for several menthe past been found. The body of the uufortumate girl in the Galician case Vrlll found with certain marks, particularly with the head shaven, which have caused the murder to be attributed to Jewish perpetrators actuated by religious motives. In sup- port of this view even the Talmud is quoted by the prose- cution. There tire no fewer than forty-five witnesses to be examined in this trial, including Dr. tiudemaan, the chief rabbi of Vienna. The real explanation of the crime, it is conjatured, from what has already transpired, is that Ritter took the girl's life in order to hide his own immorality, the object of the subsequent mutilation being to prevent identi- fication.

TRAORDY PARIS.—The nen de Richelieu as On Tueiday morning the scene of a terrible crime. At about seven o'alock a womaa, with blood profusely streaming from her breast, was seen leaning from the window of the fourth floor of No. 89, and crying 'Help!" "Murder!" A medical man, who lives in the same house, and another neighbour immediately hestsned upstairs, and. before the door of the apartment whence the cries proceeded were met by the servant belonging to it. The three then, entering the dwelling, went to the room at the window of which the woman bad been seen, and there found her extended, with notbinc on but her chemise, in a pool of blood, across her bad, at the foot ef which a wet dagger was lying. A moment's examiaation showed that she had ceased to breathe. On going into an adjoining room they found a man bleeding from a bullet wound in the head, lying dead en the floor, his right hand still clutching a newly dis- charged revolver. On the chimney-p:ece was the velvet sheltb of the dagger with which the woman had been killed, and a letter written in a firm hand, addressed to a police commissioner, and another letter begging a Jewish benevolent society to see to the burial of the two bodies. The man proved to be one Repaport, a diamond merchant, and the woman his daughter, a girl if 18 years of age. From the indications there is no reasonoble doubt that she was murdered by her father, and that immediately afterwards he eammitted suicide. Repaport and his daughter, who is etated to he of great personal attractions, had for some time lived there, and were well known and respected by their neighbours. The motive for the deed has not transpired, but rninour says that it is to be attributed to the father's shame at the ruin of his daughter. EGYPT.

Ismail Pasha Eyoub's appointment to the Ministry of the Interior has, the correspondent of the Standard telegraphs, created a. very favourable impreLsion amongst all classes of Egyptians in Cairo, and it is considered as an earnest of the intention of the British Government to protect Egypt against the oppression of the dominant race. Riaz Pasha's influence, how,..,ver, (says the corresponednt) is still visible in the violent articles published by such of the native papers RS are immediately inspired by him. "In these journals the English pelicy in Egypt is most vehemently attacked, and Arabi is, curiously enough, abused as having sold the sountry.to the British."

The arrangements rendered necessary by Cetewavo's return to Zululand are on the eve of completion, aid he will shortly set out for that country. From Rome we learn that the Duke of Sermoneta, who was President of the Provisional Government after the entry of the Italian troops..into the present. capital of Italy, in 1870, is dead. Colonel Stewart reports front the Soudan that the False Prophet's forces have beea repulsed, and that Kartoum is in no danger. The Gazeite of India contains the returns for 1881 of wild animals and poisonous snakes killed in British India during the year. The total number of wild animals killed was 15,79; 5nake5,254,908. The total number of persons killed was 21,427, against 21,990 in 1880. Serious riots are reported from Toulouse, in the south of France, beginning in the University and gradually extend- ing to the streets_ The precise origin and motive of the demonstrations have not been clearly demonstrated. The Italian Premier has brought in a bill for the settle- ment of the "Be' adlaugh difficulty." It enacts that any deputy who refuses to take the oath, or shall not have taken it within two months after his election, shall be expelled from the House. FALL OF A, BRIDGE: SEVEN PERSONS KILLED AND SIANY INJURED.—An accident has occurred on the Mexican Pacific Railway extension through the falling of a newly-oonstructed Iron bridge. At the time of the occurrence over 100 work- men were engaged on the bridge, seven of whom were killed. There were a large number injured. SERIOXS, FIRE IN MADRID: TWENTY PERSONS INIIIRRD. —A tire broke out at the Ministry of War on Tuesday morn- ing, and a portion of the building was burnt to the ground. Twenty persons were injured—one of them seriously. The library and part of the archives were destroyed. The King was present, and assisted to subdue the flames.

DISASTROUS FIRE w JAMAICA: £6,000,000 DAMAGES.— At New York, on Tuesday, a despatch received here from Kingston, Jamaica, announces that the business quarter of that town was destroyed by tire on Monday. The loss is estimated at £0,000.000. Hundreds of persons have been rendered homeless, and as several banks, wharves, and ware- houses and stores containing supplies have been burned, food is much needed. DEATH OF A, Famous JOCEET.—The death is announced of a famous American jockey, Gilbert Watson Partriels, who for 50 years was well known in racing circles. He is reputed to have made over 5,000 mounts, and to hays come off vic- torious in four-fifths of thern—a record which is said to be

div.p: TRADE NOTES.

Tees INIII3EBS' WACIIIS QUISTION.—Mr. Pickard, secre- tary of the Evuth Yorkshire Miners' Association, addressed a meeting at Sheffield on Wednesday night on the subject of restrietion. He stated that at the Leeds conference next week it would be proposed that miners throughout the country work five days a week and eight hours a day. He likewise stated that he was now engaged upon a soheme for an additional advance of 10 per cent. wages, and that a demand for that ,increase would shortly be made. TRH LANCAOESIRE IRON TRADIL—The iron market con- tinues in a depressed condition. The. concessions in price which have been made during the week do not appear to hays been sufficient to meet the views of buyers, and where offers are made they are at figures below the reduced prices which makers are asking. There is, however, very little disposition even to make offers, the general feeling beimg to wait the turn of the year. For delivery equal to Man- chester, district brands are quoted at 475. 61. to 48s. 61., less 21, but the figures are not being realised; local brands e still nominally quoted at 495. to 505., less 2, but a re- duction in these seem to be only defined, and there is a dis- position to entertain offers at lower figures. In the finished iron trade there is no material change to notice. liii LANCASRIRR COAL TRADR—Although there is still an absence of anything like animation throughout the coal trade of this district, the severe weather of the past week imparted more activity to the market, and any further down- weld movement in prices has been checked. A good deal of coal has been thrown upon the home market by the scarcity of vessels both at Liverpool and Garston, which hes prevented the executidn of orders for shipment, and these is a large quantity of coal held under load at many of the collieries which would readily be moved away if vessels could be obtained to take cargoes. The extra, demand brought about by the severity of the weether has been chiefly for house-fire coals, orders for which have been coming in pretty freely, but other descriptions of fuel, such as common round-coal for iron-making and steam purposes, have not been 'affected to any very material extent, and still move oft oely moderately. At the pit moath prices are steady, at about 105. to 10s. 6d. for best coals, 83. to S. ed. for seconds, 6s. 9d. to is. for common house coals, 6i, to es. 6d. for steam and forge coals, 4s. 9,1 to ss. for burgy, and Sa. 6d. te 43. per ton for good slack. For ship- ment prices are rather low, steam coal delivered at the high level, Liverpool, or at the Garston docks averaging Bs., and seconds house coal 9s. per ton. Tnz LABOUR MAuxerr.—The labour market is in a fairly satisfactory condition, although the recent inclement and stormy weather has at some of our leading centres of industry impeded work, but on the whole employment is up co the average:, The building trade in London as well as elsewhere .has been-interfered with Ly the severe frost, but the disas- trous fires of the last few days at various places augur well for increased labour in the near future. At Birmingham business is fairly good, especially in the jewellery and lamp, stove, and electric lighting branches. The Wolverhampton iron manufacturers are doing a steady trade, and the coal leads is active. Iron ship and marine engine builders at the northern ports are very busy, and at the Government dockyards at Chatham and Sheerness the men are working overtime, and a large number of extra haruis have been tbleen on. Several parts of the mining districts are in an unsettled state in relation to wages. At Newcestle-on-Tyne shipbuilding is brick. At Sunderland the glass bottle makers are on strike, and ship and marine engine builders are very buoy. At Barnsley the mills and foundries are well employed, and coke makers are busy. Steel makers at Barrow-in-Fur- mese are fairly employed, and shipbuilding is active. At the Hartiepools the shipbuilding yards are on full time, and the Iron trade good. The textile trades show no important changes. At Bradford two-fold yarn spinners are busy, lint in other branches trade is quiet. At Kiddermineter the manufacturers are completing orders on hand, but trade in worsteds is quiet. At Nottingham there is a fair demand for Valenciennes and Maltese lace, and manufacturers of Irish crochet lace and Sviiss embroideries are fairly busy. The hosiery trade as well as the shoe trade at Leiceeter is quiet. At Northampton and Stafford shoe manufacturers complain of want of orders. Several large contracts for constructing railways and docks have just been decided, and the works are to be at once commenced. Several others are in progrees, and at some good hands are wanted.—Labour .2re1103.

THE ERSKINES. The family of Erskine is poor in possessions, but rich in itles, and richer still in honours—in honours chiefly won by one of its cadets, who rose by sheer force of ability from penury to the Woolsack, and who wrote upon his escutcheon the proud motto, "Trial by Jury." The name of Erskine is born by the Earl of Buchan, the Earl of Kellie, and Lord Erskine. - Besides these, there is Goodeve-Erskine, Earl of Mar, and St. Clair Erskine, Earl of Rosslyn. Not one of these appears to possess an estate of 10,000 acres. This relieves me for once from the tedious task of tracing out the sinister and tortuous ways by which wealth has been derived, and affords me an ample opportunity of dwelling upon the brilliant career of one whose eloquence was only equalled by his lofty patriotism, and whose services to his country deserve to he held in imperishable remembrance. To me this is a congenial task. lam jealous of the historic continuity of English Liberalism. I can understand and pity a Russian Nihilist to whom yesterday is as great a blank as to-morrow; for an English Nihilist I cannot but feel contempt.

The Earldom of Mar was in existence at the period of the Norman Conquest, and its origin is lost in antiquity. At various times its possessors have played an important part in Scottish history. In the fourteenth century a grand- daughter of one of the Earls of Mar married Sir Thomas Erskine, and one of their descendahts was elevated to the peerage with the title of Lord Erskine. The direct male line of the old Earls of Mar having died out, Queen Mary, in 1565, restored the title to the fifth Lord Erskine. In the Civil War the family suffered greatly, and, although the estates were restored on the accession of Charles 11., a great part of them had to be sold. The Earl of Mar took an active part in the Jacobite Rebellion of 1715, and was attainted in consequence. In 1824 the title was revived in favour of one of his descendants, who was succeeded-by his son; but, he dying without issue, the Earldom passed to the son of his eldest sister who had married Mr. William James Goodeve. The Earldom of Kellie was obtained through the marriage of one of the Erskines into the family which held that ancient Earldom. The Earldom of Rosslyn is a modern creation, obtained by Alexander Wedderburn, Lord Lough- borough, who was Lord Chancellor in 1793. At his death the title paSsed to his nephew,anErskine,who was descended from the seventh Earl of Mar.

This seventh Earl of Mar was the favourite of James 1., from whom he received lar4e grants of confiscated Church lands, formerly belonging to Dryburgh and other monastic houses, which were erected into the Barony of Cardross, and passed to the issue of his second son, who, married the Countess of Buchan. By the middle of last century the Buchan branch of the family was almost in as unfortunate a condition as the heirs of the attainted Earl of Mar. Possi- bly they had suffered in political troubles, for some of them were staunch Covenanters; certainly, one of them had squandered a large portion of his inheritance. The fifth Earl was reduced to a miserable income of £2OO a year, lived in a flat at Edinburgh, and was compelled to move to cheaper lodgings at St. Andrews. He had three sons .; the eldest, his heir, succeeded him, and contrived in half century to increase his income from £2OO to £2,000. The second became an able and successful practitioner at the Scotch Bar. Of the third, who ,afterward became Lord Erskine, I am about to speak more 'particularly. Thomas Erskine, as a lad, was anxious to be educated for a learned profession; but what could a poor lord, with but £260 a year, do for a third son, save provide him with por- ridge and kail, which seems to have been the lad's ordinary fare? He could not even buy him a commission in the Army, so the boy was sent to sea as a midshipman. Four years passed, and young Erskine returned home, soon after, attending the funeral of his father, which was conducted at Bath by Whitfield, of whom the Earl was an adherent. With the small legacy bequeathed him, Erskine purchased an ensigncy, and, with only his pay to support him, he was rash enough at the age of twenty to rush into matrimony with an amiable young lady of no fortune. After enduring two or three years of poverty as a subaltern in a marching regiment, Erskine's casual attendance at the Assizes fired him with the resolve to make a determined effort to forsake the Army for the Law. He entered himself as a student at Lincoln's Inn, and also as a student at Cambridge—he, as the son of a nobleman, having the right to take a degree without examination, which degree, once obtained, shortened his legal probation by two years. It was a hard struggle. He Wok lodgings for his young wife in Kentish Town, and had to be content with mean fare and shabby clothes. He had no legal connections to push him forward; and, as he himself said, when he obtained his first brief, he had barely a shilling in his pocket. But he had only been at the Bar a few months when a happy accident brought him fame and fortune_ at a single bound'. Ssme men, equally worthy of success, have to fight their way inch by inch for half a life- time. Fortunately for Erskine and for England it was other- wise with him.

An action for libel had been brought against Captain Baillie, lieutenant-goverifor of Greenwich Hospital, because, after vaiply appealing to the Government to redress the flagrant abuses in that institution, he had published the facts of the case. Shortly before the trial, Erskine, who was quite unknown to Millie, was present at a dinner at which Baillie attended, and happened to express himself strongly in con- versation on he case. Baillie asked hia attorney to retain Erskine as junior counsel for his defence. The fee was but one poor guinea, and four senior counsel had to appear be- fore him. Ai ter the othe s had spoken the case was adjourned till the next morning, and then Erskine rose anil electrified the Court with a speech which was a masterpiece of invec- tive, in which he attacked the prima author of the abuses, Lord Sandwich, with withering scorn. captain Baillie won his case, with costs, and -Erskine's fame at the Bar was at once secured.

A few months after, Erskine acted as legal adviser to Admiral Keppel, who was tried by court-martial on a groundless charge of incapacity, and the Admiral, on his acquittal, presented him with £l,OOO. In four years and a half Erskine was computed to have not only paid his debts, but to have made £9,000; and to have acquired a practice of 13,t!00 per annum. From 1783 to 1806 he is said to have had, on the average, a dozen special retainers a year, with a minimum fee of 300 guineas each. In all he is said ta have made £200,000; he appears to have invested his money un- wisely, and to have died- comparatively poor. For many years Erskine was the chief legal advocate of English liberty against the infamous attacks of tyrannical Tory Governments. In defending Lord George Gordon, he made a successful stand against the attempt to bring a man to the scaffold on a charge of constructive treason. In the case of Stocknale' the publisher, he made an equally success- ful stand against libel prosecutions by vote of the House of Commons In the case of Thomas Paine, for publishing "The Rights of Man," he vindicated the independence of the Bar by accepting a retainer for Paine, though warned that if he did so he would lose his office as Attorney-General of the Prince of Wales. But his crowning triumph was his successful defence of Hardy, Horne Tooke, and Thelwall, who, as members of the London Corresponding Society, were tried for high treason.. Hardy, the brave shoemaker, whose tombstone any one may see against the railing of Bunhill Fields when passing up the City Road, was tried first. Scott, afterwards Lord Eldon, spoke for nine hours for the prosecution, and a whole week passed before the pro- secution closed. For seven hours Erskine spoke in Hardy's defence, till his voice failed, and hardly rose above a whisper amid the hushed stillness of the court. At the' close of the trial, his exertions were rewarded with a verdict of "Not guilty." The trials of Horne Tooke and Thelwall followed, and in each case Erskioe was equally triumphant. In another trial, Erskine earnestlyacontended that in libel cases juries should be judges, not merely as regards the publica- tion of the libel, but as to the libel itself—a principle after- wards embodied in Fox's Libel Bill. Once he appeared to prosecute in a case affecting th 3 liberty of the Press, at the instance of the S ,cirety for the Suppression of Vice, who pro- ceeded against the publisher of Paine's "Age of Reason ;" bat on it appearing that the Society pressed for a vindictive punishment he repudiated its action, and refused to appear in its behalf span. - - _ -

As a debate;.in Parliament, and as Lord Chancellor, Lord Erskine did not achieve remarkab'e success, and he was severely blamed for appointing his son-in-law a Master in Chancery just before his retirement. That solitAry act of nepotism, however, is venial indeed when we compare him with those who, Game before and those who followed after. Almost the het public act of his life was to write a pamphlet ia which he earnestly pleaded the cause of the oppressed Greeks. Well might Lord Brougham write of this true nobleman—"He resisted the combination of statesmen, ard princes, and lawyers--the league of craft and cruelty formed to destroy our liberties—and triumphantly scattered to the winds the half-accomplished scheme of an unsparing proscription. Before such a precious service as this, well may the lustre of statesmen and of orators grow pale; ard yet this was the achievement of one not only the first orator of his age, and not amongst its foremost statesmen, because he was beyond all comparison the most accomplished ad- vocate, and the most elogrAnt that raodern times have pro- duced."
