div.p: At Liverpool, on Monday, Mr. Edrard Driffield, County Coroner for Lancashire, resigned his office. On Saturday morning the Printe of Wales paid a visit of inspection to the scene of the great fire in London. It is stated that the aggregate sum assured seems to be about £850,000 on the various stocks in trade, and £150,000 on the

buildings. The Rey. A. H. Mackonochie having resigned the living of St. Alban', Holborn, the vacant living was offered by the Dean and Chapter of St. Paul's to the Rev. R A. J. Suckling, of S. Peter's, London Docks, and the latter living was afterwards offered to Mr. Macho ' sochie who aecepted it. The Bishop of London has confirmed both appoint-

ments. Lady Strangford has written from Cairo appealing for funds for the hospital established by the St. John's Ambulance Mission. The hospital has already done good work, and, it is hoped, may be placed on a permanent basis, supported by the Egyptian Government, but under English control. Unless funds are forthcoming, however, it must be closed. At tie Marlborough Police Court, on Saturday, a lad, nulled Lawrence, was seat to prison for 14 days for craelty to a colt at the Manton racing stables. Because a valuable colt named My Lud, which resently cost £l,OOO, would not move when ordered, Lawrence threw a pitchfork, point foremost, into its quarters. The fork was embedded four or five inches, and it is doubtful whether the animal will recover. A LITHRPOOL EXPRESS IN COLLISION. On Monday evening, a collision occurred at Dinting, a.station between Manchester and Sheffield. Whilst a slow train out of Man- chester was standing in the station it was run into by an express from Liverpool to Hull. Four persons were in- jured, one of them so seriously that he is not expected to recover. The goods van of the slow train was smashed, and also a passenger carriage next to it. It was in this the in- jured persons were. The collision seems to have been caused by the engine-driver not seeing the signals. Much delay of traffic has resulted. Tan Tflurr OT FORNION BONDS.—John Carr, aged 54, and Joseph Wilson, aged 51, who were convicted at the September session of stealing and receiving foreign bonds of the value of £l,OOO from on board a vessel at Rotterdam, were brought up for judgment at the Central Criminal Court, on Saturday. A point of law was reserved in their favour as to whether the robbery was under the jurisdiction of a ; British court of justice, but that was decided against them, ; and they were brought up fur sentence. Mr. Justice Haw- kins sentenced them to five years' penal servitude, to be ,• dated from the period of their conviction. He also ordered I that they should pay the costs of the prosecution. ITill BrYB CROFTBRS AGITATION.—Arnong the parlia- ; mentary papers issued on Tuesday, is a letter from the Lord I Advocate to the Sheriff of Inyernesahire respecting the dis- turbances among the Skye crofters. The Lord Advocate ; says the Government have come to the conclusion that they ought not to sanction the employment of a military force under existing circumstances, but that the county authori- ; ties should provide or obtain the service of such a force of Ipolice as they may consider necessary. Should they resolve ; to increase their own police, -6ir William Harcourt will grant his consent to whatever addition they consider usquisite. I Tam Sr. Luis's MySTRRT.—At the Ceatral Criminal Court, on Monday, the trial of Franz Felix Stutnm, baker, I for forgery, was brought to It conclusion. The case Was connected with the mysterious disappearance of Napoleon Stanger, baker, Stat Luke's. The evidence having closed, and I counsel having addressed the jury, Mr. Justice Hawkins summed up. and directed the jury to eliminate the question lof the murder of Stanger, and consider merely whether the prisoner was guilty of forging the mortgage deed. The pre- tended letters from Stanger in Germany were admitted by Miss Stanger to be forgeries. The jury found the prisoner ' guilty on all the counts and the judge passed a sentence of ten years' penal servitude. STEALING HUMAN HAIR.—At Birmingham on Tuesday, Ernest Lotz, a German, pleaded guilty to stealing 871bs. of Swedish human air, value £4OO, from his employer, Mr. Schletter, merchant, Navigation-street. At the request of the prosecution, the case was dealt with summarily, the magistrates imposing a sentence of six months' imprison- ment. since his incarceration, prisoner has given informa-' Lion tending to criminate different hairdressers in the town, one of whom, Henry White, Stafford-street, was, en Tues- day, arrested and remanded. White, as alleged, received nearly £2OO worth of the choicest specimens of women's hair from Lola for £l5 "on credit." Other locks were dis- posed of at as low a price as horse hair. THN PRINCa OF WlLlis AND THH NIPPY Curt OF Lox- DON SCHOOL—The Prince and Princess of Wales on Tues- day afternoon opened the New City of London School, on the Thames Embankment, Blackfriars, the erection of which cost about £lOO,OOO. The Lord Mayer, the Lady Mayoress, and Sheriffs attended in State. The Prince and Princess arrived at three o'clock, and were received with due honour, Dr. Ablyott, head master, conducting their Royal Highnesses over the building. In replying to an address, the Prince expressed a hope that the school, which had prospered so well for thirty of forty years, would continue ever to do so. Many of its pupils had taken high degrees at the universi- ties. The ceremony concluded amid cheers. DESTRUCTION OF A Cartmcm—The Presbyterian Church at Plymouth, which was erec'ed at a coat of several thousand pounds about 12 years ago, was destroyed by fire lon Monday morning. The warming apparatus was attended to in the usual manner on Saturday night, and it is supposed it must have become so fiercely heated as to ignite the woodwork. The exterior of a nunnery attached to the Roman Catholic Cathedral was damaged, and for seine time ; a panic prevailed among the mans and some hundreds of 1 orphan children maintained there. The last instalment of i debt on the building was paid on the recent celebration of I the twenty-first anniversary of the pastorate of the Rev. IJoseph Wood; and when the news of the fire was conveyed to that gentleman he was seized with a paralytic stroke, and has not since spoken. FIRS AT 1 BOLTON Inoxwotnrs £lO,OOO.— Shortly before midnight on Monday a fire was discovered lon the premises of Messrs. Musgrave and Co., Limited, Globe Ironfoundry, Kay-street, Bolton. Flames were first observed in the central room of the pattern-making-depart- ment, and the watchman was communicated with. The Brigade connected ;with Messrs. Dobson and Barlovea works, Kay-street, was first on the spot, quickly followed by the borough brigade and that of Messrs Ormrod aid liardcastle, I cotton spinners. Difficulty was experienced in getting at I the scat of the fire but ultimately nine jets were at work, and the lames, which blazed fiercely, were subdued, not, however, till the roof had fallen in and a large quantity of valuable patterns had been destroyed. The brigades continued at work until four &clack on Tuesday morning. The build- ing was 90ft. long by about 251 t. wide, and was situated in the centre of the works. The damage amounts to £lO,OOO, and is covered by insurance. THEATRICAL faTr SUIT.—In the Queen's Bench Division. on Saturday, Mr. Justice Field and Mr. Justice Stephen had before them the case of "Sennett v. Clarke," an action which was brought by an actor and his wife, an actress, to recover from the proprietor of the Carecian Theatre damages for wrongful dismissal, and which was tried the other day be- fore Mr. Justice Day and a common jury. The trial having resulted in a verdict for the plaintiffs for £250, Mr. Kemp, QC., now moved on behalf of the defendant for 'a rule calling upon the plaintiffs to show cause why the verdict should not be set aside, or why there should not be a new trial on the grounds of the verdict belt g against the weight of evidence and of the damages being excessive. Their lordships granted a rule on the second ground, but refused I to interfere on the first. PAnaTur. AFFAIR AT WATHRLOO.—A solution of a pain- ful mystery at Waterloo was reached on Monday. On tlre 30th ult. the young wife of a Liverpool sharebroker, who had been in a desponding state of mind through illness, and who was staying for her health at the residence of her father at Waterloo, was missed from the house. When last seen she was without jacket or bonnet. Every effort was made to discover her whereabouts, and a reward of £lOO was offered for that result. On Monday the body of the lady was found in a pond in the grounds of Mr. Cornelius, a Liverpeol corn merchant, residing at Waterloo. The deceased lady, who was stilly 21 years of age, bad called upon the family of Mr. Cornelius on the day of her dis- appearance, and it is supposed that on leaving the house she commit ted suicide by throwing herself in the lake.

EXTENSIYE Finn AT DMIZARTON. A telegram from Dumbarton, on Monday afternoon, stated that the town buildings were at five o'clock in a perfect conflagration, and the efforts of the fire brigade appeared to be entirely futile. The fire was discovered about 4.30 p.m. The town buildings belong to the Corporation, and contain school accommoda- tion for over 600 pupils, two large halls for public meetings, and a number of smaller balls. Workmen had for some (line been employed making three largo class-rooms, in which it was intended to carry on a school of art under tlite Govern- ment. It is stated that one of the workmen with a lighted candle had come in contact with some felt which was being put in the ceilings. The fire spread with alarmino• rapidity, that defeated all efforts to check its progress. The fire bii- gade in town were soon on the spot, but, owing to the inflam- mable nature of the building and the want of pressure on the town's water mains, the firemen were only partially suc- cessful. The roof of the front part of the building soon fell in, and the firemen then directed. their efforts to saving the adjoining properties and the larger public hall. In this they were fortunately successful. The damage done will amount to £s,ooo or £9,000, but is covered by insurance. THE DANGIRS Or VSGETAIZIAN DIBT.—The wife of the celebrated Dr. Tanner has lately taken up her abode in •France, having obtained a divorce from her eccentric hus- band under the following circumstances :—Dr. Tanner, it appears, is pecnliarly addicted to extraordinary fancies ; and, some time since, he thought that be ,had found out that the human character becomes modified according to the food taken by the individual, and especially in relation to the vegetables consumed. Carrots, he avers, make people tidgetty and sly ; turnips produce extreme amiability; while a prolonged diet of French beans induces great irritability of temper. The carrying out of this theory has brought great trouble into Dr. 'tanner's home. He made a heavy wager on the question with some friends, and experimented on Mrs. Tanner with French beans, giving her to eat about three pounds of this vegetable daily. It is not altogether to be wondered at, if, after such a "regimen, Mrs. Tanner became rather more irritable than was perhaps contemplated, and threw a jug at Dr. Tanner's head. The doctor, however, gained his bet;; and, more thoroughly convinced than ever of the truth of his theory, put his wife on the turnip diet, so as to make her as amiable as she was before the French bean regimen. This time, however, the result was not so strictly , in accordance with the theory. Mrs. Tanner objected to be L any longer a subject for these vegetarian experiments; sued for a divorce, and, what is more singular, obtained it.— British Medical Jottrital.

The Egyptian Government has chartered a steamer to I convey Arabi, Toulba, Samy, and the other exiles from Suez to Ceylon. Madame Sarah Berrihardt has paid 40,000 f. of the 100,000 f. to which she was condemned for breaking her engagement with the Theatre Francaise. The Midland Railway Company have purchased a block of property in Derby for the purpose of extending their Central Works, where 1,030 additional men will be em- ployed. News reached Kirkwall on Thursday afternoon from the outlying island of Papa Westray that a boat and three men lost in the gale of the 2nd inst. had been found in Papa Sound. The names of those drowned are William Nuller, John Reid, and Edward Bigland. We understand that in answer to an appeal from Sir Ughtred Kay-Slauttleworth, as chairman of the North-East Lancashire Liberal Registration Association, Lord Derby has consented to become a subscriber of £5O a year to the funds of that organisation. Mr. Justice Stephen is setting an admirable example in his method of dealing with the street ruffians in London. Two youths who pleaded guilty before him to a robbery and assault on a married lady were each sentenced to fifteen years' penal servitude, and the "cruel brute" who actually inflicted the violence complained of was also ordered to be flogged. I public worship and public-house Sunday census has been taken at Kilburn with the following curious result, There are 25 places of worship in Kilburn, and the number of persons attending such places on the evening in question was 5,570. There are 35 public-houses in the place, and the number of persons who entered such houses between the hours of six and eight on the same night was 5,591. Sentenee of penal servitude for life was passed at Sligo, on Thursday, by Mr. Justice Lawson on the leader of a gang of "moonlighters," named Tubbridy, for an outrage in Galway. Tubbridy was shot in the back by the farmer whose house the party attacked, and the Judge said that the fact that the prisoner was deserted by his comrades showed that the tie which bound such men together was merely a rope of sand. On Thursday morning the Dublin Co-operative Stores , were destroyed by fire. The conflagratioa was a most disas- trous one, the whole of the extensive premises being con- sumed. The building was packed With goods from top to bottom, and nothing was saved. The vaults were filled with explosive materials, bat fortunately no explosion occurred. Ills rumoured that a caretaker aud his family living in the house have been burned to death. A Bolton carder, named Brough, was committed to the sessions, on Thursday morning, by the Bolton magistrates for defrauding his employers, Messrs. G. Knowles and Sons, Limited. The prisoner had drawn the wages of two work- men, and had falsified the pay sheet so as to make out a larger number of hours than they had worked. He banded the men the correct sum, and pocketed the difference Bs. 101

The Dublin police made two arrests on Thursday, sup- posed to be in connection with the Phcenix Park murders. Two men living in the Coombe, whose names will not be given as yet, are the parties captured. They were taken to the Castle by detectives immediately after being arrested, but of course the proceedings were private. Considerable importance appears to be attached to the capture. It is expected that the men will be brought up at the police court. The Liverpool Mercury is informed on the best authority that Mr. Rodway, the Tory legal agent, has been busily engaged since Monday, aided by the chiefs of the party, in endeavouring to obtain material upon which to found a case with the view of petitioning against Mr, S. Smith, M.P. It is hinted that Mr. Rodway has discovered sufficieut ev;dence with whick to proceed, the main allegation of the con- templated iadictment being briber*, personation, endue influence, and delay in opening several of the polling booths on the morning of the election day. In the event of proceedings taking place, the seat will net be claimed on behalf of Mr. Alderman A. B. Forwood. BISHOP LIGHTFOOT ON THE SALVATION ARMY.—Bishop Lightfoot, in bis triennial charge to the diocesan clergy in Durham Cathedral on Thursday, said if the Church bad het succeeded in evangelising the masses, neither had the Non- coaformists. Would the Church be satisfied with picking one up here and there, gathering together a more or less select congregation, forgetting the Master's command to go into the highways and compel them to come in? The Sal- vation Army had taught them a higher lesson. Whatever might be the faults of the Salvation Army, it had at least recalled them to the lost idea of the work of the Church. THREATENING THE PRINCE OF WALES AND Ma. GLAD- STONE—At Bow-street, en Monday morning, John Crunder, 47, was charged on remand with sending a letter threatening his Royal Highnees the Prince of Wales and the Right lion. W. E. Gladstone. The prisoner was arrested by Inspector Swanson, of Scotland Yard, at 19, Wilson-street, Gray's Inn- road, and admitted having written the letter, which was published last week. Mr. Pollard now attended on behalf of the Treasury; and asked:that the prisoner might be further remanded, and formally committed for trial on another day. Mr. Flowers remanded the prisoner until Monday next. MR. LEITHAIL, M.P., AT HUDDEIRIFIRLD.—Mr. E. A. Leathern, M.P., addressing a meeting of his constituents at Huddersfield on Tuesday evening, said that the political outlook seemed to be brightening. Peace prevailed through- out Europe, and the dangers which once threatened us, in connection with our colonial empire had been averted. Ireland was slowly returning to that allegiance to which nothing but the active application of Liberal remedies could have restored her, and once more there was a hope that she might be retained as part of the United Kingdom by other means than those of force. Parliament itself was now loosed from the trammels which of late years had fettered her, and under the guidance of a great leader would, he doubted not, accomplish legislation which would have its place in English history. SHOCKING GUN ACCIDENT NEAR HUDDERSFIELD.—On Thursday afternoon, two brothers, named Thomas Mellitr, aged 36, mason, and George Mellor, mason, a little younger, of -Meltham, near Huddersfield, went out in search of hares, and about 1.45 they were on some land near the Convalescent Home, on the south side of the village. George Mellor had a doable-barrelled gun, both barrels of which were loaded with No. 5 shot. They saw a hare, and Thomas Mellor said he would try and catch it alive. He made an effort but did not succeed, and then he went behind a snow-drift so as to watch its further movements and to direct his brother. He then directed his brother to fire at the hare and ha did so, but the shot did not take effect, and just as he fired the second barrel Thomas jumped up from behind the snow-drift and received in the back of the head the full effect of the shot. He fell and death resultedinstantaneously. THE ANNIVERSARY OF PRINCE CONSORT'S DEATH.-Thurs- day being the anniversary of the deaths of the Prince Consort and Princess Alice, the Queen, Princess Beatrice, the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, the Duke A. WRY MR. MACKONOCHIE RESIGNED. A copy of the communications which passed between the late Archbishop of Canterbury and the Rev. A. A. Mack- onochie, of St. Alban's' which led to the latter resigning his living, has been published. The Archbishop, writing from Addington on November 10, says his thoughts, so far as he was able at present to give steady thought to public matters, had dwelt much upon She troubles and difficulties in con- nection with the resent Ritual prosecutions. He was ex- ceedingly anxious that :the result of the Royal Commis- sion on Ecclesiastical Courts should be such as to allay dis- quiet, and by meeting any reasonable objections to existing procedure to set men's minds free for the pressing duties which devolve upon the church in the face of prevailing sin and unbelief. Anything which increased bitterness of feeling might do permanent mischief to the cause they had at heart; anything which tended to preserve peace would make a satisfactory solution of their difficulties far easier. He, therefore, ventured privately to ask him whether he aould in any way contri- bute to minimise the present feeling of bitterness which undoubtedly exists in sore quarters. He had no wish to dictate a course of action, but if he felt it possible, consist- ently with his duty, to withdraw voluntarily, by resigna- tion of his benefice from further conflict with the courts, he felt sure he would be acting in the manner best calculated to promote the real power and usefulness of the Church. , The Archbishop concluded by saying he made the appeal ;under the strong sense of responsibility, and commanded , Mr. Mackonochie to prayerful thought and the guidance of , Almighty God.—Mr. Mackonechie replied next day that he would seek after Divine gaidance before replying, and , regretted that say of his concerns shonld add to the weight of his Grace': illness.—On the 21st of November the Rey. Randall Davidson wrote to Mr. Machonochie that the Archbishop was daily asking if Mr. Mackonochie I, had replied, informing him, that although the Archbishop i was so mach worse, he would be justified in writing him. —On November 23rd, Mr. Machonochie writes that he will , acquiesce in his Grace's wish, and resign his benefice. It , was to himself and his people a great sorrow, but on which he hoped they would be willing to hear. If the true peace of the church could be obtained by his compliance, he was contented to give up his peace for hers. He accepted the lino of action indicated, in deference to his Grace, as supreme representative of tie Lord Christ in all things spiritual in this land, and not as withdrawing anything he bad said or done in reference to those courts.—Mr. Davidson, acknowledging this letter, mentions the pleasure with which the Archbishop received it.—The remainder of the correspondence refers to Mr. Mackonochie's nomination to the benefice of St. Peter's, London Docks.

THE EXLMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 16, 1882. LORD DERBY AT MANCHESTER. I Lord Derby was, on Wednesday evening, entertained at I the Manchester Reform Club by the President (Mr. William Mather), and delivered a speech on current politics which will be read with deep interest. Referring to the fact of his having joined the Liberal party, his Lordship said that that "was a step long, carefully, and deeply considered, and once taken it would not be retracted." His next words were words of congratulation on the position now occupied ky the Goverament and by those who sympathise with their suc- cess. Measures affecting Ireland, he said, had beet adopted which in the ordinary condition of etialety would not have been required, and, not being requited, would not have been justified. As a consequence of this a considerable defection might not unreasonably have been expected. There had, however, been no defections numerically important. They were, he held, justified in saying that Mr. Gadstone'e Cabinet was as much trusted, after three yeais' trial, as it was trusted before, and that the commission which it received from the constituencies in 1880 would, if opportunity offered, be renewed to-day. Referring to Egypt, the noble Lord expressed his belief that the sudden withdrawal of France before the outbreak of hostilities, did more than arything else to encourage the military party in Egypt to a resistance of which otherwise they would never have dreamed. That, in his view, was the explanation of the whole transaction. "It was an unlucky affair, and he was quite sure that Lord Granville and Mr. Gladstone were the last persons in England to be flattered or pleased by that shout of exultation which went up from a section of English society when it was seen that there was a,chance of blood being shed and public money expended." There could be no difference of opinion on one point, namely, that the Ca'ainet, in giving the order to fight, only on the conviction of imperative necessity. What- ever plans the Government had in view regarding the future of Egypt, one thing was clear, we had no business there a day longer that was necessary to restore order. The idea of annexation, or the establishment of a protectorate, was not to be entertained. Our duty was to set the Khedive on his legs, to support him in making necessary reforms, and then, if it be possible, let him stand by himself. Our in- fluence in Egypt—which would, of course, be paramount— need not exclude that frank and friendly consultation with our French neighbours which, he was happy to believe, was now going on. The French were a sensible, though, it might be, an excitable people, and .they must recognise that It was by their own act, and net by ours, that they did not at this moment hold the same position which once they held in Egypt. As to Madagascar, we had no interest which would justify active intervention, however much we might disapprove the proceedings of France. Referring to Ire- land, he expressed his belief that Irish affairs would be mar chief difficulty for some time to coins. He pointed out the obstacles in the way of creating a peasant proprietary, and expressed his belief in emigration as a remedy for distress, adding that now was the time to push it forward. Some millions spent in promoting Irish emigration, if Parliament and the Cabinet saw their way to it, he believed, would pay us well. Lord Derby referred to possible legislation in the future—amongst other things to the problem of municipal govern- ment for London, the Corrupt Practices Bill, and the Licensing Laws. The latter, he thought, might remain un- disturbed till the agricultural labourer can have a voice in their settlement. His Lordship expressed himself favour- able to the scheme for dividing the House of Commons into committees—a process which he believed would increase the working power of the House three or four fold, and the results of which be hoped we should He is snore rapid as well as more oareful legislation. In conclusionlie counselled unity in the Liberal ranks. Upon the motion of Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., seconded by Mr. H. Dunckley, the thanks of the members of the club were accorded to Lord Derby; and a vote of thanks to the president, proposed by Mr. Ming- worth, M.P., and seconded by Mr. J. K. Crou, M.P., terminated the proceedings.

RUNCORN 2ND T. ST. HELENS RINGERS 2ND (12).— These two second teams met at Runcorn on Saturday, the Rangers turning up with only twelve men. After a very one-sided game, the home teara won by two goals (one dropped by Speakman), six tries, and four minor points to Rangers' nil. The tries were obtained by Speakman (4) and Roberts (3). W.I.IIINOTON WAYDEREIR T. nor &nom —The Wanderers journeyed on Saturday to New Springs, to play a match with the above club. Bolton kicke4 off for the visitors. Both sides being evenly matched, a very even game was the result. The ground was completely covereat with snow, which was detrimental to good play on the part of the backs. The game was only of half an hour's dura- tion, and resulted in a draw, neither side mooring a single point. LATCHFORD (2ND TRAM) T. Sr. ANN'S RINGFIRS (Ise Ittem).—This match was played at Latchford on Saturday. The visitors, who, owing to the ground being covered with snow, were unexpected, were represented by their strongest team; but Latchford was minus four men who had been originally selected to play. During the first half of the game the playing of the home tertm backs and forwards was excellent, they having scored three tries (got by Jack- son, Taylor, and Acton) and six minor points to nil. The second hair, however, was not so pleasantly contested, as the visitors kept repeatedly playing off-side, and a good deal of the time allowed for play was taken up in wrangling. They, however, claimed to have got two tries, but they were disputed. A. most unsatisfactory conclusion was, therefore, arrived at, Latchford winning by one try and one minor point. NORTHWICH VICTORIAS.—The tie in the second round of the competition for the English Association challenge cup between these two favndus clubs—the helders of the Welsh and Cheshire challenge cups respectively—was played off on Saturday in Wynnstay Park, Ruabon. Very soon after the game began it was evident that the Northwich men were overmatched, though they played pluckily to the end, and the goal-keeping of Palin was greatly admired. The first goal was scored three minutes after starting, by' Albert Jones and before half-time two more were credited to the Druids by Bowen and Cross. Change of ends did not im- prove matters for the visitors, and the game ended in a win for the Welshmen by five goals to ail. The two goals obtained in the second half were secured by Albert Jones and J. P. Owen. The game was very amicably played throughout, but there were a few minor casualties, Vaughan sustaining a sprained thumb and Davies a cut lip. EaIiaLISTOWN ASSOCIATION (2ND) T. HAYDOCK ST. Jamis's.—Theas two teams met on the groand of the latter on Saturday afternoon last before a fair number of spectators. Two of the Earlestown first tekm—R. Green and Darsbury—played for the second team of Earlestown, while the Haydock eleven contained about equal number of the first and second teams. The home team won the toss, and chose to play uphill during the first half. Earlestown kicked of, and after about quarter of an hour's play scored a goal after some splendid passing. Up to half time the Earlestown 'team severely pressed their opponents,and made several capital attempts to score. On the change of ends the game became very fast and more even, hut the visitors still maintained a slight advantage. flo score was made, ! however, and the match thus resulted in a win for Earlee- town by one goal to none. Rurtcoalt v. ST. Hamm Riatomus.-1. match between these two clubs was played at St. Helens on Saturday, when a finely-contested match of only 40 minutes' duration was played. The home team started the oval, Wainwright returning effectively. Borth wick and Gregson on one side, Wright, Atherton, and Wilkinson on the other, played a good game. The visitors pressed the Rangers in the struggle, and Lewis dribbled the ball up to their lines, where he picked up and crossed close to the corner flag. The place being very difficult, he failed. The Rangers then touched down. Borthwick dropped oat, and a tight scrim- maging took place, both teams being evenly matched. After scrimmaging, Wright emerged through the pack with the ball at his feet, dribbling up into the home 25, when he smartly crossed the goal line, gaining a try. Gatley took the place, nicely adding the premier point. After half- time, the game became very fast, the forward play of both teams being worthy of notice. Gregson gained possession of the ball and made a splendid run, Hughes tackling him on the goal line. Hughes rolled him into play. Gregson, however, asserted that he had grounded the leather before it being worked into play. The visitors gave way, but the kick at goal proved unsuccessful. No other point was registered to the call of "No side," Runcorn winning a pleasant game by one goal, one try, two minor points, to Rangers' one try. Teams Runcorn—Wainwright, full back ; Broady, Larkin, and Johnson, three-quarter backs; , H. div.head: SERIOUS FIRE AT HAMPTON COURT
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE AT HAMPTON COURT
PALACE.

The burning of the Alhambra Theatre and the destructive ire at the Wood-street warehouses has been succeeded by a conflagration far surpassing them In interest. On Thursday morning smoke was seen to be issuing from the eastern wing of the Hampton Court Palace, and flames speedily burst forth despite the efforts of thosuresiding within its precincts .and the military stationed at the Palace. It was soon evident that the east wing was doomed, and every effort was forthcoming to prevent the fire spreading to the other parts of the building. This, happily was effected. In the apartments at Hampton Court reside many ladies having claims .upou the country, to whom this home has been granted by Her Majesty. These have, it is believed, all escaped, but one woman is stated to have been suffocated in the dense smoke which enveloped the building. It appears that the fire broke out between seven and eight o'clock, in the private apartinenti of Mrs. Crofton, which are situated immediately above the picture gallery at the east end of the building. The alarm was lest given by one of the ladies, who raised the cry of "Fire" from one of the windows of Mrs. Crofton's apart- ments. The officials of the Palace were at once communi- cated with, as also the men of the detachment of the 14th Hussars, stationed at the Palace, messengers likewise being I despatched to Kipgston, Twickenham, and other neighbour- ing towns for the volunteer fire brigades. Until the arrival of the latter,' the soldiers' officials, and police stationed at the Palace worked with great energar, and with the aid of the Palace fire-engine did , excellent service. The flames spread with great rapidity, ' and the contents of a number of the private apartments were destroyed before their fury could be arrested. Great excitement prevailed among the inmates of the palace, but no time was lost in removing articles of value in the lower rooms to a place of safety. At ten o'clock, by which time some half-dozen fire brigades were upon the spot, all further danger was at an end. The whole of the eastern portion of the building is gutted, especially the upper rooms, and it is feared that many of the pictures in the galleries are seriously damaged. Shortly after the outbreak the dead body of one of Mrs. Crofton's female servants was I discovered by the soldiers in one of the upstair rooms, the cause of death being no doubt suffocation. The damage has been roughly estimated at £430,000. Some, however, kielieve it will greatly exceed that amount. The palace is situated upon the banks of the Thames, about 15 miles from London. The original palace, which consisted of five quadrangles, of which oulv two remain, was built by Car- dinal Wolsev, who presented it to Henry the Eighth, by whom it was subsequently enlarged. A third quadrangle wasadded by Sir Christopher Wren for William the Third. The Palace consisted of three courts, the first of the age Wolsey, the second of Henry the Eighth, and the third, as before mentioned, of the age of William the Third. ,Hamp- ton Court contained many valuable pictures, by Holbein, Lely, Kneller, and West, besides seven of Raphael's most famous cartoons. Edward Sixth was born there, and here was held the Conference between the Puritans and established clergy which led to a new translation of the Bible.

The reason why so many are unable to take Cocos is that the varieties commonly sold are mixed with starch, under the plea of render:ng them soluble ; while really making them thick, heavy, and indigestible. This may be easily detected, for if Cocoa thickens in the cup it proves the addition of starch. Cadbury's Cocoa Essence is genuine; it is therefore three times the strength of these Cocoas, and a refreshing .beverage like tea or coffee.—Advt.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY ELOPEMENT FROM
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY ELOPEMENT FROM
EARLESTOWN.

On Monday last an elopement took place from the neigh- bourhood of Newton Common, Earlestown, and as yet the runaway couple have not been induced to return themselves nor to return the valuable articles and a sum of money with which, it, is stated, they decamped. I: appears that for some months past a collier, employed at Collins Green Colliery, has had lodging at his house a man, wrio was also employed as a collier at the same pit. Up to Monday last nothing was noticed to cause any suspicion on the part of the basband, and everything, on the contrary, appears to have gone on smoothly and well up to that -day. Before the spouse proceeded to his work, on Monday morning, how- ever, his lodger complained of being sick, and that was his e.a.cuse for stopping away from his work, and as his land- lord thought, stopping at home also. But when the latter returned, about two o'clock in the afternoon, he was con- siderably surprised to find that his sick lodget had not only gone away, but what was more perplexing the leudlord's rife was missing. The children were asked about so strange an occurrence, and they stated that their mother had gone on an errand to Earlestown, whilst the lodger had gone in the same direction carrying a bundle. The husband looked round the house and ascertained that a quantity of wearing apparel had been taken and on going upstairs he found that his hard-earned sav- ings, amounting to £27, had been abstracted from a drawer. He at once proceeded to Earlestown, and on making enquiries there, ascertained that the ruiazvay couple had together booked for Manchester. The husband quickly fo'- lowed them, and-on arriving at Manchester, sought the assis- tance of the police. Unfortunately the husband was compelled to return without having gleaned anything as to the whereabouts of his faithless wife and her partner. He, however, has not given up all hope, and during the week he has been to Warrington, and there taken out a warrant for the apprehension of his former lodger. It is freely stated that the parties have booked to America, and on Wednesday P.C. Lloyd visited Liverpool with the object of obtaining definite information, but in this he was unsuccessful. Nothing further has been heard of the couple. •

div.head: LIBERALISM AT LYME.
div.p: LIBERALISM AT LYME.

On Tuesday evening a melting was held in the Assembly Room, at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, under the auspices of the Lymm Liberal Association, for the purposes of hearing an address by Mr. J. C. Pie!den, of Manchester, on "Coming legislation." There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. Brewtnall, of Thelvrall, and there were present Messrs, R. Dutton, D. Boyd, Swanwick, W. Long, and ethers. The CIAIIILLN said he had the less hesitation in occupym ing the position in which he had been placed that night, . inasmuch as he knew that a very able speaker had to follow him, and therefore very little was required from him. Ile had also the less difficulty, as be had perfect sympathy with the subject of his address—Coming legislation. Ho had the feiling, and he thought the feeling was generally shared, that this legislation had been a long time coming; that they had been waiting for it, longing for it, and striv- ing for it, for years upon years, and yet very little of it had come. It was a hundred, years this year, 1852, since reform was first broached in the Heine of Commons. Ost the 14th May, 1762, Mr. Pitt first intrcduced the subject of parliamentary reform:in the House of Commons, so that we had now been one hundred years labouring at the im- provement of our machinery for legislation. For 50 years these labours were totally barren, for it was oily in 1832, after 50 years ex rtione, after the country had gone through all sorts of agitation in favour of the changes that were caught, and%t last was brought, as the Duke of Wellington allowed, within 24 hours of a revolution—it was only then anything was done, and the great Reform Bill of 1832 was passed. Then it took 25 years to emetic' that very imper- fect measure, and only after seven abortive reform bills were introduced was it that the Bill of Mr. Disraeli in 1867-8 was passed; so that we could not congratulate ourselves on the speed with which we had progressed in the work of parlia- mentary reform. Our neighbours, who started about the same time with us,had been eminently more successful and rapid in their movements than we had. The French during that time had revolutionised the condition of their country, had totally changed the character of their land laws—laws which we had never yet been able to touch—and hact introduced a peasant proprietary which was the pride and mainstay of the coun- try. But they had to do it at the expense of seven revolutions and at the sacrifice of three dynasties. We had been satis- fied to move in more measured:terms, and in a slower, and perhaps in a safer fashion, in the end. We might have been satisfied perhaps with these slow movements whilst they had been safe and sound ones if after all we had attained the end we had in view, if the machinery of our legislation had been completed and those objects , more perfectly and more fully realised. But even yet the matter of reform was before Parliament. Whilst we had enfranchised the middle classes and done a little to- wards the enfranchisement of working men, we still had very large arrears to reform and accomplish for the counties; and no one could say how skit2n that might be accomplished, although it was certainly on the cards and could not, :humanly speaking, be lorg de- layed. We might have endured all this, if after all we had made the best use of the means of legislation which we had ; but our parliamentary annals had been disgraced by ots- struction. (Hear, hear.) After all this delay and all this evil Parliament had become an immovable machine. It had lost its momentum. It would no longer go, no longer pro- duce the effects for Which it was instituted. He confessed to them that as far as Irish obstruction went he had some little sympathy with it—not with obstruction as obstruction but with the objects which the Irish patriots had in view for no doubt the condition of Ireland was very very serioais indeed. The land laws of England were bad enough per- haps, and the only land laws beside them in Europe which had not been reformed and brought up to the wants of so- ciety in its present condition, but the land laws of Ireland were very much worse. The condition of the agricultural population was extremely had, and all efforts to remove the evil had beim negatived in the usual Tory fashion, for just as the Chandos :clause was introduced to spoil the effects of the great Reform Bill,, so the Bright clauses whieh were introduced in the Glad stone Land Bill of 1880 were removed by the obatructiv° policy of the Tory party; and it was only when obstruction was introduced in the troublesome and often rather degrad- ing fashion it was, by the Irish members, that the great reform that they so much needed was brought about, Although they deplored the scenes through which Parlia- ment was dragged, and were humiliated when they looked back to the means which seemed necessary in order to bring that great measure of Irish land reform through Parliament, still they, to some extent, must acknowledge that the Irish members had a good object in view fs4 far as land-law reform was concerned. But there was another element of obstruc- tion with which he had r.o patience, for they must have observed the most bitter, malicious and malignant kind of obstruction that Parliament had recently suffered, had been obstruction brought about by the Tory party—(hear, hear) —obstruction intended to prevent legislation--obstruction no doubt begotten of the apprehension that great changes were about to follow—changes:which would have a disastrous effect no doubt on the privileges of the Tory class; —(hear, hear)—and when they considered the means and agents that had been at work in producing all this hubbub in Parliament their scorn and contempt could not help being roused to the extreme. (Hear, hear.) That Lord Randolph Churchill should make the figure in Parliament that he bad done, and that he should beard the beat and greatest of minis- ters England ever saw in the fashion he bad, was enough to stir the blood of every patriotic Englishman. Whilst he firmly believed all this obstruction of the Tory party had a reference to the great coming legislation—legislation which would touch the privileges of the privileged class, the Tory landlords and Tory magistrates throughout the country, he had a secret suspicion that Lord Randolph Churchill must ibe touched and moved by some personal considerations. (Laughter.) They all recollected something of the John Churchill who lived 160 years ago, or thereabouts. He was perhaps the greatest military genius that England ever pro- duced, and no doubt did great service for his country, bat he secured great retards,—(bear, kear)—and amongst the rewards was something which still continued, and which Lord Randolph Churchill might perhaps in his apprehension fear the coming reforms would touch to his disadvantage. (Hear, hear.) He could not imagine the virulence, acidity and perseverance with which Lord Randolph Churchill had pursued this object, unless he was touched and influenced by some motive of this kind. No doubt when this great reform did come we should see great changes—not before we needed them—changes which would come to our very doors, for everyone—those who had thought the least about political matters here—must know that all the great privileges of the country were in the hands of the Tory party. (Hear, hear.) In spite tf all they had done, in spite of all the labours of reform in Parliament, endeavouring to introduce Liberal measures, the Tory party possessed all the plums that the country had to bestow. Look at their own condition in Cheshire. How was it thatatheir friend, who so ably took the chair on the list occasion there, was refused the chairmanship of the Quarter Sessions in Cheshire! (Hear, hear.) It was acknowledged on all hands to have been his due, that he was exceedingly well able to fill.the position which his educa- tion, as a barrister, and his knowledge of law, and the pro- ceedings of courts, admirably fitted him to fill, and which 'personally he was so well able to fill, for they had had proof repeatedly of his ability, his clear heacledness, his knowledge of the law, and of the customs and usages of the country generally. He would have made an ad- mirable chairman of Quarter Sessions, and yet, forsooth, he was thrust aside for a Tory nominee because he was a Liberal. (Hear, hear.) They needed a little change even in Cheshire. He had referred to the land laws as the great backbone of Tory power and Tory pre-eminence. He might refer to some other very substantial props of that power—the church amongst the rest. (Sear, hear.) Here they had a great political institution, intended from the irst to influence the politics of the country and to make religion subservient to political purposes. No one could deny that, and well had it served its purpose. How very few, how exceedingly and melancholy tow Liberal clergy- men did they find (Hear, hear.) He had heard it asserted that there was only one Liberal clergyman in Cheshire. He did not vouch for the assertion, but he aid vouch for this, that he had beard of one, and that Liberal clergyman was boycotted because lie was a Liberal clergy- man. It was by this means, these things that the props of the Tory power and influence were kept strong and active, and were used on all occasions. Now, these were things which in a reformed parliament, a parliament that was not clogged by an antiquated mode of procedure, they would get remedied; and these were things which the Tory party feared would soon be remedied. (Applause.) Mr. FIELDRN, who was received with cheers, said how thankful he was to see such an audience. It proved to him that in thequiet little district there was a very considerable activity amongst the people in the direction of polities. See- ing that they losd in that vicinity many men who had political judgment, which had been exercised by their chairman in the speech to which they had just listened, he was not surprised to find that there was more than an average interest taken in politics in that neighbourhood. There was, somehow, a spirit abroad to decry politics and politi- cians, but he held that a politician practically occupied the same relation to the evils that affficted society as a physician held to the evils that afflicted the human body. After speaking at length upon the position of affairs when the present Government came into office, he reviewed the legis- _talon of the present Government, mentioning the Hares and Rabbits Act, the Liability Act, the Land Act, anctremarking that they had done a great deal in making secure the operatiops of merchants. Speaking of coming legislation, he maintained that the first great measure we were likely to have was a scheme of County Boards, which he ventured to say would occupy a prominent position in the Queen's Speech. (Applause.) On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. Was. ff LONG, it was resolved—. That this meeting desires toso. er Wto the Right Hon. .E. Gladstone, Her ltel jubilee of opf"iinise minister, its heartiest congratulations t On h parliamentary life, and tinies of this great nation." kspared to guide the d, fervently hops that he may be ion The meeting concluded with the usual votes of thanks t being accorded.

To these ghoul-like visages, inspired at Truth's if not Beauty's shrine; Masks wrinkled by lines of thought twisted by grimace, writhing under toothache; emotenances that mirror the souls of Macbeth, Ctomwells, Mirabeaus, Dantons and Robe- pierres, Clowns and Poets, the wise and the otherwise. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
-SATURDAY, DECEMBER 16, 1882.

ON H of the most notable epochs in the life of the PRIME MINISTER too) place on Wed- nesday, when the right hon. gentleman attained his Parliamentary jubilee. This is an event on which Mr. GLADSTONE and the whole Liberal patty may be heartily congratu- lated, and the occa,,tion may be profitably improved by recalling a few of the leading points in the career of England's greatest Statesman. Fifty years ago Mr. GLADSTONE was chosen by the electors of Newark as their representative, and from that time he has been a prominent figure in public life, as we sincerely hope he may remain for many years yet to come. The young politician was then only 23 years of age, and he had just closed his college career, where he had taken high degrees, but had betrayed none of the Radical tendencies which he is now believed to possess in a very marked degree. He was ' in fact a Tory, and seemed to have very little '1 sympathy with the Reform Bill, which had ; just been wrested from Parliament. In his I address to the electors of Newark he referred i to the desire for great changes which the tadvocates of Reform manifested, and the following, passage taken from that address shows how much he dreaded change. He said: "We must watch and resist that un- enquiring and undiscriminating desire for change amongst us which threatens to pro- duce, along with partial good, a melancholy preponderance of mischief, which, I am per-

div.head: ExAMINER, SA TURPAY, I)ECEmBER 16, 188‘..;.
div.p: THE ExAMINER, SA TURPAY, I)ECEmBER 16, 188‘..;.

suaded, would aggravate beyond computation the deep-seated evils of our social scale, the heavy burthens of our industrial classes." Little did he then think that in a compara- tively short period of time he would lae the earnest and no less sincere advocate of reforms much more sweeping than almost anything that had gone before. Mr. GLAD- STONE'S Parliamentary career is a most remarkable one. His ability and eloquence very soon marked him out for favour, and Sir R. PEEL, who was never slow to recognise merit in his followers, appointed young GLADSTONE, soon after his election, one of the junior lords of the Admiralty. So early as 183.4. he was promoted by Sir ROBERT Under Secretary for the Colonies, but his tenure of this office —the duties of which he discharged with commendable ability—was of short duration, for the PREMIER found it necessary to resign in 1835, and was suc- ceeded by Lord MELBOURNE. On Sir ROBERT PEEL'S return to power, however, in 1841, Mr. GLADSTONE was appointed Vice- President of the Board of Trade and Master of the Mint, in which office, by passing through the House a bill for the revision of the Tariff, he displayed a great knowledge of the details of commerce. In May, 18.4_3, on the death of the Earl of RIPON, Mr. GLAD- STONE became President of the Board of Trade, and for the first time entered the Cabinet. The agitation for the repeal of the corn laws was then gaining ground in the country, and Mr. GLADSTONE contributed , largely by his advocacy to the success which attended that movement. He stuck man- fully to his leader in the noblg step which he then saw fit to take in repealing the obnoxious imposts, and shared with him the abuse which was heaped upon those who, by advocating repeal, were regarded as deserters of their party. The abuse, how- ever, was as much undeserved at that time by Mr. GLADSTONE as the vituperation which is hurled at him at the present day by ,his political opponents. In the general electioni of 184.7 Mr. GLADSTONE was returned as member for ,Oxford University, and one of the first questions introduced into the new Parliament was one to remove the disabilities of the Jews. Mr. GLADSTONE gave it his unqualified support, much to the disappoint- ment of his constituency, and this it was that led him to sever himself from the Conserva- tive party, which was at that time led by Lord DERBY. It is rather singular that at the present time Mr. GLADSTONE should be re- ceiving into his Cabinet Lord DERBY'S son, who has also seceded from the ranks of the Tories. In consequence of his change of views Mr. GLADSTONE had to fight for his seat for Oxford University in 1852, but he was successful in retaining it; and he then entered Lord ABERDEEN'S Coalition Ministry as Chancellor of the Exchequer. Proceeding in his course of fiscal reform, the aptitude for which he had shown at the Board of Trade, the young Chancellor of the Exchequer passed the Succession Duties Act, and ever since he has distinguished himselfj in finance. The Coalition Ministry wasl broken up by Mr. ROEBUCK'S motion with ! respect to the misfortunes of the Englishl troops before Sebastopol, and Lord PALMERSTON became Prime Minister, with ! Mr. GLADSTONE again as Chancellor ofj the Exchequer. Finding, however, Lord PALMEF STON was ready to give way on the question of appointing a committee to inquire into the sufferings of the troops, as suggested , by Mr ROPBUCK, Mr. GLADSTONE resigned his office, but resumed it four years subse- quently.. In the meantime he had received! at the hands of Lord DERBY the appointment ' of Lord High Commissioner Extraordinary, to the lonian Is;ands, which were at the time in a disturbed state; and the hon member'sl mission only terminated when the Home Ministry advised Her Majesty to decline to ! grant the prayer of a petition from thel lonian Legislative Assembly in favour of a union with Greece. This union was, how- ever, granted in 1864. by a Liberal Govern- ment. The acceptance of this appointment was believed by many to be a forerunner of Mr. GLADSTONE'S return to his old political school; this, we all know, has been fullyl falsified by events. On his return from thej lonian Islands Mr. GLADSTONE again servedj under Lord- PALMERSTON, and also Lox& RUSSELL, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, his budgets being pitductive of increased j revenue and reduced taxation. His Liberal ; tendencies resulted in his being thrown over by the University of Oxford in 1865, but he was returned for South Lancashire,,and in the next: Parliament took up the post of leader of thel Opposition. In that capacity, paradoxical ; though it may seem, he opposed the Reform I Bill of 1867-8, promoted by Mr. DISRAELI. The last, session of this Parliament was I signalised by Mr. GLADSTONE succeeding in passing resolutions in favour of the dis- establishment and disendowment of the Irish Church, and at the generall election which followed in 1868 he was returned to power by a large majority. From 1868 to 1874 he was PRIME MINISTER, but in the last-mentioned year he was defeated at the polls. Subsequently he resigned the leadership of the Liberal party, which was afterwards led by Lord HARTINGTON, but at the general election of 1880 the Liberals were again victorious at the polls, and by one acclaim Mr. GLADSTONE was selected to form a Cabinet His career ever since he left the Conservative ranks has been one uninterrupted run of success. In finance he has proved himself amaster,and in domestic legislation the measures which he has passed are generally acknowledged to be the best which have been placed upon the statute book. With respect to Irish affairs—which must always be delicaebly handled—he is, we think, the only PRIME MINISTER who ever attempted. to rule the sister isle -without coercion and according to Irish ideas. He has fearlessly passed measures which he knew would grant relief. He has boldly struck at the very root of Irish disaffection, successfully grappled , with every difficulty, and he reaps the reward in seeing the country gradually assuming a ' peaceful and contented attitude. His Irish legislation is, we should say, the crowning glory of his administration so far. Mr. GLAD- STONE'S services to his own country have never been equalled, much less excelled by any contemporary statesman, and his brilliant talents have also been the means of doing good to other countries. At a time when the Neapolitans were groaning under the oppres- sion of King BOMBA., Mr. GLADSTONE'S 'Two letters to the Earl of ABERDEEN on the State Prosecutions of the Neapolitan Government," struck a sympathetic chord in every heart, not only in England but throughout the civilised globe. For the purposes of these letters Mr GLADSTONE visited the prisons in Naples, conversed with the prisoners and witnessed their sufferings, at the same time exploring underground dungeons, and it must be a satisfaction to him to know that his disclosures resulted in a considerable, remission of punishment in many cases. In the Greeks

he has always taken a profound interest: and it is evident that they have fully appreciated his exertions on their behalf, for a telegram comes from Athens to the effect that the Greek Government are about to erect a statue to commemorate his Parliamentary jubilee. His scathing denunciations of the Bulgarian atrocities are still fresh in the memories of our readers ; whilst his desire to hand over Egypt to the Egyptians is another evidence of his intense desire to assist struggling nationalities- No statesman has more honourably earned the rest to which he is now so justly entitled, and yet there never was a time when his services were more coveted by his country. Let us hope that the changes now taking place in the Cabinet may relieve the PRIME MINISTER to some extent, so that he may the better nurse his energies for the passing of those great measures of reform which ho has yet promised the country.
LOCAL ARTIFICIAL NAVIGATION. No. I.

Now that public attention is being directed to the Man: chester Ship Canal, we have gathered from various sources some little information respecting the artificial navigatious of the district, which we think will interest our readers. The canals or artificial navigations pining the Mersey, are the Weaver Navigation, Sankey Canal, Bridgewater Canal, Mersey and Irrrell, or Old Quay Canal, and the Shropshire Union Canal. Those, with their numerous branches and connections, permeate the country both north and south- wards, and for safety and cheapness of transit are no mean rivals to the railway companies. The Weaver Navigation seems to have beendeone of the earliest attempts to press into the service of the district a tortuous and unnavigable stream, the success of Which has been continuous and re- markable. The river Weaver derives its source from Ridley, Pool, close to Cholmondeley Hall, and pastes Nantwich, Minshall, Weaver, Winsford, and Northwich, where it is joined by the river Dane, from hence it turns westerly, and in a very eriading course flows to Frodsharn bridge below which it falls into the Mersey. It receives several tributary streams in its course, and has been made navigable by means of various locks and weirs. The plan upon which this was effected deserves to be noticed. The gentlemen of this county observing the vast expense of land carriage from the salt towns to Liverpool, and other maritime places, determined to make the Weaver navigable, and accordingly, In 1720, an Act of Parliament was obtained, which em- powered them to raise a subscription of £40,000 to defray the necessary expenses. The subscribers were to receive five per cent. on the principal, and one per cent. on the risk, and also certain instalments arising' from the tonnage of vessels on the river till the money advanced was reimbursed ; but afterwards the whole amount of the tonnage, when the charges ot necessary repairs and management have been deducted, was to be employed from time to time,,,for and towards amending and repairing public bridges within the county, and such other public charges, and in such manner as the magistrates should yearly direct. So great was the success of this venture that in a comparatively short period the debt was repaid and the surplas revenue devoted to county purposes. The length of this navigation is 20 miles, in which course it has a fall of 45 feet 10 inches divided by 10 locks. As showing the very large development of trade on the Weaver navigation we qaote by way of comparison from an account of the Inland Navigation Return to and from Liverpool in the year 1783,— "Between Liverpool on the river Mersey, and Northwich and Winsford on the Weaver, 110 vessels are employed in carry- ing timber, salt, coals, and merchandise to the amount of 164,000 tons annually. The carrying capacity of these vessels ranged from 20 to 100 tons burthen.:" The above account was published many years ago, and since that time subsequent Acts of Parliament have been obtained for im- proving the navigation with the result that it is now a ship canal for vessels of 300 tens burthen, many of which are propelled by steam; exclusive docks and wharves are situate at its janction with the Mersey at Weston point, and each recurring tide witnesses to its importance and ever- increasing trade. E. Leader-Williams, Esq., C.E., the engineer of the proposed Manchester Ship Canal, was for many years the engineer and .manager of the Weaver Navigation Trust, and it was under his direction the Widening and deepening of the Weaver As successfully accomplished. During his management a very remarkable hydranlic lift was erected at a point near North- wich, where the Trent and Mersey Canal and the Weaver are contiguous, though on very diverse levels, by ;which locks are entirely dispensed with and barges transferred fro.n the one canal to another with the greatest ease and dispatch, the modes operandi being two iron docks or caisons, into which the barges are floated, and being shut in by water-tiglet stops are either lowered or raised as cir- eurnstences require te the respective canals, the stops being then raised and the barges continuing the journey. The next in period of time is the Sankey Canal, which is said to be the earliest artificial navigation in England. It was begun in 1755, and opened in the following year. It leads from the coal pits of St. Helens to the Mersey at Widnes, and was cut for the purpose of conveying coals from St. Helens and district to Liverpool. Originally it joined the

Mersey at Fidler's Ferry, below Warrington, the length of thro-ani-a-half miles from thente to Widnes being cut in 1830. In its length of about twelve miles it has a fall of seventy-eight feet, with ten locks. The entire navigation was amalgamated with the st. Helens Rill way in 1845, and

passed with that railway into the bands of the London and North-Western Railway Company in 1864. Several years ago it was projected to still further extend it to the west side of Runcorn Bridge, and the excavation actually corn- manced, but from some cause was never completed. This extension would have secured a deeper and better river channel, with convenient docka' and warehouses on West Bank. Quoting from the before-mentioned "Account of Inland Navigation," the number of vessels employe in 1788 was about 80, with an annual aggregate tonnage of 115,888 tons.

present than it was 12 months ago, their funds will scarcely allow them to carry out the project without extraneous help. They, therefore, will be under the necessity of soliciting subscriptions, and I feel sure that there will be a hearty response to aid so worthy an object. I should like to know where Vie contractor to the Commissioners and his men have been during- the past few days. The footpaths and roads have been in an, if not unpassable, at least highly inconvenient and dangerous condition. 'Widnes Local Board, too, seems to have as little thought for the comfort of pedestrians ' for the footpaths in that town are equally bad. There is an adage to the effect that evil may be done that good may come, and the Genezal Purposes Committee of the Runcorn Commissioners seem to I have invented one of a somewhat similar tendency. It is to this effect: "Cheat the State to help your own finances." In order the better to accomplish this they say to the hawkers of vegetables in the town, "Pay us 4s. per month, and aid us in breaking the law, or we will prosecute you for not complying with its requirements." This, in my opinion, is the meaning of the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Board, .when Dr. MacDougall stood forth as the champion of the shopkeepers, and was in consequence quietly twitted with being a Protectionist by Mr. L'Ake. Runcorn ought to be grateful to the gardened and farmers of Frodsham and Helsby for larineing their produce into the towu and disposing of it at a cheap rate, as it was acknowledged they did. If it is a benefit to the seller it is equally a benefit to the buyer, and I would like to point out to Dr. MacDougall that, in the majority of cases, the gardeners and farmers return home with purchased goods almost equal in value witn the produce they have sold. FLACCITS.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK. —At 'Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. J. L. Evans and Mr. E. K. Muspratt, Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the School Board, appeared to presecuto a number of persons for contravention of the Education Act. The following were each fined ss. :—John McCann (two cases), Edward Mulvey. Archibald Grloyne, Thomas Dunne, John Shandley, Thomas Painter, Elias Roberts, John Johnson, and Elizabath Williamson. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—The forthightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present—the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner (in the chair), the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. George Whitlow, James Derbyshire, W. Picliering. Th6mas Norman, E. A. Wallington, John Weir, William Fisher, and William Handley.- The Finance Committee reported that they had examined accounts amountin!, to £4::) 13s. Id., which weve recommended to be paid. The usual Christmas fare was ordered to be provided for the inma.es. _

OBSTRUCTING FOOTPATHS AT RUNCAN : A WARN- ING.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, a young man, named James Gough, was summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 3rd December, unlawfully obstructed the footpath in Church-street.—P.C. Thompson stated the defendant was in company with a number of other young fellows at the time, and refused to move when requested to do so.—Defondant was fined ss. and costs.— Superintendent Williamson amid the police had a great deal of trouble with young fellows like the defendant in Run- corn. Frequent complaints were made to him of people standing on the parapet, but the offenders set the police at defiance. He did not bring these cases before the Bench unless the conduct had been very bad, but he should like it to go forth to the public that obstruction of the foot- paths would not be tolerated. A ItErENTANT Pniso:gra. AT RUNCOVl.—Oatherine Kenealy, a woman well known to the police, was charged at Runcorn Petty Sesssions, on Monday, with being drunk and disorderly in Lock-street on Saturday night, and , also with breaking one window of the house occupied by Joseph Pegg.—lt appeared that the prisoner was thrice ejected from Pegg's house, where she had been creating a disturbance. On the last occasion she smashed a pane of , glass.—For being drunk, the prisoner was fined 205., and fie. 41. costs, and for the wilful damage she was sent to gaol one month.—The prisoner, who could be heard send- ing forth dismal bowls in the cells long before she was placed in the deck, sheel "tears of repentance" during the whole of the time her case was being beard, and at the conclusion she was conveyed •‘ below" moaning dismally. HUTTON TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—A miscellaneous con ' cot, in aid of the Fluyton Temperance Society, was given on Tuesday evening in the Huyton Park schoolroom. The contributions to the entertainment comprised a musical party under the leadership of Mr. Joseph Cantor, the mem- bers of which were Miss Linda Cuthbert, Mr. S. Kirkham, Mr. E. Edwards, and Mr. Jimes A. Muir, while valuable service was rendered by Mr. Queen's glee party. The pro- gramme presented a varied selection of glees, part songs, and airs, by some of the best composers, and the audience testified their appreciation of the manner in which most of these were executed by frequent demands for repetition. In the course of the evening Mr. W. D. Stoha gave an amusing reading in the Laucashire dialect, descriptive of " Owd Billy Fitton's visit to the Earl of Derby." On the motion of Mr. E. S. Eccles, seconded by the Rev. M. Walker, a vote thanks was given to the performers' who gave their services gratuitously, and Mr. Queen responded on their behalf. The entertainment was altogether one of the most successful the society have had. WIDNES BRANCH OF THE CHURCH MISSIONARY SOCIETY. —The annual sermons on behalf of the Church Missionary Society were preached in Widnes Parish Church on Sunday by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, of London. On Monday even- ing a meeting was held in Waterloo-road school-room. end and there was a large audience. The Vicar, t!,e Rev. J. Wright-Williams presided. Amongst those present were the Revs. J. D. Thomas (deputation), W. H. Duggan, and Messrs. W. Treacey, J. B. unison, Balmer, Lord, Lc. In a short opening address tlee Chairman remarked that those who really believed Ctra God had sent Ills son into the world to save the world, should remember that as He was the light His people should at least be lights ; and those , who could not go forth as missionaries, had, neverthele.ss, opportunities of pushing forward the great cause in other ways. He pointed out that their collections on behalf of the missionary cause were not made in one big effort as they were by some religi sus bodies, but that they had no less than four societies in connection with foreign missions. He quoted figures showing that the sum raised for the mi:- sions in Widnes had gradually increased during the past few years. The collections on the previous day amounted to £lO 4s. Old., of which £3 131. Old. were the offerings of the children. He considered this a noble offering from the children to the Church Missionary Society. He had asked Mr. Lord to accept the post of secretary to the Widnes branch of the society during the ensuing year. and he hoped be would accept the office.---The Rev. J. D. Thomas related his experiences as a missionary in India, describing the habits and customs of the people.—A 'vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Thomas, on the motion of the Rev. W. H. Duggan, seconded by Mr. Treacey, and supported by Mr. Lord, who said having seen something of India, he could vouch for the truthfulness of Mr. Thomas's narrative. THE RAILWAY FATALITY AT RUNCORN: HoSPITAL ACCOMMODATION.—At the Coroner's Court, Dale-street, Liverpool, on Saturday, before Mr: Clarke Aspinall, an inquest was held on the body of Thomas Larkin, 34 years of age, residing at Newton, and in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway. Deceased, on Thurs- day last, was engaged at his occupation as platelayer outside Runcorn station, and when suddenly attempting to cross the line a passenger train ran over him, his leg being seriously injured. A doctor was sent for, after which, owing to there being no accommodation in Runcorn, deceased was brought to the Liverpool Infirmary, where he died.—The Coroner, in summing up the evidence, said it was a singulaily sad acci- dent, but from the evidence they had had it did not appear there was anybody to blame. The accident only proved what he bad said before, that accidents might take place in a way that was almost unaccountable. He, however, wishe'd that some of the populous places outside Liverpool would see their way to having more hospital accommodation than they seemed to have. He should himself venture to write to the authorities just snggesting that possibly they might see their way to do something in that direction. He knew enough of Runcorn people to know if they had anything of that sort pointed out to them they were likely to take the suggestion kindly, and what was still more im- portant, to act upon it in a practical way if the need really existed. He should, therefore write to the chairman of the Improvement Commissioners upon the matter.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." THE VICAR Or RUNCORN ON THS LATE PRIMATE.— The F mad G Companies of the Earl of Chester's Rifle Volunteers attended divine service at the Parish Church, on Sunday. The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., in preaching from the 10th verse of the cxliv. Psalm, adverted to the death of the Archbishop of Canterbury. He observed that if all who were soldie.re of Great Britain were also soldiers for Christ it would be of little moment whether they gave ' up their lives to God in the chamber of the quiet home or on the battle field steeped in blood, for "wherever the song was required, the language of the departing spirit still would be "I have fought a good fight. I have finished my course. I have kept the faith ; henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness. Such, if he might advert to a topic which, though not suggested by their subject, yet naturally occupied his own thoughts, might well have been the dying exclamation of him in honour to whose memory the oficials of the church had arranged that a misfiled peal should be rung on this Sunday after his decease. Re felt assured that no member of that congrega- tion, whether a constant worshipper or only an occa- sional visitor, would grudge such a tribute of respect to one who was for 14 years the chief pastor of the English Church, and who, as was universally allowed, dis- charged the duties of hie high office in a manner which commended him to men of all denominations and shades of opinion ; indeed, it might be said of him that he belonged to no party, for he was tkoroughly catholic. So while natural,y devoted lo the doctrine and discipline of the Church over which lie so worthily presided, yet he was tolerant to those who differed widely from him on theological points. He sympathised with almost every variety of Christian work, and cultivated the 'friendship of good men of the most divergent parties. Their chief memory, how- ever, was not of the high position be held as occupant of the chair of St. Augustine, nor of the talents which he used so industriously, but that he lived to do good through a long, useful, and honourable life, from which he had at length been called to his rest in the Lord, in whom he so absolutely trusted, and whom he so simply and fervently loved.

The town's meeting held at Runcorn, on Tuesday week last, performed a useful purpose in showing how strong was the feeling of the ratepayers against the mode of conducting Commissioners' elections which has hitherto prevailed. The war note was sounded that no longer should the community in its public afTairs be under the domination of one interest. The Examiner has frequently demonstrated. the injustice of.the system, the somewhat farcical nature of the nominations, the need of the ballot box, and of some organisation. To some extent the Ratepayers Association supplies the latter requirement. Its establishment was an indica- tion that the usual "fast and loose" fashion of election would have to give place to a better method, and it gives signs of having, unlike its predecessors, a healthy and vigorous existence. The committee includes many good men and true; and they have already set to work to rectify abuses and institute reforms. lamin a position to state that the Asso- ciation intends, if it has not already done so, to forward a petition to Government asking that elect- tions for Commissioners should be carried on under the Ballot Act, and I think that there is little doubt that so reasonable a request will receive imperial attention. The introduction of the ballot box would be a heavy blow at class interests, which, although then able to obtain their fair share of representation —and that they are entitled to a share nobody will deny—would be unable to over-ride the free will of the people. The Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association have broached a project which does them great credit. They intend shortly after Christmas to provide a tea for the old people of both sexes who reside in the town. No charge will be made, and, although the association is in a much better financial position at
