div.p: Twtttero to the xiitor.

AN EXPLANATION. Sir,—ln your report of the last meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners there appears a statement reflecting on me as the clerk of works for the new hospital. As I believe the statement must have been made under a misapprehension of the facts of the case, and as I was not even asked for an explanation, I have sent a letter to the chairman of the hospital committee, which will no doubt be read at the next meeting of the Board, and which I think will show their aaion to have been rather hasty, and calculated to do me (though it may be unintentionally) an injustice.—Truly yours, JOHN WILSON. Greenway-road,Runcorn.

THE SHIP CANAL TO MANCHESTER. Sir,—As Mr. Diggle felicitously remarked on Wednes- day evening, in reference to the chart of the Ship Canal which he had before him, "We are asked to be partners in this block-line," the said line being the course of the canal aN training walls from Manchester to Garston. Mr. Diggle sternly advised the principle of total abstinence in the matter; in fact, to abjure the canal and all its works. Without going so far as that, however, we might safely take a position of "temperance in all things," even in admira- tion of, and enthusiasm for, the Ship Canal scheme of Man- chester. In the fitiSt place, a reference to the map of the pro- posed canal in the Warrington district, discloses the fact that immediately after passing under the future high-level bridge of the London and North-Western main line, the canal ascends by locks to twenty feet above its former level, that is, above the level of the river, and it continues at this height for some miles beyond Warrington. Speaking diffi- dently, as in absence of fuller information one rg bound to speak, the result of this seems to be that the surface of the water in the great dock will be twenty feet above the level of the river, which is to be used as sabsidiary docks at this point, and to get into these subsidiary docks, twenty feet below the level of the groat dock, there will have to be further locks. That is to say, a ship bound for, say, the Mersey Mills, will sail up the canal from opposite Otterspool, go up twenty feet through locks at Walton, sail alonc, to the great dock, and then go down twenty feet through locks at the subsidiary dock. One would like to ask why are these locks put at Walton ? Would they not do quite as well a mile or so on the east side of Warrington rather than a mile or two on the west. If this harbour could be reached with- out any intervention of locks, and be quite open at all times to the tide, would it not be an advantage to Warrington, and ne loss to Manchester? Indeed, one is rather at a loss to see what particular good the *4 nal is to be to Warring- ton if vessels are to go up locks, and then go down 19(Ais; and then only get to the despised old Mersey after all. Look- ing anxiously for a little information upon this point, I am, your obedient servant, ENQUIRER. .I.sth Daceiaber, 1”2,

THE BRITISH WORKMAN PUBLIC-HOUSE COMPANY (LLMITED). Sic—ln the days before men built castles in the air and expected them to remain firm, a self-willed man, thinking to be in advance of his age, built a house chiefly made of apright posts supporting a substantial roof. the house served its purpose for a long time ; but, after a while, he thought to add to his accommodation by building another house a little distance from the first one. Now, instead of going into the woods and felling new timber or the new house he thought to show his skill in calculations and mechanical contrivances by constructing the second house eut of the surplus woodwork contained in the first, and thus demonstrate the truth of his (till then) new idea, that castles could not only exist in the air of imagination, but also in that of real substance. Had he been a wise man, he would have first seen whether there was any such surplus woodwork to spare; but lie was anxious to mike a display of hii cieVernag,7Bo he began gradually to take out, one by one, the props of the old house in order to set up the new one. A friend of his, " Libra "by name, (because he was fond. of keeping a just and even "balalaCe " in everything, especially in such matters as roof-supporting), often and anxious reasoned with him upon the madness of his design, but in vain. For, in truth, the clever builder prided himself in making a castle really an truly stand upon nothing, such was his confidence in his calculating and combining powers ! Doubtless, had he lived in these days, aid had been secretary to a coffee-house company, he woald have been crying "dividends" when there are no dividends, "profits" when there are no profits; and he would have thought that if he took a part of his working capital out of the concern, and (in spite of facts as natural and necessary to be allowed for as the heat of summer and the cold of winter) declared the part so taken to be profits, he would be doing an exceedingly business-like thing. But this builder lived long ago; for wlro now-a-days (when common sense guides all men's conduct) ever hears of a manufacturer taking all his surplus as prolt, without leaving wherewith to pay for broken or seed-up machinery, unless he gets up for a cuter person than ordinary! For I suppose nobody denies or even doubts that wear and tear does depreciate furniture to some extent at least, after a time. Heedless of the warnings of his friend, he continued to elaborate and construct one building at the expense of the other—fear- lessly livink in the old one all the time—till one night a strong wind from the desert blew on the weakened hailing, and, as its owner was quietly sleeping, and perhaps dream- ing of the still greater wonders he was to perform in the future, the fabric collapsed, burying the, philosopher in the ruins. So shall it be with the men of this generation, if, when they know that facts are against them, they say in the language of one if old, "So mach the worse for the facts."—Yours, DERVISH. Warrington, December, 1882.

THE BRINSMEAD CONCERT AT WARRINGTON. On Saturday evening a miscellaneous concert was given by the Br:nsmead Concert Company for the benefit of the funds required for founding and endowing the proposed Royal College of Music. We regret to record that, with this professed object, the efforts of the distinguished artistes who took part in the concert should have met with only scant support. Despite the attractiveness of the pro- gramme and the general excellence of its performance— qualities which might confidently have been predicted in regard to the concert—the Public Hall was not more than half full. The artistes were all of established repute, and ineluded Madame Sinico, Madame Mudie-Bolingbroke, Mr. Harper Kearton, and Mr. Frederick Bevan, as vocalists, and the Chevalier Niedzielski and Herr Heinrich Kohler in the respective capacities of violinist and pianist. Madame Sinico is a cantatrice of such well-known ability as to call for little critialtsm, adverse or otherwise. An encore being a foregone conclusien—as it provel on this occasion—to her performance of the bravura air "Roberto o to che adero," from Meyerbeer's opera, Madame Binico showed a wise discretion and at the same time demonstrated her versatility of style by selecting for the response "Home, sweet home," a ballad in every respect the direct antithesis of the excerpt just mentioned. Madame Mudie-Bolingbroke, though, perhaps, less knows to the musical world, is amongst the best of the contralto vocalists of the present slay. Her voice is of exceptionally rich quality, the tones of the middle register rivalling the chalumeau of the clarionet in mellowness and volume. "0, rest in the Lord," from Mendelssohn's Elijah, was sung by her with all the fervour and ;intensity of feeling "which should characterise this theme, perhaps the purest and most sublime which its gifted composer has left us. The songs, " It only " (Marzials) and " Joyous life " (Randegger), confirmed our high opinion of Madame Bolingbroke's singing. "The Angel at the window" (13. Tours) was the les opportunity the tenor, Mr. Harper Kearton, had of distinguishing himself. We must own to a feeling of disappointment, however, at his interpretation of this telling song, beautiful in its sentiment and masterly in its setting. Towards the close the many changes in tempo and marks of expression were almost entirely over- looked, and the whole performance lacked the finish of the artiste, easing the word in its truest _sense., "The old and the young Marie' (Cowen), Mr. Kearton 's second song, is a difficult one to render effectively on account of the some- what involved little story sought to be told in the words, and the obstacles—only partially . overcome-7hich. they present to musical treatment. Mr. Kearton did his best i• tbis song, and received the applause his efforts merited. Mr. Frederick Bevan sang " Hvbrias the Cretan" with the super- abundant vigour and in the robust bass voice which he must have who essays this very effective and clever song: ".The wreck of the Hesperus" (Weiss) tells with an audience rather by its graphic word-painting than the musical colour which has been imparted to the picture by the com- poser.. Mr. Bevan, however, gave more than an ordinary rendering, and secured prolonged applause. The per- formances of the vielinist were in every respect masterly. True, a certain extravagance amounting almost to grotesque- ness is the leading feature of Paganini's variations on "La Carnival de Venice," but these are indulged in only in the

exuberance of conscious ability to cope with the stern diffi- i culties and deep subtleties of "The Krentzer Sonata:: The Chevalier Neiclzielski possesses a command of the teehniczbe of his instrument which leaves little in the way of improve- ment to he striven for or even imagined. As a pianist,l Herr Kaler must rank high amongst the virtuosi of the' i day. We need only mention Chopin's Ifocturne and the 1 Finale to Mendelssobn's G minor Concerto played with the greatest refinement to attest this gentleman's taste and marvellous powers of execution. All the instrumental pieces were loudly applauded and manifestly enjoyed.

div.head: LONDON MISSIONART SOCIETY.
div.p: LONDON MISSIONART SOCIETY.

MEETING AT RUNCORN. In aid of this society sermon, were preached in Bethesda Chapel on Sunday; in the morning by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, and in the evening by the Rev. E. Le Mare, mis- sionary from Salem, gouth India. In the afternoon Mr. E. Le Mare delivered an address to the Sunday scholars. There were good congregations at each service. On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held in Bethesda chapel under the presidency of Mr. Joseph Bell, of Creasing- ton. On the platform were the Revs. E. Le Mare, M. Williams J. D. Thomas, and Mr. William Handley. The CrqIAIRMAST said the London Missionary Society had a history, and God had blessed it in a remarkable manner. He had been reading the report of the society and found that the work to be done was growing. The society was crying out for more funds. Those present were at home sat at ease, while the missionaries were hard at work in far- off lands, apd it was the least they could do to supply them with money and so encourage them in their work; and he always thought that when a deputation came from London they ought to try to make the meeting as large as possible, not only that they might themselves get good, but that the missionary might see that the people at home tookan interest in his labours. Of course they were all human and liked human sympathy, but there was a higher thing to look for which was the profession of Christ. Missionary meetings were to bins like milestones, which marked the various .stages in their lives. Many present had no doubt been privileged year after year to assist the society, and he himself could look back to the days of his boyhood, and the missionary meetings lie had attended seemed like milestones iu his life time. Much had been talked about hero worship. He confess.±.d that he had a sort of idol worship, and if he were asked who was his idol, he should tell them Robert Moffatt. (Applause.) From his boyhood to the present Vote missionary work had had a great hold of him, and ho always felt it a pleasure that they had such men connected with it. He could assure them that other countries were taking an interest in foreign missionary work. Recently difficulties had arisen in Madagascar with the French Govern- ment. No doubt France regarded with little favour the missionary work that was being done there, but he hoped England would take a loaf out of Oliver Cromwell's .book and see that there was no interference with the free publica- tion of the Gospel. (Applause.) The Rev. J. D. THOMAS said the London Missionary Society was founded gg years ago, when it was thought, during the first year, the income of the society might roach £l,OOO. Since that time the society Lad growl. List year the total income was £112,478 gs gd., and the expenditure amounted to £114,917 03 sd, an excess over the income of more than £2,0(0. This deficiency, however, was met by withdrawing certain monies which had been invested by the society, and when the accounts were closed in May there was a balance of over £l,OOO in favour of the society. This sounded very agreeable, bat it was not progressive. Mr. Thomas alluded to the fact more than one-half of the sum sent by Runcorn branch had been collected and given by the children. Owing to the opening up of new fields of labour, and consequent increase of missionaries, there was required £5,000 mere than 4ast year. Where was this to come from? They might depend that there would be a large deficit next May intim a, of course, contributions came from the churches and private individuals. He referred ti the motive which ong•ht to intluoacs them in giving, and said the London Missionary Society dig. not spread any sect, nor did it extend the powers of any denomination. Its aim was to send the Gospel pure dnd simple to the heathen nations, without fettering missionaries with aly ecclesias- tical polity. He exhorted them to be generous in their gifts to the society, because of what Christ had done for them, and for the blessings they enjoyed through Christianity. (Applause.) The Rev. E. DI Mann gave:many descriptions of mis- sionary work in India, where lie had laboured for several years, remarking upon its unique character and its difficul- ties. He said he was convinced that their work in India must be done through native agency, or Christianity would never be propagated to any great extent. The importance of education was touched upon. Mr. Le Mire observing that the whole of their departments of learning Were, adeording to the ideas of the people of India, and the teaching of their books, regarded as sacred. But education had made groat strides in the country, and the superstitions, idolatries, and mythologies, upon which religion rested, were being swept away and Christianity taking its place. He commented upon the fact that many of the people were materialists and atheists at heart, and that the works of Bradlaugh and other English atheists were being translated into the vernacular, and broupt forward in opposition to the teaching of Christianity. There was, however, great hope and en- couragement to be derived from the fact that many of the people of India, not only belonging to the lower classes, but persons of the highest caste, were Protestant Christians. (Applause.) The Rev. J. D. TnasLas said fine following was a list of subscriptions of the Runcorn Circuit :—Collections: Widows fund, £2 Os. 21.; new year's offerings, £9 Bs. 41. • school boxes, £9 12s. 4d.: subscriptions, £3 7s. ; collections, £l2 6s. id.; total, £3O 14s. 31 (Applause.) On the proposition of the Rev. E. WILLIams, seconded by Mr. Wm. HANDLEY, votes of thanks were accorded to the deputation and the chairman, and the meeting concluded.

div.head: RATING OF NEWTON LAKE.
div.p: THE RATING OF NEWTON LAKE.

JOHN LANE AGAIN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and Al C. MeCorquodale, John Lane, of Newton, was summoned, at the instance of the Newton Improvement Commissioners, to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to pay the sum of .£1 10s., improvement rate, for which he was assessed in respect of premises belonging to him in the township of Newton.—On the case being called, Mr. Gillespie observed that as he sat on the eomniittee at which the rate was levied he would leave the Bench.—Mr. Lane (the defendant) : You may tay, sir, if you want. Don't run away from shame.—Mr. Gillespie took a seat at the back of the Bench.---Mr. Worsley, solicitor, Warrington (law clerk to the Commissioners) said that he appeared on behalf of the Commissioners to demand payment from Mr. Lane of a rate which was laid by the Commissioners on the sth June last, and which amounted to the sum of £1 103. That rate was founded upon the poor rate, which was duly levied and signed by their worships on the 29th April last. The powers of the Com- missioners to recover its rates, he scarcely thought it neces- sary to state, were oreltntwn. They had power under their Act, which was the Act of the Newton Commissioners, 18th and nth Victoria, 'chapter 100 to lay certain rates, powers which they had exercised in proper manner as evidenced by the rate book. The mode of ascertaining the rate was laid down by the Act which stated that the rate was ascertained from poor rate. There was a course of appeal which any person di- satisfied with the rate could pursue, but in connection with the case in question that time had long since passed. There was also a clause that the rate book should be evidence. He would produce the rate book for the current year signed and allowed by their worships—Mr. Robert Houghton and Mr. Thcs..Comber—on the 28th April; and also produce the rate book of the Newton Commissioners under their seal duly passed and allowed at a meeting of the Commissioners on the 6th June. After doing so he would submit that they were compelled to make an order for the rate upon the de- fendant,—Mr. Henry Houghton (ensistent overseer and col- lector) was then sworn. He said he produced the rate book duly signed by the magistrates. He also produced the New- ton Improvement Commissioners' rate book which was duly allowed as stated. Mr. Lane, as appeared in the book, owed the Commissioners for current rates the sum of £1 103. He had made application for it. He had had a demand note. The rate was still due.—Mr. Lane: Da you mean to say that you sent me a bill for 303 for Commissionere'rates 7—Mr. Houghton: I have.—The defndant: Who by?—Mr. Houghton: By the boy in my office.—The defendant: What month 7—Mr. Houghton : I cannot state what month—it was sent directly after the dispute about the rate for 1881 was settled.—The defendant said he had never seen one.—Mr. Houghton said he possibly might not have seen it, because his daughter in- formed him that if any more papers about the Lake were sent to the'r house she would throw them behind the fire. He added that he had aever asked the defendant fcr it per- sonally except on the previous Monday week, when he asked both him and his daughter in his office.—The defen- dant: I should like to call a witness to that fact to prove whether he is right or wrong.—Mr. Worsley : That is a point that is not material.—The defendant: "Give me a chance of defending this, sir. If I cannot call a witness to prove what he says is false it is no use me coming here to stand my trial. I can prove that he is wrong.—He then handed up to the Bench some account he had received from Mr. Houghton, and asked them to "just overhaul that—we don't want any dirty work here." He continued a long statement, asking Mr Houghton if he had paid his rates, and stated that the latter had made a blunder in adding up the account he had given the Bench. He (Mr. Houghton) had also made two blunders about another summons he (the defendant) had received. He made one in making out the summons, and then took out another, but the magistrate made a mistake in signing, and he (Mr. Lane) had to put them both right before he could appear -before the magistrates. (Laugh- ter.)—The magistrates ultimately made an Grder for pay- ment within seven days. int

SUDDEN DELTA AT ST. HELENS.—About eleven o'clock on Saturday morning a very sudden death occurred in a St. Helens thoroughfare. James Johnson, aged sixty, who was employed as a vreighman at Messrs. Pilkington's glassworks, complained of being unwell, and another ma* was put at the machine to enable him to go home. He started, but befote he had proceeded far down Grove-street, he fell down and instantly expired. His body was conveyed 0 his late home, 83, Peachy Cross-lane. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA7aTTIDAY DECEMBER 16, 1882.

LIBERAL 'MEETING AT WARRINGTON, SPEECH BY MR. MCMINNIBS, M.P. A. well-attended meeting of Liberals of the South-West Ward was held in the Warrington Co-operative Hall, on Monday evening. Mr. J. G. McMinisies, M.P., presided, and he was supported by the Rev. R. Pitcher, 8.A., Rev. J. Tenge, Councillors F. Monks, Greening, and W. Pierpoint, Major Cartwright, Messrs. E. J. Guest, BA., M. Bowden, W. Burn, T. Birchall, A. Rathhone, S. Dunbobbin, J. Bonnet], G. Holford, W. Cresskill, and H. Roberts (secretary). Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from the Rev. Thomas Rippon, Councillor Platt, Dr. Smith, Messrs. Z. Armitage, C. S. Burgess, and F. Roberts. After the election of the Ward Committee, The Ceateumeer explained how it was he came to be in the chair, and after stating the next business was the election of the chairman of the ward, said: I am very sorry our friend Mr. Crosfleld does not feel himself st liberty to take the chair. I can hardly say lam sorry for the reason he would give if he were here, which is that he has the honour to le the mayor of Warrington. (Applause.) lam sure we are all glad to see him in that position. We are glad to see him in that position under all the circumstances of the case—(laughter)—which I dare sly may be more satisfactory to us than to some of our friends on the other side. (Laughter.) I have no doubt at all that Mr. Crosfield is, as he always has been, most earnest and zealous in the Liberal cause— (hear, hear) —and if it had not been for this fortunate circumstance he would have been here to-night. You will have to make the best of the matter under the circumstances. While I cannot undertake the office of chairman of the ward, I can, in the poeiton I now occupy, ask you to name a chairman, and I think I may say that you could not have a better ehairwa than Mr. John Crosfield. (Applause.) . On the proposition of Councillor Drxosr, Mr. Cromfield was re-elected chairman. Mr. W. Burn was re-appointed vice-chairman, and Mr. Wm. Cresskill secretary. The other formal business having been disposed of, Mr. BURN moved the following resolution :—"That this meeting of the electors of the South-West Ward begs to express its unabated confidence in John Gordon McMinniee, Esq., M.P., and its best thanks for his assiduous attestion to his parliamentary duties; and, further, pledges itself to use every possible legitimate effort to secure his triumphant return at the next election by a much increased majority." (Cheers.) He remarked that he took up a newspaper that day and fourld that Mr.McMinnies was sick, that he was tired of the job—(laughter)—and that he had not given that atten- tion to his duties which they required of him. (Laughter.) Now, that was eeid advisedly. But he did not think Mr. McMinnies looked ill—(laughter)—and he thought he would be the last man in the room to get tired. He thought Mr. McMinnies would not forsake the 529 yet awhile. (Laughter.) They had also been complaining of another matter, but he thought Mr. McMinnies was quite right in the course he had taken. There had been plenty of talking in the I:loupe withou him saying anything. (Applause.)- If they had talked less and done more work, there was no doubt we should have been in a better position to-day than we were. (Applause.) There had been a great deal of talk about Grand Committees and the Closure. People said Mr. McMinnies had helped to curry them out. There was so doubt he had, and wisely so, too, for they must bear in mind they were in operation in other countries. The "grand old man" had bees harassed enough, but he hoped he would live long, and that we should yet see some great and goad measures that would be of lasting benefit, and carry his name down to posterity. (Applause.) He then referred to their position in the Council, which he was sorry to say was not what it ought to be, and urged thorn to be true to their principles. He had pleasure in moving the resolution. (Applause.) Major Ceerrernisfar, who was greeted with applause, seconded the resolution. He remarked that nothing gave him greater satisfaction than to support the resolution that had been so ably proposed by Mr. Burn. Why did he support that resolution? Because ha believed in the gentleman:that they had betore them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McMinnies was what he termed an all-round man. (Laugh- ter.) He had no enemies—political enemies. Now that was a great thing to say. They would find, if they had followed him, as he had followed Mr. MoMinnies through his parliamentary career, he had always supported the Liberal party—(hear, hear)--stedfastly. There had been no equivocation. He said when he went up he went for the purpose, and he (the Major) was sure Mr. McMinnies had satisfied them. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He coupled with Mr. MoMinnies the new member for Liverpool, Mr,Salith. (Applause.) He verily believed there were no two mem- bers of the House of Commons who would be more straight than they would be. (Hear, hear.) He verily believed that Mr. Smith had won the election at Liverpool by his Integrity and straightforwardness. (Hear, hear.) He said at the commenc&nent what he meant, and he curried it out, and it carried him. (1 aughter.) He was straight to the backbone, and if a man went straight, in the long run, although he might meet with defeat over and over again, it would back him up. (Laughter.) Oh, he (the Major) had found that out. (Loud laughter.) There was no mistake about that. In his friend, Mr. McMinnies, they had a man as straight as an arrow. They would nearly always find him in his place, and if he was not able to attend, that must be, he felt certain, on account of his ailments. Well, they were all subject to that. (Laughter.) Whenever Mr. McMinnies had been at the elbow of the present Prime Minister he had supported him. (Hear, heat.) He went for a purpose, and he carried it out. They never found him deviating. He hadn't it in him. (Lanehter.) He was re- solute and so long as Mr. McMinnies thought proper, and Mal lit:111th would permit him to represent the borough in Parliament, nothing eould touch him. (Loud applause.) It was a true bill. (Loud laughtel.) Nothing could touch him simply for this reason his opponents thought vreil of him. (Hear, hear.) Well, reason, MoMinnies was the first mare that ever he knew who represented Warrington in Parliament whose opponents i.hought well of him. (Hear, hear.) Therefore they would easily understand the pleasure that he had in supporting the resolution that had been proposed by his friend Mr. Burn. He knew in supporting the resolution he was satisfied in his own mind, and he had always a greet deal of faith, that so long as Mr. McMinnies represented them they had nothing to fear. (Applause.) It was not aggrandieernent he sought; It was not that he wanted atone to pick. (Laughter.) He did not care one jot in regard to position. His position was simply that of member for Warrington, and he cared net so long as he felt within himself that he was doing his duty to his constituents; and so long is they had a man of that sort they should support him up to the hilt. (Hear, hear.) Me was worthy of it. He knew no better man, and so long as he desired to represent this borough there would be no "go" on the other side. (Applause.) They might rest contented about that, but they must not rest satisfied. Whenever the opporunity offered itself all they had got to do was to think of the past and look to the future, and support one of the best men that ever represented Warrington. (Applause.) The Rev. J. YONG 3 said at the risk of their thinking the Board of Guardians was going to consume the evening— (laughter)—the resolution haying been moved by a Guar- dian, seconded by a Guardian, and now supported by. a Guardian—(loud laughter)—he'would venture one or two remarks. He thought they were perfectly convinced that the resolution was true in every word. They felt in 1880 that there was no man like Mr. McMinnies. (Hear, hear.) They then did all they could to help him to success, and their efforts were crowned with glorious victory. He did not think there was a member of the Liberal party in War- rington to-day who regretted that victory--(hear, hear)— and who had any reason whatever to feel- any abated con- fidence in the hon. member for the borough. He believed that their increased acquaintance with him politically as member for the berough, had increased their confidence in him, and had wen for him a more earnest personal esteem than ever he possessed before. (Applause.) A little dog barked last week. He did not know whether it was in that room or the large one—the Public Hall—but somebody of the name of Kerr—he did not know him—(laughter)— carried out the well-known line of Dr. Watts, which said "Lot dogs delight to bark." He did not bite, of course. His bark was a great deal worse than his bite... He was pleased to say the hon. member for the borough —and, as Mr. Burn, had told them, he said it advisedly, though he was disposed to think it was one of those cases in which tie spoke unadvisedly with his lips—was sick and tired of his job. They could judge themselves that night of the sickness, although if the Cabinet secrets were before them perhaps they would know their friend was present at some little risk, inasmuch as he was suffering from cold, and if ho had taken his (Mr. Tonge's) advice he would have sent a little note instead of coming. But Mr. MeMinnies did not attend to his duty, and so he was present. He thought that was a suite sufficient answer to Mr. Kerr or any other cur who might bark upon that subject. He thought if gentlemen eroald take the trouble to read the division lists of the session just closed they would have anether reason to understand that their hon. member had not neglected his duty. He had attended more divisions than a great many younger men attended. He had been there all sorts of hours, and had attended, he thought, two-thirds of the whole num- ber of divisions which were taken in connection with recent important debates. Thirty-eight, if he remembered the figures correctly, was the number of divisions that Mr. McMinnies took part in, and when they remembered the whole member was only something like 60. he thought they ought to be proud that a gentleman like Mr. McMinnies exposed himself to all sorts of atmospheres, and at all sorts of hours to carry out their work in the House of Commons. (Applause.) After a reference to the Liverpool election, the rev, gentleman said some of them were amused that morning in looking over the Liverpool and Manchester papers to see references made to the probable retirement of Mr. Gladstone. That kind of thing had been told over and over again any number of times during the last two or three years. But they earnestly hoped he would be spared as Premier to carry with equal success all those other measures of a liberal character which he had fore- shadowed in days pest. (Hear, hear.) They should not for- get that the Liberal programme was only partly achieved, and it was to be hoped now the new rules were passed some other matters which had so long been in abeyance would be put iato effect, and Mr. Gladstone would have the proud honour of achieving new laurels for his immortal fame in this country. (Loud applause.) The resolution was carried with cheers. The CHAIRMAN, who was loudly cheered, said : Gentlemen, I am very mnch obliged to you for the kind, and I suppose I may say, unanimous m timer in which you have carried this resolution; and I wish also to express my thanks to the mover and seconder and supporter of it, for the kind terms in which they have alluded to me. I can hardly express the sorrow that I feel that my Parliamentary conduct has not been satisfactory to those who did not vote for me. (Loud laughter and cheers.) I shall have to be as

happy as I ":a in the knowledge that you have given me a vote, awl.. that the other wards have given me a vote that my crenduct has not been unsatisfactory to the Liberal party. (Hear, hear' and cheers.) I went to Parliament to support the Liberal Government, headed by Mr. Gladstone ' —(hear, hear)—and I have done it to the best of my ability, when I could conscientiously do so. (Hear, hear.) There had been circumstances, and there have been measures, when I have found myself unable to do that, but they have been few and far between. (Hear, hear.) During part of the seseion that had elapsed since the adjournment I have felt great interest in the proposed new rules of procedure, and while it is quite certain that I have not attended every division, because, you know, a fellow must feed sometimes, I have not been absent a single night from the House dun: ing the time that those rules of procedure have been con- siiered in that House. (Cheers.) I believe myself that whatever there has been that has made those rules less rigid and less strict has been a mistake—(hear, hear) ;—but I hope that they are still rigid and strict enough to make possible that kind of legislation which hitherto has been obstructed by those who are very anxious to obstruct all legislation whatsoever. (Cheers.) I believe that the Tories would be delighted if there was no legisla- tion whatsoever in the way of improvement. (Hear, hear.) That is my experience of them, and has been my experience all my life,—(laughter)—and I have seen a great deal of it during the last three years in the House of Commons. Well, now, gentlemen, I also have noticed, or it has been explained to me, that certain speeches have been made in Warrington during the last week at a great meeting of the Tory party. (Laughter.) I arn told that on that occasion there was a very eloquent speech made by it gentleman who saw great hope of promise for the future success of the party in the fact that they were so united. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) I remember reading an anecdote some short time ago of two gentlemen who lived in Boston named Charming, one the great writer and great divine of -that name, and the other was a medical man of the Same name, Dr. Channing. They were at a party one night, these two Channings, when the servant came in and said "Dr. Channing is wanted." The medical man got up, and he said " Which Dr. Channing—the man whe preaches or the one that practices ?" (Loud laughter.) Now, I am bound to say if. our friends on the other sid'e preach unity they don't practice it. (Laughter.) If you look at what has occurred to this great united party during the last six weeks—(laughter)—you will find that on one occasion they met together, recommended a candidate for a particular ward, and then the very next day they put up one of their own party to oppose him and thwart him, and he was returned, I believe, by the votes of the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) WelYthere is another instance of the harmony of this great united party which you saw on the 9th November, when two very able and very influential members of the party attacked one another in the Council Chamber with a fury perfectly remarkable to everyone there. (Laughter.) Then there is this gentlenten who sees in the union of his party such a great promise of success— this very gentleman himself, in order to pre- vent one of his own party being elected mayor, went and canvassed another member of his party to Stand as mayor in order to throw the other one out. How these Christians love one another! (Loud laughter.) I remember a story of a Mr. Mallam, who lived at 67, Wimpole-street, in London. He used to ask his friends to visit him, and he used to say to them at the same time "You will find us all at six's and seven's." Now I think the Tory party must live at 67 in some street, because not only here but elsewhere we ind them all six's and seven's. While it is very comforting to us and very encouraging to us to see all this, we should make a mistake if we think that it is certain to continue. (Hear, hear.) Ily experience of the Tory party is that they quarrel and make it up again, aid I think it is very likely We shall find this quarrel,and other quarrels probably, made up again. What we have to do is not to depend upon any difference that may exist in the ranks of our opponents, but to make ourselves safe in our own ranks. (Cheers.) I urn very glad to think that at these ward meetings a very large section of the working *less are takiag an interest in the proceedings if the party. We should make a very great mistake if we lest sight of the fact that political power now rests with the working classes (Hear, lean) When I began to take an interest in War- rington politics we had 700 electors in the town, all of whom paid at least £lO a year rent. We have now 7,000, and the great bulk of that increase is an increase on the part of the working classes. Now, what I want in the interest of the Liberal party is that the working classes should by a large infusion of strength increase the number of our sommittees, and of the managers of the party. (Hear, hear.) We shall do no good unless we have the working classes helping us in the management of this great party, and if we have you may depend upon it that our success hereafter is certain. It is a small matter to me, it is a s.nall matter to any men in this room, who represents the party in Parliament, but it is a great matter that the Liberal party should be represented in Parliament by somebody. (Hear, hear.) Therefore, it is that I am glad to see that at all these ward meet- ings the working class have taken an interest in the success of the Liberal party. So long as I have health and strength —(hear, heir)—and so long as you choose to extend to me that confidence which you gave to me in April 1850, I will serve you to the best of my ability,—(loud cheers)—honourably and honestly. If you choose to withdraw from me that confidence, I shall accept the withdrawal of it with regret, but also knowing that you had a perfect right to withdraw it if you thought I was not promoting your interest in the way I ought to do; but so long as you do extend to me that confidence, and so long as you cannot find a better man, I'm your man. (Loud cheers.) The Rey. R PILCIIE2 said he had had a resolution put into his hand quite unexpectedly. His friend Mr. Yonge had told them that the unexpected always happened. His friend was a Warrington Guardian. (Laughter.) But there was another "Warrington Guardian" that told them the other day, in a leading article, that the result of the Liver- pool election was not unexpected, so that they saw the -expected sometimes halipened. He had always noticed that when a certain class of men wanted to say what was untrue and did not want to tell a lie —(laughter)—they put their opinions negatively. They wpuld not say, for example, that the result of the Liverpool election was expected, but they would say that it was not unexpected. (Laugh- ter.) There was a nice distinction there, and perhaps to a Guardian's mind it might have proper weight, but perhaps his mind was not like that of every Guardian. He was not a doctor fir example—(laughter)—who supplied seraphic syrup to his friends and neutralic acid to his foes. If they wanted to see hew neatly the doctor interpolated this last all they had to do was to look round in unaccustomed corners, the epitome of news, for example, and they would see, AS he had done from time to time, with considerable curiosity, no end of sly kicks against the great man about whom he was about to move a resolution. ("Shame.") They had beard of the dog that was baying at the moon in Shakespeare; they had heard from Mr. Yonge of another dog that was bay- ing at their great local sun in this neighbourhood ; and it would occur to them also that there was another dog in Sankey-street that liked .to bay at their great central sun, the present Liberal prime minister. Well, it pleased him, and he (Mr. Pilcher) did not suppose it hurt the luminary at whom he bayed. (Hear, hear.) He was perfectly satisied of this, that the great mass of the Eaglish people, whatever their politics might be, had too much at heart the steady growth in the character of Mr. Gladstone (hear, hear) and the steady growth in the ~widening Liberal principles which he had shown, and the steady on-marc4 towards the carry- ing out of those Liberal pr'ipciples—(hear, hear)—there was not a man in this country, whatever his politics might be, but at heart felt proud that the country could produce a man like that. (Hear, hear.) It was, flung against Mr. Gladstone by my Lord Salisbury, and it was echoed by small local Salisburys (laughter) that Mr. Gladstone changed his opinions years ago. Well, this could not be said of the Tories. They made fools of them- selves 50 years ago, and they had gone on consistently making fools of themselves ever since. (Loud laughter.) It was no proof of wisdom that a man should continue in a given course. It might sometimes be a proof of mere pig-headed- ness and folly. When the great Peel saw that the time was come when the fetters on trade, and especially the fetters upon corn, should be removed, should he have said "I have always upheld the Corn Laws, and I must go on therefore rigidly to oppose them still ?" Why the ver- dict of the country long ago, the verdict of the Conservative party long ago, was that Peel was right, and they were wrong. And was Mr. Glad- stone, because he, by an unfortunate circumstance, happened to be born a Tory, and to be brought up a Tory, to sly " I shall love darkness better than light ? " and keep in the darkness of Toryism, or even in the twilight of Liberal- Conservatism ? Ah, no. Mr. Gladstone was a man of another mould. He was of such a type of mind that when a great truth seized hold of him he was forced to fohow and obey. He was perfectly satisfied that Mr. Gladstene's name and fame would live in history. —(hear, hear)—when all his detractors were dead and forgotten. The Jew in the " Merchant of Venice" said of a certain ring to which he attached tender memories, "I would not have given it for a wilderness of monkeys." So England in the future would say, when the name and fame of Mr. Gladstone came to memory, "I would not give such a man for a wilderness of Salisburys,"—(ap- plause)—and they might throw into the bargain 10,000 wildernesses full of Churchills. (Hear.) He had pleasure in moving this reselution :—" This meeting desires to offer to the Right ,Hon. W. E. Gladstone, Her Majesty's Prime Minister, its heartfelt congratulations on the jelii:ee of his parliamentary life, and fervently hopes he may long be 'spired to preside over the destinies of this great nation." I (Cheers.) Mr. M. BOWDEN secohded the resolution, and said if ther e was one man in this nation he esteemed more than another it was William Ewart Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone was not what he should call a class man, and he fancied that was why the Tories did not like him. He was not a man who would not undertake anything for the benefit of a certain class. His work was broader than that. (Hear, hear.) He worked for the general good of the majority of the nation —(hear, heat,)—and that was why he honoured him. (Cheers.) Mr. E. J. GUEST, in supporting, said he believed Mr. Gladstone would be pleased to receive that resolution from them, and he deserved it at their hands. Above all, Mr. Gladstone was a true Christian, and Christianity was at the basis of oar 'social fabric. It was only as Christian prin- ciples were maintained in the country that we should be a great country, and those principles were defended and expounded by Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) The CHAIRMAN pordially endorsed all that had been said, and remarked that it was a delight to him to support Mr Gladstone's measures in Parliament.
The resolution was carried with enthusiasm.

On the motion of Councillor MONKS, seconded by Mr. H. ROBERTS, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Mc'Hinnies for presiding. The CHAIRMAN, in reply, said he had met with nothing but kindness from the Liberal party since they did him the honour to return him as their representative in 1880. He would be glad in any capaeity to serve there, and he hoped all their efforts as a Liberal party would in the long run lead to the extension of just and opal laws for every one of the three kingdoms. (Cheers.) The meeting then terminated.

WESLEYAN METHODIST TEMPER- ANCE SOCIETY, RUNCORN. In common with all the Wesleyan Methodist Chapels throughout England temperance sermons were preached at the Wesleyan Chapels in Runcorn on Sunday. In the morning, the Rev. J. Robinson in St. Paul's, and the Rev. Geo. Hack in the Halton-road chapel, delivered a sermon on temperance, the latter minister also delivering a sermon hav- ing special reference to teetotalism in St. Paul's in the even- ing, when there was a large congregation. On Tuesday evening the annual temperance meeting in connection with the circuit society was held in Brunswick School. There was only a moderate attendance, Mr. J. R. Frith presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. George Hack, Mr. T. Simister, and Mr. S. C. Beckett. The Cream- KAN said it afforded him great pleasure to say a few words upon the temperance question. He recollected the thne when the temperance cause was a feeble one; when the advocates of temperance were looked upon with disdain, were almost thought to be a little out of their mind; but the time had arrived when people began to think that those who were not temperate were a little beside themselves. Out of small beginnings some of the greatest results had been achieved. If the history of our country was reviewed, it would be found that from small beginnings great results had followed, and those who commenced the crusade against drunkenness were not afraid of their small beginning, bat, like noble warriors, although hard pressed on every side, they were not ashamed of having taken up the cause, and, in the midst of difficulties, fought it to the bitter end. And those who had lived through any years and fought hard were rejoiced at the present time to see that the little one had become a thousand and the small one a great people. They remembered that a few years ago the Wesleyan Conference would not take any step towards helping on the cause of temperance, most of their ministers were opposed to it, and most of the people in connection with the Wesleyan denomination were opposed to the for- mation of temperance societies. But leo4 had times changed; and it was now with pleasure they read in the minutes of conference that that day was set apart for the special crusade against drunkenness. Last Sunday was set apart by conference for special sermons to be preached by the ministers, and he trusted they were all as faithful as Mr. Hack was at Halton-road on Sunday morn- ing. They had a good many ministers now aesongst them who were not ashamed to wear the blue ribbon—(applause) —but stood forth boldly stating they believed in the temperance principles, and were forwarding the cause as fast as they conld. When they thought of the formation of the societies in connection with Wesleyan Methodism, one was almost astounded at the number of members which were enrolled in the societies throughout the country; it was something marvellous. Mr. Frith referred to the result's which could be obtained by perseverance, and re- marked That they ought not to be disheartened when they had difficulties to deal with in the temperance cause, be- cause they had not only the welfare of the bodies of their fellow creatures in mind when they went forth in this crusade against intemperance, but they had also the welfare of their souls in mind. How hard it was to see some of the youths of their Sunday schools, when they attained manhood, become drunkards. He adverted to the many better Uses to which the money spent in drink could be applied, and exhorted them to help on the good cause, and they would soon see the public-houses closed on the Sabbath days, and he hoped, by God's help, on every day in the week. (Applause.) He was glad that the temperance question had been brought forward so prominently in the Liverpool election. (Hear, hear.) Ho rejoiced greatly at the result of that election—(applause)—net because he was a Liberal, but because his heart and soul were in the tem- perance cause. (Applause.) Mr. SIMISTRR, in an earnest addrese, remarked that he had been a total abstainer for 43 years—(applause)—and he Saw more reason every day why people should embrace the principles of teetotalism. The Rev. Gam. Hacx related several incidents of the evils arising from drunkenness which had come under his own observation, and concluded by referring to the Liver- pool election, which he thought was a grand sign of the times. It was a remarkable thing that at the last general election, when the beer interest was arrayed against the present Government, the Government went in with a majcrity almost unparalleled in the history of any Govern- ment, and it was a remarkable thing that at the recent Liverpool election when the whole of the beer interest went against Mr. Smith, Mr. Smith was victorious. (Applause.) He was thankful for that election on that account, and also for another reason. There had appeared. articles in the Liberal and in the Conservative papers commenting upon the election. The Liberals said it was testimony to the wisdom and ability of and confidence in the Government, and the Conservatives tried to minimise the whole thing. He read both papers but he had his own opinion, and he hollered that Mr. Smith carried the election because the Liverpool people recognised in him a man of worth, of integrity, and of Christian principles. It was a grand sign of the times that men of principle and integrity, men who came before the country with an honest pro- gramme gained the confidence of the large constituencies, and by and bye they would gain the confidence of the smaller constituencies. He rejoiced because Liverpool had sent a man to Parliament who was thorough going in his temperance principles. (Applause.) The meeting closed in the usual way.

NEWTON, IIAYDOCK, AND GOLBORNE BUILDING SOCIETY. The ntans,Ypers of the above society have issued a circular to the members, in which they clearly set forth the state of affairs. It will be remembered that the annual balance sheet, issued in May, showed a large amoint of capital " written off," as loss on property in the society's hand. The amount was ascertained by having the whole of the property revalued, and comparing the revised list with the amount originally advanced and the subsequent expenditure in repairs and improvements. The revaluation was 'unwel- come to those pecuniarily intereated, but as a business undertaking the course adopted by the managers was sound. Many members, however, decided to withdraw their investments. The ',tanagers, anticipating a run on the society, decided (in accordance with tke rules) to retain 20 per cent, from all with- drawals, Which had the effect of materially reducing pressing claims. From May to November, including with- drawals unpaid at last balance, notices of withdrawals.have been received to the extent of £8,731 7s. id. Taking 20 , per cent, from this the figures are reduced to £6,985 is. Bd., and this sum is further cut down by £1,588 55.*81 already paid to withdrawing members, leaving £5,306 16e. still to pay. At all the meetings the withdrawing members were strongly advised to cancel their notices, and notices were cancelled tO the amount of £2,100, which is not included in the above figures. Commenting on the present state. of the affairs, the managers say :—" The solicitors have, as a matter of legal security, advised the trustees to withdraw their guarantee for overdraft at the bank for the present. It would appear that the managers cannot borrow money to lend on mortgage or make any advances until the with- drawing members are paid off or their notices can- celled. The members will see the difficult positidia in which the management is placed. New business cant not be transacted until all the withdrawing members are paid or have cancelled their notices. The monthly receipts of the society are about £430, so that it must take a considerable time to pay off the present notices, and in the meantime the solicitors advise that a dividend cannot be declared under existing circumstances. The managers are doing their utmost to raise money to meet their liabilities, but think it would be unwise to make forced sales of property in these depressed times. They are, however, pleased to say the Tyldesley property has been sold for £1,030, which sum is a little under the recent valuation." The circular continues: "The managers consider the respective properties well worth the attention of members desiring investments, the valuations having been made at the present low price ruling, and there is every probability of a considerable rise in their value in the next few years." The managers have declined to dismiss Mr. Adams, secretary, as decided by the shareholders, and they will, as a body, resign at the next general meeting.

ARRIVAL OP Brrrna OnatiGms.T,The steamship Roelas, which arrived in the Mersey on Monday night, direct from Seville, brought the first consignment of bitter oranges, so essential to the makers of. genuine marmalade, numbering 600 cases, to the order of Mr. W. P. Hartley, for his exten- sive and celebrated works at Bootle. SXITING Rice AT Bum/gem—On ,Wednesday afternoon last a considerable number of persons assembled on the Car Mill dam, Billing?, to witness a skating race between a young man named Gaffeney and another young man re• siding at St—Helens. The race was for £5 a side, and the distance one mile. The ice was not as smooth as could have been wished, owing to the snow, with which it was coverel, and Ivhicb had to be wept off before the race took place. Gaffeney skated extremely well, and keeping a lead nearly the whole way, won very easily. WHAT IS A WELsnua P—This was a question which the Court of Queen's Bench had to decide on Saturday. Counsel indulged in a variety of speculations, but Mr. Justice Cave pronounced an explicit opinion, and the jury showed by their verdict that they regarded it as an objectionable term. The litigants, were Mr. William*, a photographer in Hol- loway, and a licensed victualler at the Cottenham Arms, Holloway-read. The parties had known each other for some years, and quarrelled over' a bet, the publican claim- ing £6, and the photographer refusing to pay more than .£5. When next they met'at Alexandra Park races, Mr. Williams was accused of being a welsher, and was turned out of the ring, in consequence of which be said his business had suf- fered. Accordingly he brought an action for slander. After an argument as to the meaning of welsher, the judge held that it was an indictable offence to call a man by that name. For the defence, it was denied that the words had been used, and, if they had, the counsel contended that they did not have the meaning attributed to them. The jury, however, returned a verdict for the plaintiff—damages £2o.—LloYd's Newspaper.

ASHTON. CONCERT AT HEATH-LANE SCHOOLS.—The second vocal and instrumental concert, in aid of the funds of the St. Thomas's brass band, was given in the South-lane schools, Ashton, on Monday evening, before a fair and appreciative audience. The vocalists were Mrs. Nicholson (Manchester), Miss Murgatroyd (Downall Green), Mr. George Wright (Earlestown), the St. Thomas's glee and quartette party, and Mr. J. William (Ashton), the popular vocalist and comedian. The instrumentalists included

Messrs. Smith, T. Livesley, J. PiEing, and R. N. Smith. The violinist was Mr. Thomas Liveslev, and Mr. Thomas Cook ably accompanied on the pianoforte. Mrs. Nicholson gave the songs "I cannot sing the old songs" (Claribel), " Thy face" (Wrighton), "Killarney " (Balfe), and "The bridge" (Lindsay), all of vvtlich merited and receiyed the hearty commendation of her hearers. Miss Murgatroyd sang with her accustomed ability "Darby and Joan" _ _
(Molloy) and "You and I" (Claribel). Mr. George Wright thoroughly established himself as

a favourite with the Ashtonians and his songs, "The old brigade" (Barri), "The three sailors" (Marsden), and " " were rapturously applauded and received deserved encores. The ever popular Mr. Williams created prolonged applause and amusement by his comic songs, "Mander's menagerie " (Hunter), and " Poor Mr. Wright," and it is almost needless to add that he was heartily encored. Messrs. Livesley, Holbrook, and Smith very creditably gave "Ye shepherds tell me," a trio which was much appreciated. A violin and pianoforte duet, " Dm Giovanni " (Mozart), and another entitled " William Tell" (Rossini) were excellently given by Messrs. T. Livesley and Cook; as were also the instrumental quartettes " Return of spring" and " Reaper's chorus," by Messrs. W. Smith, T. Livesley, J. Pilling, and R. N. Smith. The glee party very efficiently performed their part of the concert and the glees, "Oh, who will o'er the downs" (Pearsall), "Life's a bumper" (Wainwright), and "Ye gentlemen of England" (Callcott) were duly appreciated. The proceedings were brought to a close by the singing of the National Antkem.
CONGLETON. Attention is being called at Congleton to the pollution of . _ _ _ _

the river Dane, which is contamin-ated by the influx of sew- age matter from the town. Congleton School Board finds itself in authority over 27327 children. A committee is about to pay a visit to the arions schools to ascertain whether the provisions of the Yducation Act are being carried out. FRODSHAM.

Prtonsirem MUSICAL SOCIETY.—The first concert of the season, in connection with the above flourishing society, was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Wednesday evening. A capital programme had been prepared, but owing to the severe weather there was not such a large atten- dance as could have been wished, although there was a good number in the reserved seats. The principals were Madame Bellinie Porter, Miss Frances Armstrong, and Mr. Eaton Batty. The first part of the programme was Van Bree's cantata, entitled "St. Cecilia's day," the scene being taken from Frascah, described as a beautifully-hilly coun- try in the neighbourhood of Rome at sunset, and a number of youths and maidens are supposed to be binding wreaths to deck the marble statue of St. Cecilia. This theme has inspired the poet, and has been arranged in a number of choruses and recitations, the words of which pay a fitting tribute to "music's magic sound. The choruses are of an inspiriting character, and were given by the members of the society, numbering 61 voices, in a manner which left little to be desired. The success was doubtless due to Mr. Argent's energetic teaching; and the perfect confidence which all had in his leadership showed itself in the due observance.of time and expression, resulting fn a perfect harmony of the various parts, which was most enjoyable. Although the audience were at first somewhat apathetic, the excellence of the performance soon created an interest, and secured Well-merited ap- plause to the praise of St. Cecilia. In the recitatiyes Madame Bcilinie Porter showed that she was a cultured and finished vocalist, and did full justice to the classic4l music allotted to her. The second part of the programme *paned with "Maypole dance," a duet for pianoforte and harmonium, by Mrs. H. E. Heywood and Mr. W. J. Argent, whieb displayed considerable ability and in its rendition the perfect harmony was united with a pleasing and artistic interpretation of the fantastic spirit of the dance. Miss Frances Armstrong was fairly successful ia "Darby and Joan" and "The lost chord," but the latter song was not sufficiently well sustained to shine above the brilliant accompaniment on the pianoforte and harmonium. In the song "Golden love" Madame Bellinie Porter i secured an encore, when she responded with the "Three old maids of Lee," which was redemanded. Mr. Eaton Batty was at once a favourite, and the pathos and culti- vated intonation in "'The raft" brought down the house with an enthusiastic encore. Mr. Batty was equally successful in "The postilion," and an encofe was again elicited. The members of the society occupied a prominent position in this part of the programme, and Rossini's chorus "Faith," fortunate voices, was encored and kindly repeated. The part song "Come, Dorothy, come," was highly crzditable, although some slight hesitation was observed at the commencement. The success from a musical point of view of the second season of the society augurs well for the future, and it is to be hoped that the public will show their apprecaiation of the labours of the society by patronising the concerts. ANNOYING A GOLBOXNE TRADEMIAN.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, before It. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquodale, Ems., John Cooke, a draper at Id olborne, was summoned for assaulting a lad named William Roberts on the 3011 Nov.; and George Roberts and James Roberts were summoned for using language calculated to provoke a breach of the peace, to John Cook.—Mr. Moors, solicitor, of Warrington, ap- peared for Cook.—A large number of witnesses were called, the evidence showing that the defendant Cook is a draper, and during the last few "weeks he had been considerably annoyed by lads opening the shop door and then running away. On the date in question he was in his shop, when someone burst open the door, and he ran outside. The lad William Roberts was then in the street, and Cook seized hire. It was alleged that he used unnecessary violence to him by throwing him down and dragging him across the street. This was denied, it being asserted that the lad threw himself to the door and refused to give his name. On behalf of the Roberts, the witnesses stated that the lad did not touch the door; he was simply passing on his way from school. When the lad returned horns he informed his father, George Roberts, and a brother of the latter, the defendant James Roberts. These two went down to'Mr. Cook's shop about the matter, and the parties came to high words, during which the, Robert's accused Cook of being "a liar."—After hearing all the evidence, the Bench dismissed both cases.

DRIIX.MINNESS.—At the Newtos Petty Session, on Satur- day last, John Walsh was charged with being druik and disorderly in Queen-street, Golborne, on the 25th November, and was fined Sc. and costs.—John Charles was summoned for being drusk and disorderly at Golborne, on the 25th ult. The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and two sureties of .L 5 each, or in default, 14 days' imprisonment. THB COIsTSIARTATITES OF nOLBORKE DISAPPOINTS:M.— Under the auspices of the Golborne Workingmen's Conser- vative Club, a public lecture should have been delivered in Mr. Brewis's school-room, on Wednesday evening last, by Mr. Walter Pierce, of Liverpool. The announced title of the lecture was "The poetry and literature of Ireland," though it was locked upon in some way as covering the ground for an attack on the Liberal Government and its Irish policy. During the week, however, Mr. Pierce sent word that he was iIL, and was not sure whether he would be able to attend. On Wednesday, a telegram was received that he could not come, and the ".bellman "was accord- ingly sent round the village announcing that the lecture would not be given. It is stated that Mr. Pierce said he would fulfil the engagement at an early date. HATDOCK.

NEGLECTING TO SEND CHILDREN TO SCHOOL.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, Thomas Garland, Thomas Blundell, James Porter, and Enock Jackson were each ined 53. for neglecting to send their children to school as required by the Elementary Education Act. ?ITCH AND Toss.—Before R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington. and A. C. -McCorquodale, Esqs., at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, James Swain and Thomas Pilling, young men, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss at Haydock. on the 26th November. They pleaded guilty, and were each fined 10s. and costs. HavDpcx WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—On Sunday last, speoial services were held in Haydock Wesleyan Chapel, in con- nection with the "temperance recommendations" of the Wesleyan Conference. Both morning and evening the ser- mons were specially devoted to temperance, and in the afternoon a temperance meeting was held in the Sunday school, and interesting addresses were delivered. ACCIDENT AT HAYDOCE.—EarIy on Thursday morning, a miner 'named King, residing near the Ram, met with a serisus accident whilst following his employment in the Rain pit. A large stone fell from the roof and knocked King down. Fortunately it did not fall upon him, or the conse- quences would have b3en much more serious. As it was, his back was severely bruistd, and it was found necessary to convey him home on a stretcher. Dr. Hayward is attending the unfortunate man. ANOTHER Weans DisPtrrn. Another dispute has recently arisen between the firm of Richard Evans and Co. and a portion of their hands. On former occasions the difficulties have generally been with the men, but on this occasion it is the women, or girls, as th_y are commonly called, that have caused the dispute,, which has so far advanced as to result in a strike. The girls applied for an advance of their wages, but as the firm did not see fit to grant it the girls left work on Wednesday. Their places were filled by some of the men, who at present are doing the girls work.

_ WIDIiES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held in Alfor,e_ Chambers, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. Gossege (chairman), Shuttleworth, Sadler, _ Web Johnson, Martley, Ailidwood, Wright, Forster, ,H Pankhurst, Carey, Kershaw, Dr. O'Keeffe, _ , and Mr. Allen (clerk). SPECIAL MEETING. It wai decided that the Board shoe' ...14 "Met i'hursday, the 22nd inst., to appoint the s,taff TEE CIIAIRMAN 11--xittruGl4. The CIIAIRIIAN thanked the Board in st-itahle terms for the resolution pared a' the last meeting congratulating him on his marriage. TICINCY ON TEE BOARD 07 UPPER MERSEY COMMISSIONERS. A lette7: Was read from Mr. Collier reporting a vacancy 0,,n ti',, above-flamed Board, and it was resolved that Mr. txcesage be re-appointed to fill the vacancy.—The CHAIR- MAN said he was very glad to accept the office again, especially as he expected there would Ise some very import- ant matters brought before the Commissioners, as nothing could be done with regard to the Ship Canal without the sanction of the Mersey Trust. MR A. BEAsLEY AND THE BOARD. The CLERK was proceeding to read a letter which he had received from Mr. Beasley, when Mr. KER3EIAW interrupted and protested against a private letter being published, and he complained that a great deal of correspondence had been published of late that ought not to have been.—The CHAIR- MAN thought that no member could judge whether a letter ought to be published until he had heard it read.— Mr. KERSHAW : Certeinly.—After a little conversation it was decided that the letter be published.—The CLERK then proceeded to read as follows :—Westlands, Bolton road, Goor Park, Chiswick, London, December Bth, 1882. Dear sir,—When I gave authority, for the amount due by your Board to my brother and myself to be paid over to the trustees of his estate, it was on the understanding that the money would be immediately paid, and I am surprised to find that this has not been done. I have, therefore, to give you notice that unless the money is paid evti forthwith the authority I gave for the payment to be made to Messrs. Gibson and Bolland will be revoked, and without further notice I shall Like such proceedings as I may be advised to recover the amount. It will be unnecessary for you to reply to this letter unless yours contains a remittance of the amount, or an intimation that it has been paid over to Messrs. Gibson and Bolland, as I have no desire to enter into lengthy correspondence with a person who publicly dis- cusses and publishes private letters.-1 an, yours truly, A. BEasnEer.—The CLERK said he bad written the following reply, dated Dece.uaber 11th :—I have yours of•the Btl7, which I will read, with this reply, at the Board meeting to- morrow. The only private letter I have had from you was dated October 4th, and I entirely deny that I at any time publicly discussed or published" it.—l am, sir, yours obediently, J. T. ALLEN.—The CHAIRMAN said the course Mr. Beasley had taken was a very uajustifiable one for any man of business to take,—a sentiment which was expressed by other members of the Board. GAB ANL) At a meeting of this committee, held on the Ist instant, the ENGINEER reported that the pumping engines both at Stock's Well and Netherley had, during the past month, worked in a satisfactory manner. The Glenfield Co. offered to deliver in Widnes a water meter testing apparatus for £ll ss. Tyrnwy main branch : A. letter was read from Mr. G. F. Deacon (Liverpool Corporation), stating that instructions bad been given to pat in the branch for Widnes supply at Barrow's Green as requested. Bore tubes, eitc., No. 1 Stock's Well : Letter read, dated 30th November, from Mr. Timmins, asking the Board to pay £27.155. instead of £2O as offered • and it was recommended that the offer be increased to £.25 in settlement, the tubes, etc., to be left as they are. Gas Werks offices: The agreement with the Widnes Alkali Co. was read and approved, and it was recom- mended that it be sealed. The Eegineer submitted plan of proposed alterations, and tenders for the joiner work for same. It was recommended that the tender of Messra. J. W. Carlile and Co. ba accepted. The Widnes School Board asked fotka tender for the supply of ceke to the Board schools, from Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., for 80 tons or any - lesser quantity per week, and from Mr. B. S. Biram for 1,000 to 1,200 tons during 1883. It was recommended that the School Board be quoted 75 64 per ton in the yard, and that the others he informed that the Board is not in a position to contract for large quantities over the year.—Mr. H. WYATT complained that the water in the well on John Smith's farm, • Tarbock, had been muddy ever since the main between Netherly and Stock's Well was laid, and asked that the Board would bear the expense of pipes for supply from main, the tenant to pay the water rate.—lt was recommended that the supply be given on the usual terms.—ln reference to Mr. lilidwood's complaint, which was referred to this committee, the late foreman (Hillyer) gives the following information : —"On 17th August, 1882, James Prescott, Windermere- street, reported a leakage. Report CAI be produced. On 24th August, notice to repair was served upon Mr. Midwood by Hillyer, who placed it in his letter-box. Counterpart of notice and timekeeper's endorsement of service by Hillyer can be produced. On 34st August, the work not haying been done, the engineer gave instructions to do the work, which was completed on the 4th September. Hillyer further states that the service was not properly laid in the firet instance, that as soon as the leakage was repaired and the water turned on, that the pipe burst in another place, that then a length of four or five feet of pipe was put in with a similar result; the plumber (Shepherd) then reported to the engineer and was instructed to re-lay the service. A. piece of the pipe was carefully retained in case of dispute." Mr. PANKIIIIRST moved the adoption of the minutes, and this was seconded by Mr. FORSTER.—Mr. MeDwnon said, in reference to the „minute respecting the agreement with the Alkali Company, that he understood when the Gas Com- mittee considered this question some time back, the altera- tion should be agreed to providing it *cost the Board nothing. In regard to the minute respecting his complaint, he denied that any notice had been eerved upon him, and he looked upon the counterpart simply as waste paper.—Mr. PANKIIIIRST said that in regard to the occupation of the office, all they bad gone in for was supplying the engineer with an office to do his work in. Everything that the Alkali Company would want would be provided by themselves.— In answer to a question, the ENGINIER said that the two officials employed to look after the waste of water were simply useless, and he had found it neceesery to discharge them. He had appointed one of the outdoor men to the work, which was now being done in a more satisfactory manner. Every tap under the Board could, under the pre- sent arrangement, be examined once every six weeks.—The minutes were passed.
Ali
hIGHWAY COMIIITTEE.

Mr. KERSHAW proposed, and Mr. SADLER seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of this committee. Among other things they contained the following :—Accounts, amounting to £32 3s. 3d., examined and passed for pay- ment. Wages estimated for next four weeks, £25 per week. The wages book and statement of expenditure submitted. A letter was read, dated 21st November, and plan of pro- posed alteration to gates at Waterlco-road Crossing, received from the London and North-Western Railway Co., per Mr. Worthington WAS submitted and recommended for approval as a temporary arrangement. The clerk's letter in reply stating the foregoing, and urging that a bridge be at once erected was submitted and approved. Correspondence on the Mersey-road Ferry Approach from 1877 to 1882 was submitted. The railway company refused to contribute to- wards the cost of making good the approach.—The SURVEYOR reported having called Mr. Bibby's attention to the bad state of the footpath in Ann-street, East, to Moss Bank. A letter was read, dated 16th November, from Mr. Bibby, in reply, denying his liability to repair. The Clerk was instructed to reply. It was recommended that Ann- street, East, be declared a public highway, repairable out of the general district rate. Plans of a house for Mr. J. C. Frances, and a house for Mrs. Arnolds, Gladstone-street, were approved. At an adjourned meeting, held on the 4th Inst., a letter dated 30th November, from Mr. Worthington (London and .North-Western Railway Co.) was read agreeing to pay £2O for flagging the footralk at Waterloo-road level crossing, and asking that this work be completed before the gate alterations were commenced. It was recemmended that the flagging be done, and that the road pavement adjoining be taken up, and relaid with macadam. It was recommended that the minute of 26th January, 1882, asking for gates the full width of the road, and that all shunting be discontinued, be rescinded, and the gates (two wicket and one main) as per plan, approved at the last committee meet- ing, be adopted instead, the shunting to be reduced to a minimum, and the main gates to be kept open except when shunting is going on. The Railway Company's plan of pro- posed alterations at Ann-street level crossing was considered, and it was recommended that it be referred to the General Purposes Committee with a suggestion that the gradients to the bridge should not be less than one in thirty, and that an approach road be made from Ann-street West. A plan of the Lancashire Plateway Company was submitted and can- sidered. It was recommended that it be referred to the General Purposes Committee, with a suggestion that the bridges should be 42 feet wide on main roads, and provide e for gas and water pipes; that the bridges should be in positions approved of by the Board; that tit gradients be one in fifty; and that pro- perly constructed bridges be erected over all footpaths.— Mr. MIDWOOD said that instead of the shunting beingmerely reduced, it would be better to say that it be discontinued altogether. In regard to Ann-street crossing, he said that the railway company had studied the matter for over seven years, and they could not have proposed a more outlandish scheme than the one they had. They were going to land the Board near the Catholic church, and the property at this end would be almost worthless. Then they also proposed to do away with the footbridge. He thought every member would see that the railway company had been very selfish. Referring to the footpath from the end of Ann-street to the end of the iron bridge which the company proposed to stop, he said he thought it would be a very serious matter for those who had property them—Mr. RERSHAW said, in regard to the footpath in Ann -street East, tht!t. the Board had always had a great deal of trouble about this matter. Mr. Bibby seemed to ignore everything the Beard said with regard to his liability to repair the footpath. It was under- stood that the railway company would bear a certain liability, and the Board would expect Mr. B;bby to take the other. Referring to the Waterloo-road level crossing, he said it had cost the Board much money, and it was now in a very bad state. It would be better for the Board to take up the pavement and put in a proper foundation and macadamise it. With regard to the footpath leading to the iron bridge he might say that they had not lost sight of it, but that would be a matter for the General Purposes Committee.— The minutes were passed. 4 HEALTH COMILIrrEE.
