The veterinary surgeon was present, entel explained various matters about which he was ques• tioned, and the committee agreed to allow his remuneration to remain as arranged on the 22d March, 1880.—Mr. ADLitt drew attention to the very unsatisfactory way in which the -a•shpits, &-c., were being emptied.—Mr. KBRSHAW was glad that attention had been called to this matter, for he had heard complaints in all parts of the town. Then in regard to Mr. Robinson, the veterinary surgeon, he found that the com- mittee recommended that the arrangement of 1880 be car- i ried out. He should like to know what the arrangements were, and what his salary and duties were. He thought for the very few cases the Board had for a veterinary surgeon they could very well do without him. If the Board had a case that ought to come before the magistrates, it would be better to call a man in just for the occasion.—Mr. CAREY. alluding to the neglect of the nightsoil department, said they had new a new contractor, aid he was labouring under the disadvantage of being mew to the work. If the gentlesnei who had complained of the neglect in this de- partment would give them an instance in which they com- plained the committee would be very glad to investigate the case. He might say that he had had complaints of neglect, and some he had found bona fide and others cot so. As to the question about Mr. Robinsoi, the agreement had been read several times, and he proceeded to read it again, after which he said that it might be a question whether they should employ a professional man or not. Mr. Robinson was now living at Warrington, but he came over every Saturday at his own expense and inspected the meat shops.—The minutes were confirmed. FIMINCH COMMITTRII. Mr. HANDLNY proposed and Mr. WRIGHT seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of this committee, and the pro- position was carried. Amongst other matters they contained the following :—Mr. Beasley's account; a telegram was read from Messrs. Collins and Co., asking for £164 to pay a claim; and also a letter from Messrs. Gibson aid Rolland, asking for £5OO on account. The chairman of the commit- tee and clerk were instructed to see them aid to report. It was recommended that dwelling-houses occupied in part as retail shops, whether using water for trade purposes or not, be charged after 31st December as follows :—When the gross annual value exceeds £l4, and is under £5O, on three-fourths of such value, where it ex- ceeds £5O on two-thirds of such valne ; and when water is used for trade purposes, an additional charge equal to one- half of charge as above.—After some minor business had been disposed of the Board went into committee.

THE ORDER OF THE SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN. On Tnesday night the juvenile members of the above- named order were regaled, to a free tea, given by the adult members of the Lifeboat Crew Division. About forty sat down to tea„the tables being presided over by Mesdames T. Cooke, M. L. Jones, J. Pendlebury, and J. Cotterall, assisted by Messrs. M. L. Jones, S. Henderson, and Thomas Cooke. After tea, the youngsters were served with a light desert, after which they scrambled after nuts and amused them- selves in various other ways. Afterwards, a public meeting was held, over which Mr. S. Coventry presided, there being on the platform Messrs. J. Withington, T. Faulkner, J. W. Boyle, M. L. Jones, and T. Coeke.—'llle CHAIRMAN said it gave him great pleasure to meet with so many teetotallers, especially youthful teetotallers. The boys present were the men of the future, and if they only held fast to the pledge they had taken, and they, with all the thousands of Band of Hope boys, grew up to be temperence men, he did not know what the publicans would do for a living. Per- haps they might do as a minister once suggested, namely, procure denkeys, and go round gathering rags. (Laughter.) There were many poor children who scarcely knew what a good tea was. The money which ought to have been spent in food and clothing was taken to the public-house. He trusted all the boys of that order would rise to manhood thanking God that they had been blessed with teetotal parents. (Applause.)—Mr. THOMAS FAI;IINI3R gave an address on the influence of kind words, kind looks, and kind actions. He referred to certain great men and women who, by their kindness' had lightened the load of many a suffering one. He also alluded to the moral power of Sir Wilfrid Lawson, who was exerting an influence over the nation which would be felt in years to come. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. JOHN WITHINGTON said the division to t which he belonged had made provisions by which it was in the power of all temperance men to become mem- bers of the lodge. They had reduced their entrance fee for six weeks to one shilling to all comers between the ages of sixteen and thirty-five years. Their contribution was sixpence per week, and on the death of a member £l2 was paid to his friends, on the death of a member's wife £lO was paid, and £1 on the death of a child. A member also received ten shillings per week and medical attendance during sickness. In the juvenile section they had also re- duced the entrance fee for six weeks te sixpence. The con- tributions were twopence per week, and the benefits a sum of £3 at death, and 3s. per week, medical attendance and medicine free, besides a free transfer at the age of 16 years in the adult order. (Applause.)—The programme consisted of a clarionette solo by Mr. Alfred Jones; recitation, "The twins," Master Sam Littler; song, "Our Jack's come home to-day ;" recitation, " Owd Fogey," by Master Tom ' Saunders; "When he cometh," by Miss Stubbs; "Gather in the sumbeams," by Mr. Riley.—A vote of thanks having, on the motion of Mr. J. W. Bost, been passed to the chair- man and to the ladies presiding at tea, the meeting closed.

THE STATE OF WATERLOO BRIDGE, RUNCORN. The appended correspondence explains itself : Runcorn, December 13th, 1.82.—T0 the editor Runcorn Examiner.--Sir.—l am requested by the committee of the Runcorn Ratepayers' Association to send you the enclosed copy of correspondence between them and the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. It was expected that their letter would have been read at the last meeting of the Board and thus have obtained publicity through :your report of that meet- ing, but this was not done, and as the committee think it desirable that the public should be cognisant of any steps the Association may take in the interest of the ratepayers they will feel obliged by your inserting this letter and the the correspondence in your next issue.—Yours truly, C. Coo, hon. sec.—Runcorn Ratepayers' Association., Runcorn, November 30th, 1882. To the Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioner, Runcorn. :Gentlemen,—The Committee of the Runcorn I' tepayers' Asineat ion desire me to draw the atte .tion of the Board to the bad state of the roadway over Waterloo Bridge, and the danger to pedestrians, swing to the want of a footpath. Itis understood that some time ago the Board decide Ito t-ffect extensive improvements b the bridge, and that land for the purpose has been purchased and paid for. Also that the Board have in hand money available for carrying out the work without increasing ihe rates. This being the case the committee fail to see why the improvements should be further delayed. and respectfully urge the necessity of the work being at once wade' taken.—l remain, your obedient ser- vant, C. Cc/mu, Hon. Sec. Public Offices, Runcorn, 6th December, 18 82. Dear Sir,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 30-h ult., drawing attention to the bad state of the roadway over Water- loo Bridge, and to inform you that the letter will be lall before the next meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Committee on the 14th instant.—l am, yours obediently, W. BRO9KRS. Mr. C. Cooke, Hon. Secretary, Runcorn Ratepayers' Association.

He then told him that he had a similar case , to his for £6 pending, and he wanted to try it on him first, that being the smaller case.—The plaintiff said the state- ment of the defendant was a gross misrepresentation. He wished every case to come on, so that when the question was put to him " Did you ever compromise the case ?" he should be able to say, "No, I have tried the case."—His Honour stated that the plaintiff could not recover the amount. It WAS not etipulated that a quarter's notice would be required. As long as it was not on the circular it should have been specially mentioned at the time the engagement was made.—Judgment against the plaintiff with costs. ACTION AGAINST THE RULWAY CO3.IPANT BY RUNCORN Burrcetents.—Joseph Richardson, Joseph Savage, Jacob lied- ley, and Thomas Clough, butchers, of Runcorn, claimed from the London and North-Western Railway Company the sum of £lO in consequence of damages sustained by 14 beasts and 45 sheep being bruised and kept without food between the hours of 3-45 p.m. on the 21st and 2-40 a.m. on the 22nd August, whilst being carried past Runcorn to Crewe and back, the journey contracted for being from , Stanley Park to Runcorn only; £3 for Jacob Hedley's , loss of time and personal inconvenience in the same journey; £6 for wages and loss of time of plaintiffs' servants whilst waiting the arrival of the cattle ; £5 for loss of trade in consequence of late delivery of the beasts and sheep.—Mr. 0. Leak appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Preston represented the railway company.—Witnesses were ordered out of court.—Mr. Leak said the facts of the case upon which the action was founded were as follows On the 21st August last the plaintiffs want to Stanley Market, Liverpool, to purchase cattle to be brought to Run- corn and sold at their several shops. They bought a num- ber of cattle and sheep, and left them in the care of Hedley at the defendants' station to be brought back to Runcorn by the afternoon train, which left Liverpool between two and three o'clock, and was due to arrive in Runcorn about half- past three or four o'clock. Hedley took a cattle ticket, and paid the amount charged, shipped the cattle with the assistance of:defendants' servants, and obtained a free pass for himself. All the conditions enforced by the defendants were complied with by Hedlev, and the train started on its journey. ' Instead, however, of the train stopping at Runcorn, the train passed that station at a quar- ter to four. Hedley remonstrated with the guard, whose excuse was that the cattle were not in the train, and that Hedley had got into the wrong train. However, when the train arrived at Hartford, there the two trucks containing tee cattle were. The guard then asked the station master to al- low the trucks to beJeft at Hartford and returned from there. The station master said if they were left he would be unable. to return them, and they were, therefore, taken on to Crewe, at which station the cattle were shunted backwards and for- wards all night. The cattle did not leave Crewe until about two o'clock the following morning, and on the journey back to Runcorn they were shunted at Winsford and Sutton Weaver, arriving at Runcorn at 20 minutes to three. When the cattle left Liverpool they were in first-rate condition, but when they were killed at the end of the week it was found that they were seriously bruised in consequence of being on the road all the time he had stated. Hedley had no opportunity of giving the cattle any food or water, and Hedley himself was obliged to remain in the same condition Leing all the night with the train. There was no accotno- dation for cattle at Runcorn station, and the plaintiffs were waiting tkere until the cattle arrived. On the cattle ticket it was stated that the company would not be responsible for any injuries or accidents arising from over-loading or over- crowding, but Mr. Leak contended that the injuries received in this instance were in consequence ef the cattle being shunted, thus knocking against one another and the sides of the truck.—Mr. Preston suggested that the case might be materially shortened if Mr. Leak would mention that the money had been paid into court.—Mr. Leak admitted a sum of money had been paid into court, but he did not know what particular item it was intended to satisfy.—His Honour: Paid generally without admitting any liability.—Mr. Leak said he should then have to prove each particular item, and called Jacob Hedley, who gave evidence confirmatory of his advocate's statement, remarking that when the train passed Runcorn he was "going to fight the guard all the way to Acton Bridge." (Laughter.) Five of the beasts belonged to Savage, four to Richardson, three to Clough, and two to Hedley. He killed one of his beasts on the Tuesday afternoon, and one of its sides was "bruised scan- dalous." In answer to:His Honour, witness said his honour would not like to buy a piece of bruised beef,—(laughter)— and with some difficulty it was elicited that he had to sell the meat at a less price, but he was unable to tell exactly the extent of his loss.—The court then adjourned for lunch, and, on resuming, Hedley was put through a close cross-ex- amination by Mr. Preston.—Joseph Richardson said he went to Stanley Market on the 21st August, and purchased four beasts and 21 sheep, which he left in the charge of Hedley. Joseph Savage and Thomas Clough, butchers, were also examined. They were examined with regard to the damage they had sustained, but as, with the exception of Clough, neither of them kept books, they were unable to give an exact statement. One or more of their cattle was in a bruised condition. Clough stated that he had to " pare " 601bs. of beef off the carcases —William Daniels, butcher's man, saidhe was waiting at Runcorn railway station from two o'clock on Monday, the 21st August, to twenty minutes to three on Tuesday morn- ing. He drove Clough's cattle to the slaughter-house. On the way one fell into the canal dock, and getting jammed between the dock side and a flat, it was severely crushed.— His honour said it was impossible on this evidence that the action could be taken jointly, because there was no joint interest.—Mr. Leak said he based his action upon the case of Metcalf, of the London and Brighton South Coast Rail- way Company. div.head: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.
div.p: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.

NEW LABORATORY. Although established for a period of eight years, Widnes Science and Art Classes have not hitherto been provided with a laboratory for the efficient teaching of that most popular and instructive science chemistry. This, besides being an intellectual loss to the students, has also been a pecuniary disadvantage to the committee, because Govern- ment, although the students may be thoronghly instructed in the theories of chemistry, will not make a grant of money unless this knowledge is supplemented by a practical ac- quaintance with chemical operations. That a town like Widnes, which is well called the centre of the chemical trade, should neglect to provide the accommodation and conveniences for teaching that science in which the inhabi- tants are most interested, is somewhat surprising. But, what the classes in their collective capacity were perhaps unable to do, had been done by the generous benefaction of a gentleman, who has formerly shown his great interest in the intellectual and social welfare of the town; and on Wednesday afternoon the subscribes and friends of the classes were invited by the committee to inspect a new laboratory, of which we have been 1 indly supplied with the following particulars by Mr. J. Morrison The new building, which has been erected for the committee by Mr. Carlile, is situated at the junction of Major Cross- street with Lugsdale-road. It is a two-storey building, 50 feet by 20 feet. The upper storey consists of lecture room, library, and lavatory. The lecture room will accommodate about 60 students, and is furnished by desks supplied by J. Thompson, of 47, South Castle-street, Liverpool. The library, although very unpretentious in appearance contains a very valuable collection of scientific books. It was com- menced by the committee last season, and this season Mr. T. Sutton Timmis very generously authorised the commit- tee to provide at his coat any additional technological works that would assist stadents in their studies. This has been done, and the students have shown their high appreciation of Mr. Timmis's generosity, for although the library is only open on Saturday from six to nine students have asked to be allowed to use the books every night the school is open. The lower room is used as laboratory, and is fitted up in the most complete manner. There is bench accom- modation for 32 students, and every bench is occupied. Each student is provided with a complete set of the neces- sary apparatus and chemical reagents, and he has cupboards in which to lock up his apparatus when his experiments are finished. The benches are made of pitch pine, and were erected by Mr. Thomas Sadler. The, gas and water fittings were supplied by Mr. Moreland. Captain Abney, RE, F.R.S., recently made an inspection of the laboratory an. expressed very great satisfaction with the accommodatiod provided. Re said it was a credit to the town, and that it would afford him great pleasure to report favourably to the Science and Art Department. Since his visit the Science and Art Department has congratulated the committee for completing the laboratory in such a satisfactory manner. The total cost of fitting up the laboratory (about £200) has been defrayed by Mr. F. H. Gossage. The invitation of the committee was taken advantage of to a considerable extent, and the visitors evinced great interest in the arrangements.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF (I,,'IARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF (I,,'IARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meet:.ng of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Tl,jursiay. There were present Mr. Marsh (chairman)t 'Ctre Rev. J. Barnacle, Rev. T. Finegan, Rev. T. Cham'oers, Messrs. Tyrer, Meadows, Buckley, Jack- son, Birchall, Penketh, Leatherbarrovr, Lowe, Hall, Fisher, Agnew, Matthews, Swift, and Mr. H. S. Hartley (clerk). MEDICAL APPOINTMENTS. Mr. Miliner, medical officer for Rainford, wrote to say that he was "in a fix" with rea•ard to the choice of a deputy, there being no duly qualified medical practitioner in his district or between it and St. Helens.—The matter was adjourned in order to give Mr. Millner time to get over the difficulty.—Mr. FISHER, in pursuance of notice given, moved that Dr. Edward Casey be appointed medical officer for Sutton distict at the salary of £45 per annum. Mr. LEATTIERBARROW seconded the motion.—The Rev. J. BAR- NACLE asked if it was one of tbe regulations of the Local Government Board that the medical officer must reside in the district to which he was appointed. The CHAIR- MAN: Yes. Mr. TSIZER : If there is a medical man resident in the district he must have the appointment The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Has it been taken into considera- tion whether his residence is conveniently situated for the poor people he has to treat.—Mr. FISHER replied it had been stated at last meeting. that Dr. Casey's residence was conveniently situated for the poor.—Mr. JACKSON said the district included both Sutton and Parr, and the medical officer could not live in both districts, but there was no question that if Mr. Casey were appointed he would do his utmost to meet the requirements of the two townships with regard to residence.—Dr. CAS/SY having been introduced to the Board, he stated,in answer to the clerk, that he possessed all the legal qualifications, the particulars of which he enumerated, for the office of district medical officer. He promised, If appointed, to take up his abode in a portion of, the district best suited to the requirements of the poor people of both Parr and Sutton.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS exhibited to Dr. Casey a plan of the district, and asked him whether he would be prepared to remove from his present residence near St. Helens Junction to a more central posi- tion, so as to meet the requirements of Parr, and Dr. Casey replied in the affirmative.—Dr. Casey having withdrawn, the Rev.T.FINEGAN said he was very glad he had agreed to change his residence, for he was told that the place where he now lived was very inconvenient for nine-tenths of the poor people of the district.—The CHAIRMAN said he knew that instead of remaining where he was now, near St. Helens Junction, Dr. Casey would come close on the edge of Parr, which would be the centre of the two places.—The Chair- man was about to read letters on the subject from three clergymen when Mr. HALL remarked that it was queer the Board could not conduct their business without being inter- fered with by people outside.—Mr. JACKSON: There is no doubt those clergymen have been prompted to write by illy' terested persons.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS protested against brother clergymen either in St. Helens or elsewhere being spoken of in that way. He would not allow it to be said that the clergymen were influenced by interested motives. No man knew more about his district than the clergyman, and if he felt an interest in his district he had a right to write to the chairman as to any appointment of the kind under discussion. He - simply looked after the poor, and it was for him to see that the medical man appointed was as near to them as possible with a surgery and every appliance necessary. Mr. JACKSON said he did not wish to withhold from the clergymen in question the right to write to the Board, but it was evident some interested party had gone to the expense of the map Mr. Chambers had produced and influenced the clergymen—Roman Catholic priests and one thing and another. He maintained what he had said before, that it was an interssted party who was pushing the matter.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Interested in the welfare of his poor.— Mr. JACKSON: No; interested in the welfare of his own pocket.—Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Nothing of the kind.—Mr. MEADOWS said there was no doubt that in making the appointment they should study the poor people, and taking the whole extent of the district, St. Helens Junction was a place where the medical officer ought not to reside. But Dr. Casey had promised to remove, and therefore the thing was in a nutshell ; if he was appointed it would be on the understanding that he would remove. As sensible man, they knew that the poor people were to be attended to without regard to whoever got the appointment.—Mr. HALL: Yes; but are not the Guardians competent to look after that without outsiders coming in ? Mr. MEADOWS: They ought to be.—The CHAIRMAN then read the letters which had given rise to the discussion. They were from the Rev. A. A. Nunn, St, Peter's, Parr; the Rev. P. Byrne, St. Joseph's, Peasley Cross: and the Rey. E. O'Sullivan, St. Mary's, Blackbrook ; the point in each case being that whoever might be the medical officer appointed , he should be required to reside somewhere equally accessible to the poor of Parr and Sutton.—After some further conver- sation the motion was agreed to without opposition. THIS RATING OF SHOOLS AND CHARITIES. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS asked why the Assessment Com- mittee had taken up the novel idea and cruel innovation of taxing Halewood Schools. He should like to know on what authority they had taxed charities. His schools were built by charity, they were supported by charity, and they in- volved a loss of £5O or £6O a year. The schools owed him £5O or £6O, and in addition he was asked to pay £1 ss. 6d. to the common fund of the Union. He protested against that, and respectfully declined to pay until he was shown why he should do so. He did not see why the schools should be taxed. They were for poor children, and if the children paid a paltry twopence or threepence per week that was no reason why the schools should be taxed by the Union. He did not know what things were coming to. Many of the farmers of Halewood complained that they were taxed to death, and some of them feared that they would become recipients of parochial relief themselves. Why were the school buildings taxed now, when they were not taxed before ?—The CLERK: It is a matter the Board have no control over.—The CHAIR- MAN: If you zefuse to ply, the result will be that von will get a summons.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS : I would rather be summoned than pay £1 53. 61 when my schools are in debt.—The CHAIRMAN: You will have to go to Kirkdale. (Laughter.)—The CLERK isaid that if Mr. Chambers went before the magistrates they would say they could not go into the legality of the charge, their functions being merely ministerial. He might bring it before the Assessment Committee, but it was the duty of that committee to see that all rateable property was rated, and if by chance any property was omitted, the whole rate would be bad. In a case decided within the last few years it had been decided that schools wherein schoor pence were received were rateable, inasmuch as there was a beneficial occupation by some one.—The Rev. T. Crraefennes : When was that discovered? Only this year ?—The Cleaner : When I came here I took steps to put these things in. I belieye it has been the practice to rate the schools at a nomi- nal sum.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: If you say you put it in court, you put it in now at a nominal sum. I will pay 55., but to ask me to pay £1 ss. 6d. is absurd.—The CLERK: The overseers have done that •,° not this Board. —The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: The school pence go to pay the master and mistress, and the rest is supported by charity.—The CLERK: Yes; but they say it is a bene- ficial occupation. Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Then I say it is a most cruel way of getting money for the Union. Mr. MEADOWS: I would advise you to appeal.—Rev. T. CRAM- BURS: I will appeal.—The CLERK: They rate tithes.—Rev. T. Caietnarts : Yes, but tithes are really a beneficial in- terest. 1 know you rate tithes, for out of £75 tithes I only receive £s6.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN said he had very large schools, and he thought the question was a very important one indeed. The education of a district was a great burden, and to tax charities was stretch- ing the law ' very far indeed. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he was struggling as hard as he could to keep Halewood schools up, and he protested against having to pay the tax.—Mr. LESITHERBARROW remarked that alms- houses were taxed as well.—The Rev. J. BARNACLE said he was uery glad Mr. Chambers had mentioned the matter. His schools, happily, were not taxed; but if they were he should speak in as strong terms as Mr. Chambers had done.—The CLERK: If your schools are not taxed they ought to be.— The Rev. J. BARNACLE said he should consider the taxation of his schools a great imposition. He got nothing out of the schools, and the managers got nettling out of them; but they were a burden to the managers, and it would be a very great shame to further burden them with rates. The CLERK said the Board had nothing to do with the matter. It was entirely in the hands of the Assessment Committee, and they were regulated by Act of Parliament. In fact they rated their own workhouse.—The Rev. T. CereafisEns said he should bring the subject before higher quarters. It was not right to tax church echools when they were struggling against board schools and other things.—Mr. HALL said board schools were taxed also, and ha did not see why any difference should be made between them and church schools. The Prescot Board schools were assessed at about £600. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he would bring the subject before the Assessment Committee. ECONOMY. The Rev. T. CHAMBEKS moved that no further notices be sent out of the meetings of the Visiting Committee. They cost 23. 61 a week in postage, besides paper and envelopes, and although he might appear to be posing in a new character as an economist, he thought the expense un- necessary, every member of the committee knowing the times of meeting.—The motion was agreed to. • CHEAPER GAS. A letter was read from the Prescot "Gas Company, in- forming the Board that the charge made to them for gas would be reduced from 53. 41. to ss. per thousand cubic feet with a deduction of ten per cent. if the account was paid witffin a month after delivery, making 4s. 6d. per thousand net.

BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SC HOOL BAND or HOPE .—The monthly meeting of the above Band of Hope was held on Tuesday night, and there was a god attendance of members and friends. Mr. T. Norman occupied the chair, and gave a stirring temperance address, especially dwelling on the evils of intemperance and the importance of personal influence. There was an interesting programme, consisting of songs, recitations, dialogues, &a. A recitation was given by George Caygill, 'entitled " I once a drunkard was." A dialogue, entitled " The wanderer," was also given by George Marsh, William Hazlehurst, and Charles Kniveton. A number of glees were given by the choir ; Miss Norman presiding at the piano. In the absence of Mr. J. Simpson through sick- ness, Mr. D. Bisbrown gave an address. He spoke of the encouraging signs of progress in the temperance movement, and the necesAty of supplementing modern suasion by legis- lative action. The meeting was much enlivened by the Mill Brow brass band giving a number of glees during the even- ing, under the mductorship of Mr. George Thomas.

div.head: LOCAL BANKRUPTCY CASE.
div.p: LOCAL BANKRUPTCY CASE.

RE KNIGHT, OF FARNWORTH, A BANKRUPT. It now looks as if the long litigations in this case reached it final stage in the Lords Justices Court of Appeal, on Thursday, the 7th inst. The case has had many phases, originating in the first place on the questions of the rights of the mortgagees (a Liverpool building society) under an attornment clause in their mort- gage 'to distrain for monthly subscriptions as rent in arrears. The contention of the trustees in bankruptcy has been that such attornment clause was bad as against them. If the claim could be sustained, as contended for by the building society, it meant a serious diminution in the general creditors' assets. And the legal construction of this attornment clause was therefore made the subject of much argument in the Liverpool court, from whence it went on ap- peal to the Chief Judge in Bankruptcy, and next from him to the Lords Justices, before whom the final decision was made in favour of the morgagees. By a recent statute, mertgage deeds containing an attornment clause of a similar character, are now deemed to be bills of sale, and, as such, to be subject to ' registration, whereby general creditors are in- tended to be saved from surprise, and the hardship com- plained of in this particular case. But the law as now amended has no retrospective effect. There are probably now existing hundreds of mortgages with an Attorment Clause like the one contained in the mortgage by the bank- rupt Knight. The effect of the law as now settled.in re Knight rust in such cases be of serious import to creditors of traders who carryon business in premises they have made the subject of a mortgage under the same conditions. A state of circumstances is conceivable where a mortgagor's entire trading estate to the extent of thousands of pounds may be swept away ley a mortgagee with very serious loss to general creditors without their having any means of knowing any such a power stood between them and their debtor. The Court ot Appeal having decided for the Building Society, the question between the latter and the trustees in the bankruptcy became narrowed to one of account, the preparation ef which pre- sented some difficulty, ty reason of the events that had happened and the agreements made made between the parties. There were material differences in the opposite modes of stating the accounts, and these ac- counts were therefore made the subject of repeated applica- tions to the Liverpool Court, who at last decided in accord- ance with the bankruptcy trustees. The building society being dissatisfied with the decision of the County Court, appealed to the chief jnlge, who confirmed the decision of the Liverpool Court, and the building society then appealed again to the Lords Justices, who, on the seventh instant, dismissed the society's appeal with costs. This last appeal was heard before the Master of the Rolls, Lord Justices Cotton and Bo Nen, who were unanimous in their decision, the two first of whom delivered lengthened judgments inter alia upon the rights ef landlord and trustees as affected by the law of " Disclaimer " under the existing Bankruptcy Act and Rules, which will be regarded of value in future interpretations of a perplexing branch of bankruptcy law. Referring to the decision, the Manchester Guardian of Tuesday has the following :—" The peculiar position of a trustee in bankruptcy wh, disclaims a lease is well shown by the decision ef the Court of Appeal in the case of Ex. pane Isherwood, re Knight. It is net necessary to enter in- to the details of that case, for it is only the general prin- ciple involved that can be of practical interest or import- ance. The Court below had* allowed the !trustee in bank- ruptcy to disclaim the lease upon paying certain sums that were due to the mortgagees under aclause of attornment. The mortgagees claimed more and appealed, but the Lords Justices thought they had at all events got enough, if not too much, and dismissed the appeal. A more serious ques- tion was raised as to the legality of a rule made under the Bankruptcy Act in 1871, by which trustees who desire to disclaim a lease-are ordered first to obtain the leave of the Court, and by which also the Court is enabled to make such order as it may think fit. Neither of these points was contained in the Act itself, for by the statute a trustee in such cases was given a clear right to disclaim. The Court of Appeal did not really enter into the very important question as to whether or not this rule was ultra tires, holding that as the trustee had acted under it he could not complain of its existence. But they held that it could no mean that in every case of the disclaimer of a lease by the trustee the landlord has a right to be placed in the same position as if the disclaimer had never been executed. The rule, they decided, could only apply where some special cir- cumstances were shown to exist, and in such a case the landlord might be entitled, not to rent, but to some compen- sation for the property for the period during which he had been kept out of possession. But this certainly looks _like one of those over-subtle distinctions in which it is not easy to find any practical difference. The result, however, seems to be, if this rule of 1871 is to be held valid, that the ques- tion of paying compensation to a landlord after a disclaimer depends upon the facts of each case, and is in the court's discretion; and that an order can be made for such compen- sation even though the debtor's estate has obtained no benefit from the trustee's possession of the premises. But the whole principle and practice of disclaimer is now so utterly confused that one can only hope the !mot will soon he cut by some plain provision in the coming new Bank- ruptcy Act.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Globe, commenting on Mr. Childers' retirement from the War Office, says that on the whole he filled the office with credit to himself and with advantage to the country. His chief mistake lay in refusing to introduce those 'ameliorations into the territorial scheme which ex- perience has shown would have readered it more workable and more in harmony with military feeling.
THE MAAMSTRASNA MASSACRE.

EXECUTION OF THE THREE MURDERERS. SCENE ON THE SCAFFOLD. Yesterday morning in dreary and bitter cold weather, wee suited for the occation, Patrick Joyce, Myles Joyce, and Patrick Casey, were executed in Galway gaol for the share they took in the Maamstrasna murders. The three con- demned men were aroused at six o'clock, and shortly after- wards made their confessions to the Rev. Mr. Newell and received the last sacraments of the Roman Catholic Church. They all refused, however, to eat or drink anything. The execution was fixed for eight o'clock; but it was five minutes past the hour when the Governor of the Gaol, Captain Mason, informed the large number of reporters who were waiting in the Porter's Lodge the proceedings were about to commence. They were then conducted to that part of the prison in which the prisoners were confined, and then another delay resulted while they were being pinioned inside. After the lapse of a few minutes the door was opened, and then Captain Mason came out, closely followed by Mr. Reddington, the sub-sheriff. As the latter gentle- man was descending the two steps which led from the building to the ground, he slipped on the ice which had formed on the stones, and would have fallen only he had been seized by the shoulder by the governor. This led to an order being given that the ground leading to the place of exe- cution should be well covered with ashes so as to obviate MIT of the unfortunate culprits falling while on the way to the scaffold. The representatives of the press of course were not admitted to witness the process of pinioning, but from inquiries it was learned that the culprits were each pinioned in their own cells, and that while Patrick Casey and Patrick Joyce bore the operation with the greatest firmness, Myles Joyce, during all the time it was proceeding,asserted his innocence of the crime with great vehemence, and re- sisted Marwood slightly. At a quarter past eight o'clock precisely the first of the condemned, Myles Joyce, made his appearance. He wore the same clothes as during the trial, a suit of dark grey freize, nearly new, of the old-fashioned cut and make. He was supported on each side by warders, and his arms pinioned behind him. On seeing the group of pressmen gathered round the door he uttered a nuinber of exclama- tions in the Irish language of kis innocence. He was fol- lowed by Patrick Casey, a middle-aged man of the medium height. He did not utter a word, but walked firmly along. Last of all came Patrick Joyce, known during the trial as Patrick Joyce of Shaunalieahill, to distinguish him from a prisoner of the sanie name charged with the offence. Dur- ing the progress of the trial he attracted attention by the cool manner in which he conducted himself, and now also on the eve of lais death he displayed the same coolness. As he descended the steps his foot slipped, but recovering himself with self-possession he walked firmly on. He was immediately preceded by Marwood carrying a number of ropes, and was followed by the Rev. Mr. Graven, parish priest, repeating the Litany , for the dying. Patrick Joyce alone, however, repeated the responses, which he did in a low but firm voice. The procession then proceeded about 200 yards to where the scaffold was erected, in a yard next the one in which Walsh was executed. The prisoners, with the exception of Casey, mounted the steps without assistance, and were then placed in position by Marwood under the three ropes which were dangliug from the cross beam. After this was done Myles Joyce, turning to the knot of spectators, made a number of exclamations in the Irish language to the effect that he was innocent of the crime, but the other two did not say a word. On Marwood going up to him to adjust the rope round his neck, he resisted slightly, and, apparently labouring under [great excitement, made a motion as is to push him away. The Rev. W. Graven, who had been standing at the front of the scaffold repeating the usual prayers seeing this, went up close to the unfortunate man, and uttered some soothing advice to him, and he then, though talking loudly all the time, allowed the noose to be put round his neck, and the other two men permitted a like operation to be performed in their case without the least resistance. The executioner then drew the white cap over Patrick Joyce's face, then over Casey's, and Znally over Myles Joyce's. The latter, however, who continued to talk all the time most vehemently, twisted his head in some manner after the cap had been draws over his head, and Marwood had again to arrange the noose round his throat, the other two continuing all the time perfectly passive. Myles Joyce even then did not cease speaking, and continued , thus—" I am going before my God, and lam as innocent as the child unborn. I neither raised hand or -foot against the people. I had neither hand, act or part in the murders." At this instant Marwood drew the bolt, and the three men disappeared from view. There was scarcely a quiver of the ropes by which Patrick and Casey were suspended, but there was ap- parently severely struggling on the part of Miles Joyce, for the rope he hung by violently oscillated, and Marwood could be eeen for several minutes afterwards pushing down the body with his foot, and stooping down enaeavouring to do something, it could not be seen what, with the noose. Marwood afterwards, in reply to a reporter, expressed his opinion that Miles Joyce, by some means or other, got his arm or his hand entangled in some way with the rope, and that he had been trying to push it down. Death, he was positive, was instantaneous, and nothing could have been wrorg with the rope, as be had eased it at executions before at Limerick. York Castle, Liverpool, Bodmin, Cornwall, Worcester, as well as at Galway before, in the case of Patrick Walsh, the young man who was hanged for the Leenane murders. Besides, he gave all the men a drop of equal length, nine feet. One of the other ropes he used at the executions of Dr. Lamson and Lefroy. The scaffold was a substantial-looking structure, raised about 12 feet from the ground, approached by a flight of steps, and was erected by workmen brought down from Dublin, all the local tradesmen having refused to do the work. Marwood considers he could have hung the whole eight men on it, but it would have been better to have had it larger in that case. The prison was surrounded bv centries all night, and a body of police were on duty outside in the morning to quell any disturbance which might arise, but scarcely a dozen persons assembled either at the gate or around the place even after the black flag had been run up to show that the sentence of the law had been carried out. On looking down from the platform into the trap in which the men were hanging, the upper patts of their bodies could be discerned, their heads drooping to one side. Patrick Joyce was the only man who wore his cap on the way to execution, the others going bareheaded and all wore their own clothes. Myles Joyce was a man apparently between forty and fifty years of age, and with short brown whiskers and moustache. Patrick Casey was a most. repulsive looking man, with a countenance strongly indicative of brutal ferocity, while Patrick Joyce was younger by a few years than the other two, and far better looking. Hopes were entertained of the reprieve of Myles Joyce by his friends and relations almost up to the last moment. A memorial was sent by his wife to the Lord Lieutenant stating that he was innocent of the crime, and that the other men who had taken part in it were ready to swear he was not with them on the night of the murder. His Ex- cellency, however, after reviewing the facts of the case, found he had no option but to allow the law to take its course. The three Joyces who followed the party on the night of the murders, and by whose aid the perpetrators were afterwards brought to justice, returned some days ago to their homes, after receiving the sum of £1,250 from the Government, as a rewarit for the information that they gave. The authorities offered to send them out of the country free of expense, but they positively refused to go, and have also declined protection, alleging that the feeling of the people of the district is so strongly in their favour that they do not need it.

MANCHESTER CORN, THURSDAY.—Messrs. William Warbur- ton and Co. report as follows :—There has been a steady demand at full prices throughout the week for everything except maize, which article has tended downwards for parcels on the spot, but has advanced upon the low prices current for future delivery. The weather has been extremely winterly, wins keen frost and heavy snows. Imports have been liberal of all articles, more particularly of flour. To-day's market was well attended, but the inquiry was not active. English wheat was firm; foreizu, red, and in some instances, Id per cental dearer, and white was held for fully previous quotations. Flour was unchanged. Oats and oatmeal steady, with a limited de- mand. Beans and peas rather lower. 'Upon maize a reduction must be quoted of Gd per central from the currencies of last market day. MISCELLANEOUS. the Members of the Malagasy Embassy ea Tuesday Vocended to Windsor, and bad an audience with the Queen. the Preston Town Council, on Wednesday, adopted the 'scheme of Sir John Coode for the developement of Ribble nayigation, which is to cost at least £400,000. Two men have been killed and four injured by an ex- ' Plosion of dynamite in the smelting furnaces of the Ask- ham and Mousell Iron Company, near Barrow. Sir Joseph Napier, an ex-Lord Chancellor of Ireland,-and for many years an ardent champion of Protestantism, died at St. Leonard's-on-Sea, on Saturday, in his 79th year. Sir John Coode's report en the project for making the river Ribble navigable up to Preston for the largest class of 'Vessels is published. He estimates the cost at £553,150. Alfred Harris, a co,porel of the Ist Wiltshire Regiment, . who murdered a comrade, John Edgar, at Woolwich Barracks , recently, was found guilty at the Old Bailey, on Wedaesday, and sentenced to death. It is now definitely stated that Sir Evelyn Wood has been appointed to the command of the English army of occu- nation in Egypt, and that he will leave for his new post Without delay. On Monday,whilst a gang of mere were working in a deep cutting on the Swindon and Cheltenham extension railway , works, about four tons of clay fell from the bank, and killed ' two men named John Wheeler and James Richards. - Lord Randolph Churchill is again unwell, and has been ordered to the South of France. It is hoped, however, that he will be able to return to keep his engagement at Birming- ham On February 6th, on which date he has promised to give a lesson to the Midland Tories. THE GOURLAY FEAUDS.—On Tuesday, Mr. Candeman, clerk to the Oswaldtwistle Local Board, paid to the Union Bank of Manchester £13.732 in addition to the £1,500 paid in August last, making £15,232 in full discharge .of £34,619 embezzled by Gourley, the former clerk, and claimed by the Bondholders' Association. SUDDEN DEATH IN A CHAPEL. At the Congregational Church, Belper, on Sunday, Mr. Jabez Brown, who was turning over the pages of the Bible before reading the first morning lessomsuddenly fell back and died almost instantly. For the space of fifty years he hail been senior deacon at his church, and he held several public offices. CHARGE AGAINST A MEMBER OF PARLIAME.NT.—The Ramsgats magistrates on Monday issued a warrant for the arrest of Mr. George Hampden Whalley, M.P. for Peter- borough, who failed to appear in answer to a summons charging him with obtaining by false pretences the sums of £44 and £l2 from Mr. J. Colley, proprietor of the Albion Hotel, Ramsgate. It is now definitely announced that Lord Derby is to take the place of Lord Hartington at the India Office, that Lord Hartington will go to the War Office, and that Mr. Childers, who has po muck distinguished himself while responsible for the army, will become Chancellor of the Exchequer. It is understood that other changes are in contemplation, bat as yet no aathoritative statement respecting them Gan be made. A parliamentary return, issued on Tuesday, shows that there are now in the United Kingdom 25 tramways belong- ing to local authorities, the total length open of which is 150 miles 71 chains, and upon which the total amount expended has been £1,360,742. Of tramways belonging to other than local authorities there are 109, with a length of 413 miles 31 chains, and upon which has been expended £6,401,073. A CA'PTAIN AND FOUR MEN WASHED OTERBOARD.—A Lloyd's telegram states that the iron clipper four-masted ahip, Loch Torridon, of Glasgow, from Calcutta to London, is off Falmouth, in charge of the second mate, who reports that when in the Indian Ocean, during a strong gale the captain, first officer, and three of the crew were washed over- board and lost. No assistance could be rendered owing to the tremendous sea which was running at the time. OUTBREAX OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE ON TIM QIIIEN'S FARM AT WINDSOR.—Foot-and-inouth disease has broken out on the Queen's farm at Windsor, the first animal attacked being one of ten short-horn beasts sent by the Duke of Connaught to be sold at the recent sale of fat stock. All the stock that had not been removed up to Monday night will have to be slaughtered on the farm. Some of the animate were sold to butchers at Leeds, London, Bristol, and other distant parts of the kingdom. A LANDLORD MURDERED AT STOCETON.—An Irishman named Neyland, and his wife, are in custody at Stockton -on- Tees, charged with killing their landlord, John Brennan. Prisoners were leaving their lodgings on Saturday night without paying; the deceased sought to prevent them, and in an altercation that ensued the female struck the deceased on the head with a poker, and her husband kicked and jumped upon him. Brennan died shortly afterwards. A DISASTROUS EXPERIMENT.—A, Waterford telegram states that shortly before four o'clock on Monday an attempt was made to blow the wreck of the steamer Silkstone,which was sunk in the Suir opposite Waterford Quay. The force of the explosion was such that windows in every house on the quay were shattered, and goods, furniture, ckc., were scattered in every direction. Several persons were blown_off their feet. The damage is estimated about £5OO. MYSTERIOUS POISONING.—A mysterious case of poisoning occurred at Dingwall, on Wednesday, Several days ago a 'quack doctor, named William Parr, and his wife, Came to town and took lodgings. On Tuesday, Parr complained of being unwell. The woman was to have gone with another woman of the name class to Culbokie market, but yesterday the other woman discovered that Parr was dead and his wife unconscious. The latter died in the afternoon. It was discovered that death was due to poisoning'. Cesuisox ROBSERY AT LONETON.—At Longton, on Wednesday, before the Potteries stipendiary, Samuel Thompson, alias " Teaman," was committed for trial on the charge of stealing a cashbox containing £23. The prisoner had been employed as property-man at Victoria Theatre. He saw the proprietor, Mr. Wardhaugh, place the cashbox in the pay office at the theatre, on Saturday morning, and, watching his opportunity, he broke open the strong chest in which it was deposited, and walking into the town he spent LS in winter clothing, this leading to his appre- hension. THE PARCELS POST.—The Daily Noes understands that the treasury of the General Post Office and the railway companies have all come to an agreement as to the terms on which the proposed parcels post is ter be worked. In order to ensure the successful working of a reform of such magni- tude, numerous details have had to be carefully considered, and some delay must yet ensue before the Post Office authorities will be able to give the public the benefit of the scheme. It is confidently expected that within the next two months the 'parcels post will be in effective opera- tion. EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH JAlL—Charles Taylor, 39, carpenter, was executed on Tuesday morning in Wands- worth Prison, for the murder of his wife at Old Kent-road, London, last August. Since his conviction the prisoner, who at the time of the murder had also attempted suicide, expressed penitence for the crime. On Tuesday morning be walked without assistance to the scaffold, but looked very Pale and ill. Marwood allowed a drop of over eight feet, and the condemned man appeared to die without a struggle. SUICIDE IN A BARBER'S SHOF.—A man Of Very respect- able appearance went into a_ barber's shop, at No. 114, Union-street, Borough, London, on Monday, and asked to be shaved. Mr. Cole, the barber, had occasion to leave him for a moment, when the man seized one of the razors, and before it coulel be taken from him inflicted a fearful gash across his throat. He became exhausted from loss of blood, and was removed as speedily as possible to Guy's Hospital, where he died soon after. He was subsequently idantified as John Warner, who had recently come to Lon- don from Scarborough on business. It has now been ascertained that the great snowstorm of last week has' caused the losseof many lives. In addition to fatalities already reported, it is now stated that three deaths have occurred in Wales, the body of a boy who was lost in the snowstorm at Saddleworth has been found, a labourer" has died of exposure at Rye, and in Selkirkslaire a shepherd has died in the snow. In Scotland large numbers of sheep have perished. Severe frost has been experienced over the whole country, and six persons have been drowned through venturing upon the ice to soon. SERIOUS AFFRAY BETWEEN GERMAN AND BRITISII Semorts.—A most serious affray between men of 11. M Sh Iron Duke and men of the German corvette Elizabeth, took Place at Shanghai on October the 19th. A batch of 150 Men landed on that day from the Iron Duke, and 100 menl of the corvette's crew also went ashore on leave. In the evening a disturbance arose in a public-house, where were gathered nearly all the Germans and about 20 British sailors and marines Worn the Iron Duke and the Sheldrake. The Germans drew their clasp knives and attacked the English seamen, wounding eight of them, the most serious case being that of a marine who was stabbed in the left side in the region of the heart. There was a picquet on shore from the corvette, but, though in the vicinity of the affray, they failed to prevent the disturbance. M. 13RADLAUGH AND TEE HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mr. Bradlaugh addressing a crowded meeting of delegates at the Hall of Science, London, on Wednesday night, :laid he had received a communication from the Government, in which it was stated that it would probably be in his own power at the commencement of next session to promote a discussion Whether the resolution should be renewed or not. He meant to take the seat to which he was entitled. The House might expel or imprison him, but it had no right to stand between the polling booth and the seat. He proceeded to suggest that on the day of the re-assembling of Parliament in February a mass meeting should be held of not less than , 200,000 persons. He was aware this was a grave step, but the law was on his side. Twenty or thirty thousand persons , would probably attend from the provinces. A resolution , was passed in favour of holding a demonstration on the 15th February. _THE PEIME MINISTER'S PARLIAMENTARY' JUBILEII.—On Wednesday the Prime Minister received a large number of addresses on his completion of 50 years of public life. Amongst the most noteworthy were one from 223 Liberal asseciations and cubs in the metropolis, the home counties, and some contiguous shires, and another from the Cire ek Committee of bandies. The metropolis address expressed e the desire of the Liberal party that the Premier's valuable neryices should receive recognition at a great public meet- ing, believing, as they did, that such a demonstration would stimulate the growing activity of Liberalism in the south of England. The members of the Greek commuaity recog- nised the constancy with which Mr. Gladstone has adopted and developed the principles of social and political pro- gress, the extension of equal rights, the abolition of Monopolies, the establishment of free trade, the general con- , sntlidation of liberty, and the large-minded, and humane ntrectiou of his policy in regard to foreign peoples. Amonst foreign telegrams received by the right hon. gentleman Were one from the Greek Government end One from the Khedive.
